Global financial markets experienced renewed volatility at the beginning of the year as markets reassessed inflation risks in the US. In February, global equity markets fell sharply from their late-January highs, completely offsetting the notable gains recorded earlier in the year, while the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. Over the past two years, global equity markets had risen steadily amid low volatility, as markets expected the economic environment to sustain robust growth while inflation and interest rates remained at ideally low levels. However, this expectation is now facing risks from tightening global monetary conditions, rising trade protectionism sentiment, and geopolitical tensions. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, while markets continued to function in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, total loans continued to increase, but at a more moderate pace. After a slight slowdown in the middle of last year, both property price growth and transaction volumes rebounded in the fourth quarter of 2017. Looking ahead, renewed volatility in global and local financial markets may add to fluctuations in fund flows in Hong Kong. Given the uncertainties in financial markets, as well as the ongoing normalisation of US monetary policy and persistent geopolitical risks, banks should remain vigilant about heightened interest rate volatility and potential capital outflow risks. In particular, given the continued rise in corporate leverage and the elevated level of household debt burdens, banks should assess the potential impact on asset quality should interest rates rise more than expected. Following a prolonged period during which the Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX) hovered at low levels over the past two years or more, global financial markets experienced renewed volatility at the beginning of the year. Global equity markets fell sharply from their late-January highs, with the S&P 500 Index at one point dropping more than 10%, completely offsetting the notable gains recorded in early January. Market sentiment shifted amid signs that the global economic recovery could exert upward pressure on long-subdued US wages and prices, potentially prompting the US Federal Reserve to accelerate its pace of interest rate hikes. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. The prolonged rise in global equity markets over the past two years had been premised on market expectations that economic conditions would remain favourable. In the second half of 2017, global economic growth momentum continued to strengthen, with economic activity in both advanced economies and emerging market economies picking up in tandem. Towards the end of the year, the US Congress passed a tax reform package, which included tax cuts and a comprehensive overhaul of corporate and personal tax provisions, fuelling market hopes that the strong US economic recovery would receive additional cyclical stimulus in the near term. Despite the strengthening in activity, core inflation in the major advanced economies remained moderate, further reinforcing market expectations that global interest rates would remain low for a prolonged period. Against this backdrop, global asset markets rose notably in 2017, with US equity markets in particular repeatedly hitting record highs. However, following the release of stronger-than-expected US wage growth data for January, global equity markets reassessed inflation risks. After the short-term financial market volatility, the risk of tightening global monetary conditions may continue to cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. In the US, the economy has now reached its output potential, and the anticipated cyclical stimulus to domestic demand from tax cuts could accelerate a rebound in inflation, thereby prompting the US Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy at a faster pace. At the same time, as the tax cuts will lead to a rising fiscal deficit, the US may issue more Treasury bonds in the future, which is expected to add to upward pressure on long-term bond yields at a time when the US Federal Reserve continues to advance the normalisation of its balance sheet. Outside the US, stronger growth momentum in other major advanced economies has raised market expectations that their central banks may scale back their quantitative easing programmes. If implemented, this would lead to a synchronised tightening of global monetary conditions. Policy and event risks arising from international political and geopolitical tensions could also cast a shadow over the outlook for global economic growth. The US government appears increasingly inclined to adopt trade protectionism measures to shield domestic industries from competition, with recent examples including the announcement of import tariffs on solar panels, washing machines, steel, and aluminium. These moves have raised concerns over whether its trading partners will respond with retaliatory measures. In addition, should geopolitical tensions escalate unexpectedly, this could affect global trade and exacerbate financial market volatilities. Given the aforementioned uncertainties in the global economic outlook, questions have arisen as to whether the currently elevated valuations in global asset markets can be sustained. From a fundamental perspective, it remains to be seen whether the cyclical growth in global demand and the anticipated rise in the fiscal deficit from US tax cuts will push up the natural rate of interest (R*); in addition, the normalisation of the US Federal Reserve's balance sheet is expected to lead to a rise in the term premium, which could push up long-term interest rates and thereby weigh on asset market valuations. In East Asia, economies in the region have also been in an ideal environment of robust growth and moderate inflation. Amid the strong economic performance and optimistic outlook, capital inflows accelerated while financial markets rose in tandem. However, this favourable outlook faces downside risks from a number of factors: tightening global liquidity as major central banks synchronously advance monetary policy normalisation; the US government's inward-looking trade policies; geopolitical tensions; and the possibility that offshore US dollar liquidity may become strained as US corporations repatriate profits to the US on a large scale in response to the one-off "deemed repatriation" provision under the country's tax reform. Should credit and financial markets face any shock, this could trigger a reversal of fund flows, with highly leveraged sectors and economies being the most vulnerable to a tightening of financial conditions. In Mainland China, the economy performed well in the second half of 2017, supported by robust consumption, strong infrastructure, and a rebound in industrial spending towards the end of the year. At the same time, signs of the rise of the "new economy" have become increasingly evident, with sectors such as high value-added manufacturing and services demonstrating strong business expansion momentum over the past few quarters. Looking ahead, the near-term growth outlook remains positive, but uncertainties persist. In particular, it remains to be seen to what extent the rapid growth of the "new economy" can help offset the short-term pressure on growth arising from the further advancement of structural reforms. The Mainland authorities announced in 2018 that they would continue to adopt a proactive fiscal policy stance, which may help cushion adverse economic developments if necessary. During the review period, some progress was made in both structural reforms and the control of systemic risks. In particular, following the introduction of tightening measures, the Mainland housing market showed signs of cooling during the review period, most notably in first-tier cities. At the same time, as banks tightened their loan approval standards, banks' exposure to enterprises in industries with overcapacity remained under control, while shadow banking activities also slowed amid financial deleveraging. In addition to the above positive developments, our analysis also indicates that the efficiency of capital allocation in Mainland China appears to have improved. In particular, the borrowing constraints faced by state-owned enterprises (SOEs) with weaker repayment capacity appear to have tightened, possibly due to a weakening of support provided by local governments (for details, please refer to Box 2 on page 28). On the external front, amid a stabilising economic situation and diminishing risks, capital outflow pressure remained moderate for most of 2017. Hong Kong's economy maintained sequential growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Real GDP grew by 3.8% for the whole of 2017, the fastest pace in nearly six years. Amid favourable employment and income conditions as well as rising asset prices, private consumption continued to grow robustly in the second half of 2017. Aggregate investment spending also rebounded on the back of increased corporate capital expenditure. On the external front, benefiting from improved global trade growth and a gradual recovery in inbound tourism, Hong Kong's export performance improved further. Nonetheless, as imports grew faster than exports, net exports of goods continued to drag on GDP growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution to GDP growth. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018, with private consumption, building and construction activities, and exports continuing to support economic growth. Given that HKD interest rates will eventually rise, Box 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption. The Government and market consensus forecasts project real GDP growth of between 3% and 4% and 3.0% respectively for 2018. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the aforementioned external environment, the economic performance of Mainland China amid tightening financial conditions, and the movements in Hong Kong's asset markets. Although the unemployment rate fell to 2.9%, a near 20-year low, local inflationary pressures remained under control. Nonetheless, sequential inflation momentum showed signs of picking up slightly in recent months, with both tradable goods and services prices rising. Looking ahead, the underlying inflation may edge up slightly to a level that is still moderate, partly reflecting the pass-through effects of rising fresh-letting private residential rentals. Affected by funding demand from IPO fundraising activities and seasonal funding demand, liquidity conditions tightened and the unwinding of HKD short positions increased, prompting the HKD spot exchange rate to strengthen between September and November 2017. As liquidity conditions eased and interest rate arbitrage activities became active again, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened once more from December 2017. In early 2018, despite the turbulence in global financial markets—particularly the equity markets—the Hong Kong dollar remained broadly stable. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened further in early March 2018, but the CUs were not triggered. HKD interbank interest rates faced upward pressure between September and December 2017. This was mainly attributable to funding demand from IPO fundraising activities and banks' cautious approach to managing their liquidity towards year-end. In December, the average overnight and three-month HIBORs rose by 14 and 50 basis points respectively from six months earlier, to 0.25% and 1.26%. After edging down slightly in early January 2018, HIBORs remained broadly stable and were unaffected by the recent adjustment in global financial markets. Despite intense competition in the mortgage lending business, banks' average lending rate on new mortgages continued to follow the upward trend of short-term HIBORs, rising to 2.16% in December. On the other hand, retail banks' funding costs generally remained low following a brief rise in October due to IPO fundraising activities, with the composite interest rate closing at 0.38% in December. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalise, HKD interest rates may face greater upward pressure; and if global market sentiment shifts abruptly, fund flow volatility may increase. For the whole of 2017, total bank loans grew steadily by 16.1%. Following strong growth of 10.2% in the first half, loan growth slowed to 5.3% in the second half. Among these, growth in both domestic loans and loans for use outside Hong Kong declined across most industries. Growth in foreign currency loans slowed, partly due to rising US dollar funding costs. Meanwhile, amid a favourable local economic environment and relatively low HKD funding costs, HKD loans continued to record rapid growth. As HKD loans grew faster than deposits, the HKD loan-to-deposit ratio rose in the second half of 2017, climbing to 82.7% at year-end, the highest level since March 2015. On the other hand, as foreign currency loans grew relatively slowly, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell to 63.1% at year-end. The onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates against the US dollar showed signs of stabilising between September and November 2017. Subsequently, as the US dollar weakened notably against most major currencies, the onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates against the US dollar strengthened somewhat from December. Hong Kong's CNH liquidity pool (comprising the total of RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit) rebounded slightly in the second half of the year following a modest decline in the first half, broadly reflecting changes in market expectations regarding the renminbi exchange rate. As for other CNH business, although renminbi loans continued to decline, the amount of RMB trade settlements handled by Hong Kong banks rebounded in the second half of the year. The average daily turnover of the RMB RTGS system remained at a high level. Looking ahead, Hong Kong's CNH business is well positioned to benefit from the advancement of the Belt and Road initiative and the continued internationalisation of the renminbi.

The synchronised strengthening of the global economy since late 2016 has shown no signs of abating. An improved growth outlook drove global equity markets steadily higher throughout 2017 and into early 2018. However, as the market reassessed US inflation risks, global equity markets experienced a sell-off and sharp volatility in February, marking an end to the calm that had prevailed in financial markets over the past two years. Looking ahead, the risk of a tightening in global financing conditions, together with a range of policy and event risks, will continue to cast a shadow over the global growth outlook. Amid a tight labour market, US tax cuts could accelerate a cyclical rebound in inflation, prompting the Fed to speed up the pace of tightening monetary policy. As the Fed continues to advance the normalisation of its balance sheet, increased issuance of US Central Government bonds to fund the tax cuts could add to upward pressure on long-term bond yields. The looming threat of rising trade barriers, as well as any unexpected escalation of geopolitical tensions, could also threaten the nascent global trade recovery. In East Asia, benefiting from strong export performance and stable domestic demand, real GDP growth continued to rise in the second half of 2017. Nevertheless, while the economic outlook is optimistic, it also faces a number of downside risks, such as the possibility that global monetary conditions could tighten more than expected, US inward-looking trade policies and geopolitical tensions. Should these downside risks materialise, they would also increase the risk of a reversal in capital flows. Policymakers are facing multiple challenges: on the one hand, they must guard against risks to economic growth, while on the other hand, they must limit the impact of prolonged accommodative financing conditions on inflation and balance sheet vulnerabilities. In Mainland China, the economy performed well in the second half of 2017. During the review period, some progress was made in structural reforms and in curbing systemic risks. The near-term growth outlook remains positive, but uncertainties persist, which will depend in part on the extent to which the rapid growth of the "new economy" can offset the short-term pressure on growth arising from further advancement of structural reforms. As economic conditions stabilised and risks diminished, capital outflow pressures remained moderate for most of 2017. As the momentum of cyclical economic improvement has become increasingly firm since late 2016, growth in both advanced economies and emerging market economies accelerated in tandem in 2017. Among the major advanced economies, the US saw robust growth in investment and exports, driven by optimistic private-sector sentiment and a sharp depreciation of the US dollar, while the Euro area and Japan also recorded broad-based cyclical recoveries. Exports of emerging market economies also benefited from the stabilisation of global commodity prices and increased import demand from major advanced economies. In the near term, following the passage of US tax reform, investment and consumption are expected to receive a further boost from reductions in corporate and personal income taxes. In view of the current cyclical economic upswing and the expansionary effects brought about by US tax reform, the International Monetary Fund forecast in January that global economic growth would accelerate from an estimated 3.7% in 2017 to 3.9% in 2018 (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 Real GDP growth forecasts As growth momentum in the Euro area and Japan strengthened, the market expected the divergence in global monetary policy to narrow, and coupled with a more optimistic global growth outlook, this stimulated risk appetite and capital inflows into emerging market economies, thereby putting the US dollar under pressure. Although the Fed raised interest rates three times during the year and began advancing the normalisation of its balance sheet, the US dollar index still recorded a decline of nearly 10% in 2017. At the same time, despite the broad-based acceleration in economic growth, core inflation in major advanced economies remained weak and below the targets of their central banks, leading the market until recently to expect global interest rates to remain low (Chart 2.2). Against this backdrop, global equity markets continued to rise throughout 2017 and into early 2018, with the S&P 500 index repeatedly hitting new highs, pushing the cyclically adjusted price-earnings ratio to 33.8 in January 2018, the highest level since the "dot-com bubble" of early 2000. Chart 2.2 Core inflation in major advanced economies However, since the second half of 2017, market concerns that tax cuts would lead to a budget deficit and rising inflation have driven the long-term US Treasury bond yields continuously higher, casting doubt on the sustainability of increasingly elevated asset market valuations. As the US reported higher-than-expected growth in average hourly wages for January 2018, the market reassessed US inflation risks, triggering a correction in global equity markets in early February 2018. The S&P 500 index at one point fell more than 10% from its 26 January high, completely offsetting the significant gains at the start of the year, and continued to be under pressure after the US government announced a new round of trade protection measures in early March. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high in mid-February. Market volatility rose sharply, with the Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index at one point surging to a two-year high of 37.3, marking an end to the persistent low-volatility environment of the past two years (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX) Looking ahead, after the short-term stock market volatility, US inflation risks, the upside risk to long-term US Treasury bond yields and the possibility that other major central banks may tighten monetary policy could all lead to tightening global monetary conditions, thereby casting a shadow over the global growth outlook. First, with regard to US inflation risks, the recently passed tax reform includes several provisions expected to provide a short-term cyclical stimulus to private consumption and investment. The main measures involved in the tax reform include: (1) lowering corporate and personal income tax rates, (2) temporarily allowing full expensing of capital investment, and (3) a one-off "deemed repatriation" provision that helps reduce the incentive for US companies to park their overseas profits abroad. Although it is not yet certain how the tax cuts will affect domestic demand and inflation, as the US economy has now reached its output potential, the tax cuts could push US output beyond its potential level, thereby leading to economic overheating and a cyclical rebound in inflation. Should inflationary pressures rise more than expected, this could prompt the Fed to speed up the pace of tightening monetary policy. Currently, the federal funds rate trajectory expected by financial markets is flatter than the projections released by the Fed. However, should inflation rebound unexpectedly, the risk of a sudden repricing of rate-hike expectations cannot be ruled out (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Federal funds rate projections Second, given that the tax reform could exacerbate the budget deficit, the issuance of US Central Government bonds is expected to increase going forward. As the Fed continues to implement its balance sheet normalisation plan, term premia are expected to rise; in this context, the increased issuance of US Central Government bonds could intensify upward pressure on long-term bond yields. In addition, as the market anticipated an increased likelihood of the US passing the tax cut package, US inflation expectations have continued to rise since the second half of 2017 (Chart 2.5). As a result, after hovering at low levels for most of 2017, the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield has risen by more than 70 basis points since the third quarter, partly reflecting market concerns over increased supply pressure on Central Government bonds as well as rising inflation expectations. Chart 2.5 5-year 5-year forward inflation expectations Moreover, whether the natural rate of interest (R*), a key component of long-term interest rates, will remain persistently low as most people expect is a major consideration. Although estimates of R* vary, it is generally believed to have fallen substantially since the global financial crisis (Chart 2.6). Nonetheless, US R* could face upside risk in the future, due to (1) an expected decline in the national savings rate as a result of a larger budget deficit, and (2) a possible rise in the investment rate stemming from corporate tax cuts and more favourable tax treatment for capital expenditure. A rise in R*, together with the increase in term premia expected from the Fed's balance sheet normalisation, could signal higher long-term interest rates, thereby creating headwinds for asset market valuations. Chart 2.6 US R* estimated using the Laubach-Williams model Third, the strengthening growth drivers in the Euro area and Japan have led the market to expect that their central banks may scale back monetary easing measures. Should this occur, it could signal a synchronised tightening of global monetary conditions. In the Euro area, member economies recorded broad-based cyclical expansions (Chart 2.7). As for Japan, its economic recovery also accelerated, with real GDP recording positive growth for the eighth consecutive quarter in the fourth quarter of 2017. Although the European Central Bank (ECB) and the Bank of Japan have continued to signal that they will maintain accommodative monetary policy amid weak inflation, the clearer growth outlook for the Euro area and Japan (and the continued tightening of Japan's labour market) has led some market participants to predict that they will further scale back their quantitative easing programmes in the near future. Chart 2.7 Real GDP of selected Euro area member states Policy and event risks arising from international political and geopolitical tensions could also threaten the nascent global economic growth and trade recovery. The US government appears more inclined to adopt inward-looking trade policies to protect domestic industries, with recent examples being the imposition of import tariffs on solar panels and washing machines announced in January 2018, and the announcement in early March of import tariffs on steel and aluminium, raising concerns over whether its trading partners would respond with retaliatory measures. At the same time, the UK and other EU countries are currently negotiating post-Brexit trade arrangements, a process fraught with numerous uncertainties. Should the above developments lead to increased trade tensions, they could hinder global trade flows and reduce global production efficiency. In addition, should geopolitical tensions escalate unexpectedly (such as military conflict on the Korean Peninsula, political turmoil in the Middle East and latent risks of terrorist attacks), this could increase financial market volatility globally. In East Asia, economic growth momentum strengthened further in the second half of 2017, ending the year on a strong note. Real growth accelerated to 4.3% in 2017, the fastest pace since 2012. External trade remained the main driver of growth, while domestic demand also provided steady support (Chart 2.8). The accelerating recovery in advanced economies, stronger-than-expected growth in Mainland China, and the rebound in global demand for technology products all boosted exports in the region. Chart 2.8 East Asia: domestic demand and exports Inflationary pressures have remained subdued so far. In the second half of 2017, affected by declining food inflation and stable energy prices, headline inflation in East Asia eased somewhat (Chart 2.9). At the same time, owing to slow wage growth in several economies, core consumer price inflation (excluding food and energy) remained at low levels. Chart 2.9 East Asia: headline and core consumer price inflation* Note: Since 2016, South Korea has set its inflation target at 2%, with a band of +/-0.5%. Sources: CEIC and the respective central banks. The improving economy, accompanied by substantial capital inflows, caused financial asset prices to rise significantly in 2017 and early 2018 (blue and pink bars in Chart 2.10). Capital inflows into the region's markets rebounded significantly in 2017, with total portfolio investment inflows reaching a new high since 2010. Valuations of various financial assets in the region also rose along with the markets. Indeed, credit risk premia in the region narrowed further in the second half of 2017, while benchmark equity indices across the region rose broadly. Currencies in the region generally appreciated against the US dollar.

Amid buoyant local demand and improved export performance, the Hong Kong economy maintained solid growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Economic growth is expected to remain solid in 2018. The economic outlook for Hong Kong continues to be affected by numerous uncertainties and risks, including the normalisation of monetary policy by major central banks, the stability of global financial markets, rising protectionist sentiment, and escalating geopolitical tensions. In the short term, although local inflationary pressures should remain moderate, certain upside risks still exist. The Hong Kong economy maintained its growth momentum in the second half of 2017. On a seasonally adjusted basis, real GDP grew by 0.8% quarter-on-quarter in both the third and fourth quarters, similar to the average growth rate of 0.9% in the preceding two quarters (Chart 3.1). Compared with the first half of the year, private consumption continued to grow solidly and remained one of the major growth drivers of GDP growth. Consumption growth was solid, owing to favourable employment and income conditions, still-optimistic consumer sentiment, and the positive impact of rising asset prices through the wealth effect. Although building and construction activities weakened, increased corporate capital spending caused aggregate investment spending to rise notably in the final quarter, after being broadly stable for three quarters. On the external front, benefiting from improved growth in global trade and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism, Hong Kong's export performance improved further (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as imports grew faster than exports, net exports of goods continued to drag on GDP growth, while net exports of services contributed positively to GDP growth. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contributions of major expenditure components. Chart 3.2 Real imports and exports. The sustained economic growth momentum drove an increase in employment in the second half of 2017. During the period, total employment increased by about 0.7% to more than 3.85 million people, with the most notable gains in the construction industry, the financing and business services sector, and the public administration, social and personal services sector. As real GDP growth outpaced employment growth, labour productivity showed further signs of improvement. Economic growth is expected to remain solid in 2018. On the external front, Hong Kong's export performance will continue to benefit from the improving global economic growth outlook and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism. On the local front, private consumption is expected to continue to grow, mainly due to favourable labour market conditions. In view of the eventual rise in HKD interest rates, Box 3 examines the impact of a higher mortgage payment burden on private consumption. As for local fixed capital formation, building and construction activities should grow steadily, benefiting from increased housing supply and the continued commencement of infrastructure projects. Although the improved economic environment will stimulate business capital spending, potential interest rate hikes may have a negative impact. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of between 3% and 4% in 2018, while growth forecasts by international institutions and private-sector analysts range from 2% to 4%. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook continues to be affected by numerous uncertainties and risks, including the external environment mentioned in earlier chapters, the economic performance of Mainland China under tightening financial conditions, and the movements of Hong Kong's asset markets. Local inflationary pressures remained under control in the second half of 2017, but the sequential inflation momentum showed signs of a slight pickup in recent months. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying composite consumer price index rose by 1.7% and 1.6% in the third and fourth quarters respectively, similar to the average increase of about 1.7% in the first half of the year. However, the underlying inflation rate on a three-month-on-three-month annualised basis, which reflects inflation momentum, edged up to 2.8% in January 2018 (Chart 3.3). Among these, both the prices of tradables and services rose. The pickup in fresh-letting private residential rentals since mid-2016 may also have added to inflation momentum to some extent (Chart 3.4). In addition, labour cost pressures remained moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 Different indicators reflecting consumer price inflation. Chart 3.4 Rental component of the composite consumer price index and market rentals. Chart 3.5 Unit labour cost and per-capita wages. As global inflation remains moderate and increases in domestic costs are stable, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong are expected to stay moderate in 2018, but the underlying inflation rate may gradually pick up from the eight-year low of 1.7% in 2017. For example, owing to the pass-through effect from the growth of fresh-letting private residential rentals, inflationary pressures may increase somewhat in the second half of 2018. Market consensus forecasts put the headline inflation rate at a moderate 2.2% in 2018, while the Government forecasts the underlying inflation rate at 2.5%. Although the inflation outlook is moderate, upside risks still exist. On the external front, should global inflation or commodity prices record larger-than-expected increases, this could add to local inflation momentum. On the local front, the labour market has tightened further recently, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling from 3.4% in 2016 to 2.9% in December 2017, the first time it has fallen below 3% in nearly 20 years (Chart 3.6). The current output gap is estimated to be close to zero, and a substantial tightening of the labour market could pose additional upside pressure on inflation. Chart 3.6 Unemployment rate. Following the low interest rates after the 2008 global financial crisis, the mortgage debt of Hong Kong households increased. As the normalisation of USD interest rates proceeds, HKD interest rates will eventually follow their USD counterparts higher, and the mortgage payment burden of households will increase accordingly in the future, thereby dragging on household consumption. Therefore, this Box studies the impact of an increased mortgage payment burden on private consumption in Hong Kong. The mortgage payment burden refers to the ratio of mortgage debt servicing payments (i.e. interest payments plus loan principal amortisation) to income. Chart B3.1 shows the role of the mortgage payment burden in the transmission of interest rate shocks to private consumption. In addition to the substitution effect, income effect, and the wealth effect and collateral effect arising from changes in asset prices as mentioned in general economic theory, in the presence of a mortgage payment burden, an interest rate shock also affects private consumption by changing mortgage interest payments and thereby altering households' disposable income. This impact will be amplified as the outstanding mortgage loan amount increases. In addition, the loan principal amortisation amount changes with the outstanding mortgage loan amount, which also affects private consumption by changing households' disposable income. Chart B3.1 Determinants of private consumption. To measure the impact of the mortgage payment burden on private consumption, we estimated the outstanding mortgage debt servicing ratio (OMDSR) based on outstanding mortgage debt. Unlike the current mortgage payment burden indicator, which applies only to new mortgage debt, the OMDSR covers all outstanding mortgage debt of the overall household sector, which is more closely related to total private consumption. Broadly following the methodology used by the Bank for International Settlements, we measure the OMDSR using the standard formula for fixed instalment payments: where Dt is the outstanding residential mortgage loan amount of the banking sector, Yt is the total income of owner-occupier households (proxied by the median income of owner-occupier households multiplied by the number of owner-occupier households), and rt and st are the average interest rate and maturity of outstanding mortgage loans, respectively. To assess whether the OMDSR can reliably measure the mortgage payment burden of the entire household sector, it is appropriate to compare the OMDSR with two commonly used debt servicing ratio indicators. Chart B3.2 shows the OMDSR estimates from 1985 to mid-2017, as well as the median mortgage payment and loan repayment to income ratios estimated by the Census and Statistics Department based on the quinquennial population census. In the early 2000s, both ratios showed a downward trend, consistent with the reduction in overall household mortgage borrowing following the bursting of the property market bubble in 1997 and the substantial decline in mortgage rates over the same period. Although residential property prices rose substantially after the global financial crisis, both ratios remained stable, owing to the HKMA's macro-prudential measures on banks' mortgage lending, which curbed overall household mortgage leverage. In addition, the extension of the maturity of new mortgage loans also reduced the actual amount of mortgage payments. Chart B3.2 OMDSR and the median mortgage payment and loan repayment to income ratios. We also compared the OMDSR with banks' debt servicing ratio, the latter being the actual debt servicing to income ratio of banks' new mortgage applicants. As shown in Chart B3.3, the OMDSR is lower than banks' debt servicing ratio, partly because the OMDSR covers not only new mortgages but also existing mortgages. As existing mortgages were taken out when housing prices were lower, their payments are correspondingly lower than those of new mortgages. Therefore, the outstanding mortgage payment burden indicator covering both existing and new mortgages (i.e. the OMDSR) is lower than the payment burden indicator for new mortgages (i.e. banks' debt servicing ratio). In addition, banks' debt servicing ratio is higher because banks, in compliance with the HKMA's prudential regulatory requirement, take non-mortgage loan repayments into account when calculating the debt servicing ratio. After the global financial crisis, both the OMDSR and banks' debt servicing ratio remained stable, mainly owing to the HKMA's implementation of prudential regulation on mortgage loans, which set a cap on banks' debt servicing ratio, and this measure also helped to stabilise the OMDSR. Chart B3.3 OMDSR and banks' debt servicing ratio for new mortgages. Overall, the OMDSR is broadly consistent with commonly used debt servicing ratio indicators, but the OMDSR is more timely and can reflect the burden of overall outstanding mortgage debt, rather than only the burden of new mortgage debt. Therefore, we believe that using the OMDSR can assess the impact of the mortgage payment burden on private consumption. To assess the impact of the mortgage payment burden on private consumption in Hong Kong, we estimate an error-correction model following the methodologies of Lai and Lam (2002) and Kang (2016). In this model, the long-term relationship between real private consumption (proxied by real average private consumption per household) and its determinants is represented in the short-term equation by an error-correction term. Based on existing theoretical and empirical evidence, we take real income (proxied by median household income, deflated by the composite consumer price index), real housing and financial wealth (proxied by residential property prices and the Hang Seng Index respectively, deflated by the composite consumer price index), and the OMDSR as the long-term determinants of private consumption.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened, while the local interbank market continued to function in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, total lending continued to increase, but at a slower pace than in the first half. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalise, HKD interest rates may face greater upward pressure. Should sentiment in global financial markets shift abruptly, the volatility of fund flows may increase. In the second half of 2017, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar traded between 7.799 and 7.827 (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate strengthened briefly during September to November 2017 and remained close to the 7.80 level. This was mainly due to rising demand for HKD funds from IPO fund-raising activities and banks adopting a cautious approach to manage their liquidity ahead of month-ends and the year-end, which led to tighter liquidity conditions and, in turn, slowed interest rate arbitrage activities and increased the unwinding of Hong Kong dollar short positions. As the tight Hong Kong dollar liquidity situation eased and commercial demand for the US dollar rose towards the year-end, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate softened again in mid-December 2017. Entering 2018, despite increased volatility in global financial markets (particularly the equity markets), the Hong Kong dollar continued to function in an orderly manner. During the reporting period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate against the US dollar weakened, but the CUs were not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate; Chart 4.2 Fund flow indicators. The nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar fluctuated slightly in the second half of 2017, but recently faced greater downward pressures as the US dollar weakened further (Chart 4.3). This was broadly in line with the movement of the US dollar against most major currencies. Since the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and had limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index, the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar continued to track the movement of the nominal effective exchange rate index closely. Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates. Portfolio investment by non-residents recorded inflows in the second half of 2017. The latest balance of payments statistics showed that equity securities investment by both residents and non-residents recorded inflows in the third quarter, reflecting an improved regional economic outlook and optimistic market sentiment (Table 4.A). Debt securities investment by non-residents recorded inflows in the third quarter of 2017, offsetting the outflow of debt investment by residents. A survey of global mutual funds also showed that both equity and debt investments recorded inflows in the fourth quarter of 2017, as the market held an optimistic view of the economic outlook and firms’ earnings. In recent weeks, the survey data showed that despite the correction in global financial markets, equity investment still recorded inflows, while bond investment recorded a slight outflow of funds (Chart 4.4). Chart 4.4 Market survey of equity- and bond-related fund flows. Looking ahead, as the normalisation of US monetary policy continues, the negative interest rate spread between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar will widen, which may induce increased arbitrage activities. Therefore, the possibility of the weak-side CU of the Hong Kong dollar being triggered should not be ruled out. This is a normal process under the LERS. At the same time, given that the pace of US monetary policy normalisation remains unclear and that global macro-financial conditions and market sentiment can change rapidly, the volatility of HKD fund flows and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may increase. The HKMA will continue to safeguard the stability of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate in full accordance with the Currency Board mechanism. Despite the Federal Reserve's interest rate hikes and its continued reduction of its balance sheet, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2017 and in recent months. The HKD Monetary Base rose further by 1.4% in the second half of 2017, mainly driven by the growth of Certificates of Indebtedness issued in respect of the issuance of banknotes (Chart 4.5). As the CUs were not triggered, the total of the Aggregate Balance and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes remained broadly unchanged in the second half, staying at around HK$1,226.8 billion. Of these, the Aggregate Balance contracted while outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased correspondingly. This was due to the additional issuance of Exchange Fund Bills (totalling HK$80 billion) to meet the substantial demand from banks to manage their liquidity. Entering 2018, despite the correction in the stock market, the Monetary Base remained stable. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base. Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar money supply grew further in the second half of 2017, but at a slower pace. The growth of Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) slowed from 8.9% in the first half to 2.5% in the second half. As a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits rose slightly by 2.2% in the second half (Chart 4.7). Of these, demand deposits grew faster in the second half, partly due to buoyant asset markets and rising investment demand. An analysis of the counterpart assets showed that the growth of Hong Kong dollar M3 was, on the one hand, supported by the strong loan growth in Hong Kong dollar loans (Chart 4.6), and, on the other hand, dragged down by the net outflow of HKD funds from the non-bank private sector and the contraction of banks' net foreign currency assets. Chart 4.6 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and its counterpart assets. On the other hand, the growth of foreign currency deposits was mixed. Partly reflecting the currency depreciation of the US dollar against most major currencies, the growth rate of US dollar deposits fell from 3.0% in the first half to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 4.7). By contrast, other foreign currency deposits, after declining for more than two years, rebounded significantly in the second half, rising by 8.4%. This was mainly driven by the recent rebound in renminbi deposits. As the growth of Hong Kong dollar and US dollar deposits slowed, the total deposits of AIs increased slightly by 3.0% in the second half, compared with a growth rate of 5.6% in the first half. For 2017 as a whole, total deposits recorded a moderate growth of 8.7%, broadly similar to 2016. Chart 4.7 Deposit growth. During September to December 2017, demand for HKD funds from IPO fund-raising activities rose, while banks adopted a cautious approach to manage their liquidity ahead of month-ends and the year-end, which put upward pressure on HKD interbank interest rates (Chart 4.8). Compared with six months earlier, the overnight and 3-month HIBORs rose by 14 and 50 basis points respectively, climbing to 0.25% and 1.26% in December (on a monthly average basis). The negative interest rate spread between the 1-month to 3-month Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates narrowed correspondingly. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates. Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upward but flattened, broadly in line with the movement of the US dollar yield curve. In the second half, the yield of 3-year Hong Kong Government Bonds rose by 63 basis points, closing at 1.52% at the end of 2017, while the yield of 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds rose by a smaller extent of 33 basis points, closing at 1.83% at the end of 2017 (Chart 4.9). Chart 4.9 Government bond yields, composite interest rate and average lending rate on new mortgages. Entering 2018, the Hong Kong dollar interbank market continued to function in an orderly manner. As year-end demand for funds subsided, HKD interbank interest rates fell back in early January. Thereafter, despite the correction in global and local stock market, HKD interbank interest rates remained broadly stable. The overnight and 3-month HIBORs closed at 0.43% and 1.08% respectively at the end of February 2018. At the retail level, although banks' lending rates rose along with the surge in HIBORs, banks' cost of funding generally remained low due to the still-large deposit base. Despite fierce competition in the mortgage lending business, banks' average lending rate on new mortgages gradually rose by 36 basis points to 2.16% in December (Chart 4.9), broadly following the upward trend of the 1-month HIBOR. On the other hand, the composite interest rate, which measures the cost of funding in Hong Kong dollars of retail banks, briefly rose in October due to the increased demand for HKD funds from IPO fund-raising activities, but remained soft for most of the second half, closing at 0.38% at the end of December. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalise, coupled with the possible commencement of interest rate normalisation by other major economies, HKD interest rates may face greater upward pressure. At the same time, with fluctuating global market sentiment and rapidly changing macro-financial conditions, the volatility of fund flows may increase. Nevertheless, the sizeable HKD Monetary Base can serve as a buffer, helping to moderate any excessively rapid rise in HKD interest rates. In addition, banks' prudent liquidity management and the availability of discounting through the Discount Window also help to contain excessive volatility in interbank interest rates. Bank credit grew strongly throughout 2017. The loan growth rate reached 10.2% in the first half, then slowed to 5.3% in the second half (Chart 4.10). In the second half of 2017, the growth of both loans for use in Hong Kong and loans for use outside Hong Kong slowed. By currency, owing to the improved local economic environment and the relatively low cost of funding in Hong Kong dollars, Hong Kong dollar loans continued to grow rapidly by 9.5% in the second half, while foreign currency loans rose only slightly by 0.1%. Of these, the growth of US dollar loans slowed to 1.8%, partly due to the rising cost of funding in US dollars. For 2017 as a whole, total lending recorded a strong growth of 16.1%, compared with 6.5% in 2016. Chart 4.10 Loan growth. Loans for use in Hong Kong (including trade finance) grew at a slower pace, decreasing from 9.4% in the first half to 5.6% in the second half, with mixed performance across the major sectors (Chart 4.11). The growth of loans to the construction sector and to property development and investment slowed in the second half, partly because since June 2017 the authorities have required banks to strengthen the risk management of loans to property developers. Although merchandise trade and retail sales improved further, loans for trade finance and the transport sector recorded only relatively modest growth, while loans to the wholesale and retail sectors recorded declines. On the contrary, loans to financial and finance-related companies continued to grow strongly, reflecting to a certain extent the steady expansion of the financial services industry. Chart 4.11 Growth of domestic loans by selected sector. Household debt grew by 6.5% in the second half of 2017, compared with a growth of 5.0% in the first half. Within household debt, personal loans (including credit card advances and loans for other private purposes) grew at a faster pace, rising by 12.4% in the second half. The strong growth of personal loans was mainly driven by borrowing from private banking and wealth management customers using financial assets as collateral. The growth of these loans was broadly similar to the continued growth of client assets managed by banks. The risk of such collateralised loans is within a controllable range. In addition, the HKMA issued guidance to banks on the risk management of personal loans in January 2014, requiring banks to adopt prudent risk management measures, including setting caps on loan tenor and the debt servicing ratio of borrowers. On the other hand, although residential transaction volumes increased, the LTV ratio of newly approved mortgages fell, and the growth of residential mortgage loan slowed slightly to 3.8% in the second half. Overall, the household debt-to-GDP ratio rose from 68.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 70.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12).

Benefiting mainly from the growth in net interest income, the profitability of retail banks improved in the second half of 2017 compared with the same period in 2016. Capital and liquidity conditions remained robust. After experiencing strong growth in the first half of 2017, loan growth slowed in the second half, while asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Despite the significant rise in HKD interbank interest rates, the HKD funding cost of retail banks remained low owing to low retail deposit rates. Nevertheless, banks should remain vigilant about the risks of rising interest rate volatility and possible fund outflows under the normalisation of US monetary policy, as well as geopolitical risks. As corporate leverage continues to rise and personal debt burdens remain high, banks should assess the potential impact on asset quality of interest rates rising more than expected. To enhance banks' resilience to systemic risks, the countercyclical capital buffer ratio in Hong Kong will be raised to 2.5% starting from 1 January 2019.  In the second half of 2017, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 13.6% compared with the same period a year earlier. This was mainly attributable to a substantial increase in net interest income and a reduction in loan impairment provisions, which was sufficient to offset the decline in non-interest income. However, as assets grew faster than profits, the return on assets of retail banks edged down slightly from 1.17% in the first half to 1.15% in the second half of 2017. Nevertheless, the return on assets in the second half of 2017 was still higher than the 1.11% recorded in the same period of 2016 (Chart 5.1). For 2017 as a whole, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 15.8%, while the return on assets rose from 1.09% in 2016 to 1.16%. Chart 5.1 Retail bank profitability.  The net interest margin of retail banks widened further to 1.5% in the fourth quarter of 2017 from 1.34% in the same period of 2016 (Chart 5.2). Observed evidence suggests that the improvement in net interest margin was consistent with the rise in the average spread of HKD corporate loans in the Hong Kong syndicated loan market (Chart 5.3). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks. Chart 5.3 Average spread of HKD syndicated loans.  Since September 2017, the HIBORs have risen across the board, mainly driven by IPO-related liquidity demand and banks' liquidity needs towards year-end, as well as expectations of US interest rate hikes. Among them, the three-month HIBOR recorded a post-financial-crisis high of 1.31% at the end of December 2017, up 53 basis points from the end of June, but still relatively low by historical standards (blue line in Chart 5.4). Entering 2018, the HIBORs appeared to stabilise as banks' year-end liquidity needs eased. Despite the recent rise in the HIBORs, the HKD funding cost of retail banks remained stable. This was mainly due to the low retail deposit rates during the review period. Against this backdrop, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of HKD funds of retail banks, remained low at around 0.3% for most of the second half of 2017, rising only slightly to 0.38% at the end of December (green line in Chart 5.4).  A similar situation was observed for the overall HKD and USD funding costs of Hong Kong licensed banks. In the second half of 2017, banks' average HKD and USD funding costs in the non-deposit market rose by 35 basis points, while the average deposit funding costs rose slightly by 12 basis points. Overall, the average total HKD and USD funding costs of licensed banks rose by 22 basis points (red line in Chart 5.5). Chart 5.4 Interest rates. Chart 5.5 HKD and USD funding costs and maturities of licensed banks. The rise in the HIBORs exceeded the overall funding costs of the Hong Kong banking sector, which may help improve the spreads of banks' HIBOR-based assets. However, this improvement may be partly offset by the intense competition in the mortgage market. In particular, market data show that some banks have reduced the spread between their mortgage rates and the reference rate or introduced fixed-rate mortgage terms to attract new customers. Given the expectation of further US interest rate hikes this year, banks may soon face greater pressure from rising funding costs. In view of the intense competition in the loan market, if the increased funding costs cannot be fully passed on to customers, this may put pressure on banks' net interest margins.  The consolidated capital adequacy ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained well above the international minimum standard, indicating that the Hong Kong banking sector maintained a strong capital position. At the end of December 2017, the total capital ratio increased to 19.1% from 18.7% at the end of June (Chart 5.6), while the Tier 1 capital ratio54 also rose to 16.6%, of which 15.4% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital.55 Chart 5.6 Capital of locally incorporated authorized institutions. The HKMA recently issued a consultation paper to consult on the rules for establishing loss-absorbing capacity requirements applicable to authorized institutions under the Financial Institutions (Resolution) Ordinance. While enhancing the loss-absorbing capacity of authorized institutions helps reduce the likelihood of a financial crisis and thereby benefits society, it inevitably also entails costs. Box 5 conducts a cost-benefit assessment of the potential impact of the loss-absorbing capacity requirements on Hong Kong. Our assessment shows that the implementation of the loss-absorbing capacity requirements will bring net benefits to the Hong Kong economy.  Measured by the "Liquidity Coverage Ratio" requirement under Basel III, the liquidity conditions of the banking sector remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions rose from 144.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 155.1% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 80% applicable to 2017. Although the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions edged down slightly from 49.7% in the second quarter of 2017 to 49.4% in the fourth quarter, it remained well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. The ample liquidity of authorized institutions indicates that the Hong Kong banking sector is able to withstand liquidity shocks arising from possible fund outflows from Hong Kong. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio.  The Net Stable Funding Ratio, one of the Basel III liquidity standards, was implemented in Hong Kong on 1 January 2018. The requirement aims to reduce banks' medium- to long-term funding risks by requiring them to maintain a sufficient stable source of funding for their business activities. Specifically, category 1 institutions must maintain a Net Stable Funding Ratio of no less than 100% at all times.57 Customer deposits remained the primary source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting a stable funding structure in the banking system. At the end of December 2017, Customer deposits accounted for 56.2% of the total liabilities of all authorized institutions, broadly the same as six months earlier (Chart 5.8). Chart 5.8 Liability structure of all authorized institutions.  The HKD loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions rose from 77.1% at the end of June 2017 to 82.7% at the end of December (Chart 5.9), reflecting that HKD loan and advances grew faster than deposits during the review period. Meanwhile, as foreign currency deposits grew faster than loans, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell from 65.5% at the end of June 2017 to 63.1% at the end of December. Overall, the loan-to-deposit ratio for all currencies rose from 71.4% six months earlier to 73.0%. Banks should assess the impact of the rising loan-to-deposit ratio on how they manage their liquidity. Chart 5.9 Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions.  The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained low. We estimate that under an assumed shock of an across-the-board 200-basis-point rise in interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of the interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks would be equivalent to 3.45% of their total capital base at the end of December 2017 (Chart 5.10). Nevertheless, in view of the expectation that the US Federal Reserve will continue to raise interest rates and commence balance sheet normalisation, banks should assess the impact of this situation on their interest rate risk management.
