In the second half of 2017, amid a moderate but still favourable economic environment, the growth in total loans and advances of all authorized institutions slowed from the strong 10.2% growth recorded in the first half to 5.3%. After two years of slowing growth, total lending grew robustly by 16.1% for 2017 as a whole. The asset quality of banks' loan portfolios remained sound and continued to improve in the second half of 2017. At the end of December 2017, the gross CLR and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans of all authorized institutions fell to 0.67% and 0.52% respectively, compared with 0.84% and 0.61% respectively at the end of June. For retail banks, the gross CLR and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans also fell to 0.54% and 0.4% respectively (Chart 5.11). However, given the rapid growth in recent years of loans used outside Hong Kong, banks' asset quality may be more sensitive to the external environment, and banks should therefore closely monitor their credit risk. Chart 5.11 Asset quality of retail banks.  As banks have become more optimistic about their expectations for recent loan growth, the strong loan growth is expected to persist. The HKMA's Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook of December 2017 showed that 29% of the authorized institutions surveyed expected loan demand to grow over the next three months, while the remaining 71% of the authorized institutions surveyed expected loan demand to remain unchanged (Table 5.A). The credit risk of personal loans remained low during the review period. Banks' mortgage loan portfolios remained sound, with the delinquency ratio staying low at 0.03% at the end of December 2017. The average LTV ratio of newly approved mortgages fell further from 50.1% in the second quarter of 2017 to 48.8% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.12). This LTV ratio was well below the 64% recorded before the HKMA implemented the first round of countercyclical macroprudential measures (i.e. September 2009).

The global economy continued to grow, but its momentum weakened as uncertainties increased due to persistent trade tensions, tightening financial conditions, and other idiosyncratic and cyclical headwinds. The US Federal Reserve adjusted its monetary policy stance, emphasising that its decisions would be "data-dependent" and require "patience", leading investors to rule out the possibility of another rate hike. Nevertheless, financial markets may become more sensitive to data releases going forward, particularly those that could prompt a tightening of monetary policy, such as a rise in US inflation. In Hong Kong, although the weak-side CU was triggered in March, trading of the Hong Kong dollar remained smooth and orderly. In the second half of 2018, the growth of total lending narrowed slightly, reflecting reduced credit demand amid headwinds such as the persistent China-US trade conflict and slowing global economic growth. The residential property market also cooled in the second half of 2018, with a significant decline in transaction volume and a retreat in property prices, before showing signs of stabilisation in early 2019. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector faces multiple headwinds arising from increased uncertainties in the external environment. Should these uncertainties intensify and persist over the long term, they could significantly dampen business sentiment and credit demand, thereby exerting downward pressures on banks' profitability. In view of the continued rise in corporate leverage, banks should prudently assess the impact that a possible deterioration in the external environment could have on the credit risk of their related corporate loans.  In the second half of 2018, the global economy continued to grow. However, while the US economy grew robustly, growth momentum in other regions slowed. Among the advanced economies, growth decelerated in Japan and several major euro area countries, with inflation remaining low. The slowing of global trade flows and a significant drop in oil prices both posed cyclical headwinds to emerging market economies. In view of the slowing global growth momentum, in January the International Monetary Fund revised down its global growth forecasts for 2019 and 2020 by 0.2 and 0.1 percentage points respectively compared with its October 2018 projections. Amid a dimming growth outlook and escalating trade tensions, global equity markets experienced significant volatility towards the end of 2018. The US Central Government bond yields curve flattened to levels not seen since the global financial crisis, sparking market concerns about an imminent US recession. However, the fundamentals of the US economy remained sound, and the likelihood of a recession in the short term was low. That said, the global economic outlook remained fraught with uncertainties. In the US, while moderate inflation gave the Fed room to pause rate hikes, the Fed's data-dependent policy inclination also signalled that financial markets may become more sensitive to data releases going forward, particularly those that could prompt a tightening of monetary policy, such as a rise in US inflation. Meanwhile, the outcomes of trade negotiations between the US and China, and between the US and the EU, remained uncertain. In the UK, whether a solution to avoid a "hard Brexit" could be achieved remained an unknown. In East Asia, financial markets had stabilised thanks to the slowing appreciation of the US dollar and market expectations of a pause in the Fed's rate hikes, but deterioration in the external environment could weigh on the region's economic growth. Indeed, the weakening momentum of global trade growth had already dragged on the economic growth of several East Asian economies, and inflationary pressures had also eased. While this shift could alleviate the policy dilemma faced by the region's central banks between supporting growth and curbing inflation, financial imbalances such as high private-sector indebtedness in some economies within the region remained severe. As detailed in Box 1 (page 16), another challenge facing East Asia is that if the Fed's monetary policy were to change unexpectedly, the resulting shock could spill over into the sovereign bond market of emerging market economies (including East Asian economies).  In Mainland China, growth slowed further in the second half of 2018 amid increased uncertainties in the external environment and a slight moderation in domestic demand. Looking ahead, with the China-US trade negotiations yet to reach a conclusion, the economic outlook remained uncertain. As shadow financing activities contracted significantly, the financing difficulties faced by private enterprises (especially small companies) over the past few quarters increased, and coupled with weakening economic confidence, this could also exert pressure on business activities. In this challenging economic environment, policymakers must continue to strike a balance between stabilising the economy and preventing and controlling potential systemic risks by adopting accommodative but targeted measures (such as targeted required reserve ratio cuts). Meanwhile, the authorities also adopted more supply-side measures to boost productivity growth (such as promoting competition among companies of different ownership types) and to provide a better social safety net for individuals. The official growth target for 2019 was also lowered from around 6.5% in 2018 to a range of 6.0% to 6.5%. In 2018, risk-averse sentiment dominated Mainland financial markets. Bank asset quality also deteriorated slightly during the review period, while the leverage level of listed non-financial corporates rose marginally. However, banks' loan impairment provisions increased further in the second half of 2018, and their off-balance-sheet exposure to wealth management products continued to decline; both developments helped to protect the banking system from a potential deterioration in credit quality. Another positive development was that the leverage level of listed corporates in industries with overcapacity — one of the main sources of banks' credit risk — declined further in the first three quarters of 2018. Box 2 (page 32) provides an in-depth analysis of the factors that have contributed to the recent improvement in the business performance of overcapacity industries.  Compared with the first half of 2018, economic activity in Hong Kong softened in the second half. GDP growth stalled on a quarter-on-quarter basis and slowed on a year-on-year basis, dragging full-year economic growth down from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018. The weakening of economic activity was mainly due to consumption and exports being dragged down by the direct or indirect impact of the China-US trade conflict. The slowdown in private consumption growth may have reflected increased economic uncertainties as well as the wealth-erosion effect of local asset price adjustments. On the external front, Hong Kong's exports of goods also performed worse, particularly after China and the US implemented additional tariffs in the fourth quarter. Box 3 examines more closely the impact of the China-US trade conflict on Hong Kong's merchandise trade performance and explores the near-term outlook and its associated risks. Mainly owing to the slowdown in global economic growth, economic growth is expected to slow further in 2019. Under the interplay of multiple factors, Hong Kong's export performance is expected to remain under pressure. On the local front, with the unemployment rate remaining low and household incomes rising, private consumption is expected to continue to support economic growth, but the outlook for aggregate investment spending may become more uncertain. The government forecasts real GDP growth of between 2% and 3% for 2019, while the latest average growth forecast by private-sector analysts is 2.3%. These forecasts are subject to the various uncertainties and risks described above. Local inflation rose slightly in the second half of 2018 but remained at a moderate level. The mild rise in inflation was partly affected by the growth in newly-signed local residential rentals earlier. Meanwhile, although the unemployment rate remained low at 2.8%, the lowest level in more than two decades, growth in total employment showed signs of slowing. Looking ahead, as the momentum of local economic growth weakens, local inflationary pressures are expected to remain moderate in 2019.  Following the triggering of the weak-side CU in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate deviated from 7.8500 and traded between 7.8062 and 7.8499, until the weak-side CU was triggered again in March 2019, a total of four times (as at 19 March). The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate appreciated in September and November, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trade positions amid tightening liquidity. Entering 2019, the Hong Kong dollar weakened against the US dollar, partly due to the re-establishment of carry trade positions. Although the weak-side CU was triggered again in March, trading of the Hong Kong dollar remained smooth and orderly. As a result of the triggering of the weak-side CU, the Aggregate Balance declined slightly to HK$70.9 billion (as at 19 March). HKD interbank interest rates generally rose in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting expectations of US rate hikes. Compared with June 2018, the 3-month and 12-month HIBORs rose by about 30 basis points to 2.32% and 2.74% respectively in December (on a monthly average basis). Entering 2019, HKD interbank interest rates fell overall as seasonal demand receded. The composite interest rate, which measures the average HKD cost of funding of retail banks, rose from 0.62% at end-June 2018 to 0.83% at end-January 2019. In view of the rising cost of funding, following the upward adjustment of the US federal funds target rate range at the end of September, retail banks raised their Best Lending Rates by 12.5 to 25.0 basis points. At end-January 2019, the average lending rate on new mortgages rose in line with the Best Lending Rates to about 2.45%. As uncertainties related to the China-US trade tensions and Brexit negotiations persist, fund flow volatility may intensify. In addition, the significant negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and its USD counterparts may spur arbitrage activities, leading to fund outflows. In such circumstances, fund outflows and the possible triggering of the weak-side CU are both part of the normal operation of the LERS.  Since the beginning of 2018, both the CNH and onshore renminbi exchange rates were under depreciation pressure amid market concerns over the escalation of China-US trade tensions. However, driven by optimism as China and the US resumed high-level trade negotiations, both the CNH and onshore renminbi exchange rates stabilised in November. Although the China-US trade tensions persisted, they have so far not exerted a significant impact on funding conditions in the offshore interbank market. The overnight CNH HIBOR stayed below 4% for most of 2018, while the 3-month CNH HIBOR hovered around 4%. Meanwhile, Hong Kong's CNH liquidity pool expanded steadily in the second half, with RMB customer deposits growing by 5.2% in the second half of 2018. The average daily turnover of the RMB RTGS system remained at a high level and rose further to RMB1,010.1 billion in 2018. Despite lingering concerns over the China-US trade tensions, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to continue to expand, driven by the opening up of the Mainland's capital account, the development of stock and bond connectivity, and regional economic cooperation promoted under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives.  Local equity markets rode a roller-coaster over the past six months. In the early part of the review period, the market fell sharply due to continued tightening of US monetary policy, major differences between China and the US in trade negotiations, and increasing signs of weakening economic growth in the Mainland. Subsequently, as the US economic outlook weakened and became more uncertain, the Fed shifted to a "patient" monetary policy stance, while during the trade-war truce, China took more measures to reduce its trade surplus with the US and to open up its market to foreign investors. Although the US brought a highly political legal prosecution against a Chinese telecommunications company, both sides displayed friendly gestures, indicating their determination to reach a trade agreement. Against this backdrop, local equity markets rebounded rapidly at the start of the year. However, as the two sides discuss the details of an agreement (if any), the future remains highly uncertain, and the future development of the US federal government's prosecution will complicate the situation, particularly in the high-tech sector. The Hong Kong dollar debt market grew slightly last year. Yields fell, and performance improved towards the end of the year as market expectations of a slowing pace of US monetary policy normalisation strengthened. As a result, fund flows into bond funds reversed and increased slightly in the second half. Issuance in Hong Kong's offshore renminbi market rebounded strongly after three consecutive years of decline. However, as Mainland companies continued to deleverage, total issuance remained below maturing debt. Looking ahead, the local bond market remains challenging, and its growth outlook depends on global economic developments, particularly those in the Mainland.

During the review period, the global economy continued to grow, but the growth momentum weakened somewhat under the combined influence of idiosyncratic and cyclical headwinds, particularly notable in regions outside the United States. In view of the dimming growth outlook, the Fed adjusted its monetary policy stance, emphasising that its decisions would be "data-dependent" and require "patience", and no longer provided forward guidance on further interest rate hikes. As the Fed's policy leaned towards being data-dependent, financial markets may become more sensitive to subsequently released data and may view monetary policy as more uncertain. Meanwhile, global trade policy uncertainties and heightened geopolitical risks may continue to cast a shadow over the global growth outlook. In East Asia, as signs of a slowdown in the US interest rate hike cycle emerged and the US dollar stabilised, financial markets have been largely stable since the end of 2018. However, due to the deteriorating external environment—namely the unresolved China-US trade conflict and weakening growth in advanced economies—the region may face a broad-based slowdown. In Mainland China, growth momentum slowed further in the second half of 2018, and uncertainties over the growth outlook rose amid the China-US trade conflict and financing difficulties faced by small enterprises. As a result, policymakers adopted more targeted measures to stabilise the economy and support private and small enterprises. Facing these challenges, policymakers will need to strike a careful balance between continuing to guard against systemic risks and supporting businesses and the real economy. In the second half of 2018, the global economy continued to grow broadly. However, although the US economy remained generally robust, some signs of slowdown had emerged. There were also clear signs that growth momentum in regions outside the United States had slowed. A number of country-specific shocks—including natural disasters in Japan, the implementation of new automobile emission standards in Germany, the surge in Italian Central Government bond yields due to the fiscal standoff with the EU, and social unrest in France—all weighed on economic activity in the advanced economies (Chart 2.1). In addition, a cyclical slowdown in global import growth emerged, posing headwinds to industrial production in the emerging market economies (Chart 2.2). The sharp fall in oil prices in the fourth quarter also brought new challenges to commodity-exporting emerging market economies. In view of the slowing growth momentum in the second half of 2018, the International Monetary Fund lowered its 2019 global growth forecast by 0.2 percentage points to 3.5% in January. Chart 2.1 Composite Purchasing Managers' Indices of selected advanced economies. Chart 2.2 Global import volume and industrial production of emerging market economies. In the fourth quarter, the slowing global growth momentum, heightened trade policy uncertainties, market concerns over the sustainability of US firms’ earnings growth, and the Fed's remarks that monetary policy would continue to tighten led to a sharp correction in global equity markets. As market sentiment in financial markets deteriorated, the US Central Government bond yields curve flattened to levels not seen since the global financial crisis, triggering concerns among some market participants that the United States was heading towards a recession (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 The yield spread between 10-year and 3-month US Central Government bond yields and the probability of a US recession. Nonetheless, the likelihood of a US recession in the near term is very low. US economic fundamentals remain robust, particularly the tight labour market, which is expected to continue to support private consumption. At the same time, the US output gap is estimated to have only turned positive last year, making it less likely that economic overheating would prompt the Fed to tighten monetary policy substantially. However, possibly taking into account the substantial tightening of financial conditions since the fourth quarter, senior Fed officials began in early January to emphasise that monetary policy would be data-dependent, noting that moderate inflationary pressures allowed them to be "patient" in determining future monetary policy adjustments. In addition, following its January meeting, the Federal Open Market Committee no longer provided forward guidance on further interest rate hikes, and announced that it "would be prepared to adjust any of the details for completing balance sheet normalisation in light of economic and financial developments". This shift triggered a rebound in global equity markets (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 S&P 500, MSCI World (excluding the US) Index and MSCI Emerging Markets Index. Despite the Fed's recent dovish pivot signals, the outlook for US monetary policy remains rather uncertain, hinging on inflation and other developments. So far inflationary pressures have been moderate, giving the Fed room to advance monetary normalisation gradually. Inflation expectations have remained stable in recent years, supporting the view that it "can be patient" (Chart 2.5). In addition, as Fed Chair Powell noted in January, the US economic outlook faces multiple headwinds, including slowing growth in regions outside the United States and trade policy uncertainties. In view of these developments, the Fed may need to adopt a more cautious monetary policy stance. Chart 2.5 Market-based and survey-based measures of US inflation expectations. However, the tight labour market is expected to continue to support overall US economic performance. In this environment, wage growth may accelerate, which usually signals that future inflation may pick up (Chart 2.6). Therefore, the market expectation that essentially rules out the possibility of Fed interest rate hikes in 2019 may be overly optimistic (Chart 2.7). Chart 2.6 Average hourly earnings and core personal consumption expenditure inflation. Chart 2.7 Futures-implied probabilities of the federal funds rate target range remaining unchanged in 2019 versus at least one hike. All in all, a prolonged pause in Fed interest rate hikes is by no means certain. To reduce policy errors, the Fed has increasingly emphasised that its decisions will be data-dependent, as a risk-management strategy. It follows that financial markets may become more sensitive to subsequently released data, particularly data that could prompt monetary policy tightening. The monetary policy of other major central banks is also uncertain. In the Euro area, the ECB terminated its asset purchase programme in December, while continuing to reinvest the full principal of maturing securities under the asset purchase programme, and reiterated its forward guidance to keep the policy rate unchanged at least through the summer of 2019. However, in January the ECB lowered its short-term growth assessment, describing the risks to the growth outlook as having "moved to the downside". The implications of the ECB's downward revision of its economic growth assessment for monetary policy remain to be seen. In Japan, the Bank of Japan indicated at its most recent policy meeting that it would ease its monetary policy stance if necessary amid rising downside risks. However, the headwinds to further monetary policy easing may be substantial, as its effectiveness has been questioned and the drawbacks of maintaining an ultra-low interest rate environment over the long term are becoming increasingly apparent—for example, as persistently low yields continue to weigh on profitability, the capital ratio of regional banks has fallen from 10.6% in 2015 to 9.7% in 2018. As a result, the Bank of Japan has very limited room to adjust monetary policy in the near term. In addition to the uncertainties surrounding the global monetary policy outlook, the uncertain outcome of future trade negotiations and heightened geopolitical risks are two major sources of risk facing the global growth outlook. In early December, the US government announced that it would not raise tariff on imported goods from China for 90 days, and extended the deadline again at the end of February, but whether the two sides can reach a long-term trade agreement remains to be seen. Meanwhile, the trade negotiations between the United States and the EU have made almost no progress at this stage. As the outcomes of these trade negotiations remain uncertain, they may continue to cast a shadow over the global growth outlook. Policy and geopolitical risks are also prominent. In the United States, partisan disagreement over border security funding led to a 35-day federal government shutdown from late December 2018 to late January 2019. Although the impact of the shutdown on economic growth should be temporary, tensions between the Trump administration and the Democratic-controlled House of Representatives may lead to more policy gridlock in the future. In the United Kingdom, after the Theresa May government's Brexit deal was overwhelmingly rejected in mid-January, the risks associated with Brexit and its knock-on effects surged, and it remains uncertain whether a plan can be devised at the last minute to avoid a disruptive "hard Brexit". Elsewhere, geopolitical tensions in the Middle East—such as the renewed US sanctions on Iran—may also pose uncertainties to oil prices, thereby affecting the global growth outlook. In East Asia, after fluctuating over the first three quarters of last year, financial markets largely stabilised in the fourth quarter. The US dollar has stabilised since October, and there are signs that the Fed is being patient about further interest rate hikes, easing the pressures of currency depreciation and fund outflow faced by East Asian economies. A number of currencies in the region rose slightly against the US dollar in the fourth quarter, while portfolio investment flows reverted to net inflows (Chart 2.8). Chart 2.8 East Asia: currency indices and fund flows. Despite the stability in financial markets, there are increasing signs that the region will face a broad-based slowdown. As global trade momentum weakened due to the China-US trade conflict, export growth in the region declined, causing real GDP growth in most East Asian economies to slow in the second half of last year. In fact, the new export orders sub-index of the Purchasing Managers' Index in several regional economies (reflecting near-term external trade performance) has fallen into contractionary territory since the fourth quarter, signalling that near-term growth drivers may slow further (Chart 2.9). Chart 2.9 Markit Purchasing Managers' Index new export orders index of East Asian economies. Amid the slowing growth environment, coupled with the recent decline in oil prices, inflationary pressures in East Asia have eased (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 East Asia: headline inflation and oil prices. As both recent inflationary pressures and upward pressure on the US dollar have been relatively moderate, East Asian central banks have had no urgent need to raise interest rates, which has eased the policy dilemma of choosing between promoting economic growth and curbing inflation and fund outflow. However, as private-sector debt in some East Asian countries remains high by emerging market standards, central banks still face the challenge of financial imbalances (Chart 2.11).

The Hong Kong economy softened in the second half of 2018, reflecting a slowdown in private consumption growth and a weakening in export performance amid the China-US trade conflict. As global growth slows, real GDP growth in 2019 is also expected to moderate. Hong Kong's growth outlook is affected by numerous uncertainties and risks, including trade protectionism, the future direction of US monetary policy, and the economic performance of Mainland China. Local inflationary pressures in 2019 should remain mild, and their outlook faces potential risks on both the upside and downside. Hong Kong's economic activity softened in the second half of 2018. Specifically, economic activity failed to sustain the strong momentum of the first half, and the GDP growth rate (quarter-on-quarter) turned mildly negative in the second half (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). On a year-on-year basis, economic growth also slowed, with a growth rate of 1.3% in the fourth quarter, below trend growth, which dragged the full-year growth rate down from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018.* Based on the seasonally adjusted real GDP volume index compiled from the expenditure side. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contribution of major expenditure components. The weakening in economic activity was mainly dragged down by consumption and exports being directly or indirectly affected by the China-US trade conflict. Perhaps due to increased economic uncertainties and the negative wealth effect arising from the adjustment in local asset prices, the growth of private consumption slowed somewhat (Chart 3.1). Total investment spending fell markedly amid fragile business sentiment. Hong Kong's external merchandise trade performance also deteriorated, especially after China and the US both implemented additional tariffs in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, since total imports decelerated faster than total exports, net trade still made a positive contribution to GDP in the fourth quarter. Box 3 examines Hong Kong's merchandise trade performance in greater detail and explores the near-term outlook and its associated risks. Chart 3.2 Real imports and exports. As economic activity weakened, job growth appears to have slowed in the second half of 2018. Total employment increased by only 0.1% to about 3,873,000 persons at the end of 2018, a smaller increase than the 0.8% in the first half of 2018. Owing to weak output and job growth, labour productivity remained broadly stable and showed no signs of significant improvement. As global economic growth slows further, Hong Kong's economic growth is expected to moderate in 2019. Facing challenges in the external environment, Hong Kong's export performance is expected to remain under pressure. On the domestic front, although the low unemployment rate and rising household income will continue to support private consumption, the growth of private consumption is expected to slow, partly affected by weaker consumer confidence and the negative wealth effect caused by the earlier adjustment in asset prices. As for fixed capital formation, the outlook may become even more uncertain. Although building and construction activities are still expected to grow steadily as housing supply increases, businesses may become more cautious about capital investment as economic uncertainties increase. Business sentiment indicators such as the Hong Kong Purchasing Managers' Index continue to hover in contractionary territory, and through this index's forecast of future economic growth, it signals that the year-on-year growth in GDP will slow further in the near term. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of between 2% and 3% in 2019, while the latest growth forecasts of private sector analysts range from 1.5% to 2.7%. Hong Kong's growth outlook is affected by the numerous uncertainties and risks described in the previous two chapters. Although local inflationary pressures have continued to build up in recent months, they remain at a mild level. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying composite consumer price index recorded increases of 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters of 2018 respectively, higher than the average increase of 2.4% in the first half. The three-month-on-three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, has also picked up recently, rising from 2.5% in July 2018 to 2.6% in January 2019 (Chart 3.3). The slight rise in inflation momentum was driven by increases in certain service prices. The earlier growth in newly signed residential rentals and the accelerating rise in prices for eating out continued to push up services inflation (Chart 3.4). However, labour cost pressures in recent quarters have remained broadly mild (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 Different indicators reflecting consumer price inflation. Chart 3.4 Rental component of the composite consumer price index and market rentals. Chart 3.5 Unit labour cost and per capita wage. Looking ahead, local inflationary pressures should remain mild in 2019. This mainly reflects weaker local growth drivers. However, the earlier upward trend in residential rentals will continue to pass through to consumer price inflation. Market consensus forecasts a mild headline inflation rate of 2.2% for the full year, while the Government forecasts an underlying inflation rate of 2.5%. The above inflation outlook faces risks on both the upside and downside. In terms of downside risks, the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate remained at around 2.8%, the lowest level in more than 20 years (Chart 3.6). If the labour market deteriorates unexpectedly, the current near-zero output gap would turn negative, potentially posing additional downward pressures on inflation. On the other hand, if the China-US trade tensions ease, causing local economic performance to exceed expectations, this could push up local inflation. Chart 3.6 Unemployment rate. The China-US trade conflict gradually intensified in the second half of 2018: on 6 July and 23 August, the US imposed 25% tariffs on goods worth US$34 billion and US$16 billion imported from Mainland China respectively. Following these two measures, Mainland China also responded by imposing 25% tariffs on an equivalent amount of US goods. The US escalated further on 24 September, imposing a 10% tariff on goods worth US$200 billion imported from Mainland China. Mainland China immediately responded by imposing tariffs of 5% to 10% on US goods worth US$60 billion. Since then, the two countries have begun negotiations to avoid further tariffs. As Hong Kong has always been an entrepôt between these two economies, the imposition of tariffs will inevitably have a direct impact on Hong Kong through the trade channel. Therefore, the China-US trade conflict has important implications for Hong Kong's macroeconomic and financial stability. This Box reviews Hong Kong's recent merchandise trade performance and explores its near-term outlook. We will also attempt to use more granular data to distinguish trade goods directly affected by the imposition of tariffs, so as to examine the impact of the tariffs in greater detail. To analyse the impact of the tariffs, we first extract data on six groups of Hong Kong re-export goods, which are respectively affected by the various rounds of tariffs described in the previous section. In the first two rounds of tariffs, the US mainly imposed tariffs on capital goods and semi-manufactured goods, while Mainland China mainly targeted tariffs on agricultural products, chemicals, medical equipment and energy equipment. In the third round of tariffs, the range of affected goods expanded to cover more consumer goods. For brevity, we correspondingly name the goods affected by these three rounds of tariffs as List 1, List 2 and List 3. After collecting these more granular trade data, we focus on analysing the year-on-year change in the value of Hong Kong re-exports to adjust for the impact of seasonal factors. In addition, readers should also be cautious when analysing the data for September 2018, as trade activity in that month was disrupted to some extent by super typhoon Mangkhut. Overall, the analytical results in this section should only be regarded as preliminary evidence of the impact of the tariffs. Hong Kong re-exports originating from the Mainland and affected by tariffs. Shortly after the imposition of tariffs, the relevant goods re-exported from Mainland China via Hong Kong to the US appeared to have decreased substantially or slowed in growth (Chart B3.1). For example, re-export growth for List 1 and List 2 slowed in the first month after the imposition of tariffs, while re-exports for List 3 recorded negative growth. In addition, re-exports for all three lists recorded negative growth in December. Chart B3.1 Value of goods re-exported from Mainland China via Hong Kong to the US in 2018. Hong Kong re-exports originating from the US and affected by tariffs. In contrast, goods re-exported from the US via Hong Kong to Mainland China showed varied performance (Chart B3.2). Re-exports for List 1 appeared to decrease substantially in the months following the imposition of tariffs, yet picked up towards the end of the year. Re-exports for List 2 were broadly at negative growth levels throughout the year, while growth for List 3 appeared broadly stable. Chart B3.2 Value of goods re-exported from the US via Hong Kong to Mainland China in 2018. Front-loading. As there is a time lag between the announcement and final implementation of tariffs (or simply due to the threat of tariffs), businesses may increase shipments of affected goods before the expected effective date of the tariffs. In fact, some data and news reports indicate that such front-loading behaviour was quite common. Some private sector analysts also believe such behaviour was part of the reason for the strong performance of overall trade figures before the imposition of tariffs. More granular trade data show that some signs of front-loading appeared for certain tariff list goods, but it seems to have only involved goods re-exported from Mainland China to the US (Chart B3.1). The re-export growth rates for List 1 and List 2 both rose in the months before their respective tariffs took effect. On the other hand, the growth rate of goods re-exported from the US via Hong Kong to Mainland China (Chart B3.2) showed no clear front-loading behaviour by businesses. Hong Kong re-exports not affected by tariffs. It is worth noting that Hong Kong re-exports (by value) directly affected by tariffs accounted for only about 4% to 5% of total Hong Kong re-exports. To gain a more complete understanding of Hong Kong's trade performance, we should also examine re-exports not affected by tariffs. We find that re-exports not affected by tariffs recorded negative growth in the last two months of 2018 (Chart B3.3). In addition, the growth of tariff-affected re-exports (red line) has fallen significantly more since the third quarter, reflecting the significant impact of the tariffs. The slowdown in the growth of re-exports not affected by tariffs partly reflects a broader weakening in external demand. As trade tensions continue to cause increased uncertainties, global financing conditions tighten, and geopolitical risks rise, external demand could come under broader pressure. In particular, the trade conflict has weighed on global economic sentiment and activity, as reflected in the adjustments in major equity markets. Import demand in other economies has consequently been dragged down, dampening the performance of Hong Kong's external trade. Chart B3.3 Value of Hong Kong's re-exports in 2018. Even if the China-US trade tensions ease, the near-term outlook for Hong Kong's merchandise trade remains challenging. Global growth may slow in 2019 (see Chapter 2), which is set to further dampen Hong Kong's export performance. Various business sentiment indicators show that both large and small businesses are pessimistic about their business outlook (Chart B3.4), with business sentiment in the trade sector being particularly subdued. Other trade-related sectors such as logistics may also be affected. Chart B3.4 Business outlook survey of Hong Kong's import and export sectors.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened in September and November, partly reflecting tighter liquidity brought about by expected seasonal funding demand, which led to the unwinding of carry trade positions. Entering 2019, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually softened, partly due to corporations repatriating funds raised from new share offerings and the market rebuilding carry trade positions, and triggered the weak-side CU in March. Nevertheless, Hong Kong dollar trading remained smooth and orderly. HIBORs generally rose in the second half of 2018, reflecting expectations of US interest rate hikes and seasonal funding demand, before easing in January 2019. Looking ahead, in the face of uncertainties such as ongoing US-China trade tensions, Brexit negotiations, and the pace of US monetary policy normalisation becoming more difficult to predict, HKD fund flows may become more volatile. Should the interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar remain wide, market carry trade activities may persist, causing the Hong Kong dollar to stay on the weak side for some time and possibly triggering the weak-side CU again, which is consistent with the design of the LERS. Following the triggering of the weak-side CU in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate deviated from 7.8500 and fluctuated between 7.8062 and 7.8499, until the Hong Kong dollar triggered the weak-side CU again a total of 4 times by March 2019 (as of 19 March) (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate rose briefly in September, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trade positions amid tighter liquidity, but subsequently declined gradually in October. The Hong Kong dollar stabilised again after November, due to tighter liquidity brought about by year-end funding demand, which led to the unwinding of carry trade positions. Entering 2019, the spot exchange rate weakened, partly reflecting corporations repatriating funds raised from new share offerings and the market rebuilding carry trade positions. As the Hong Kong dollar-US dollar interest rate differential widened after the year-end, this triggered market participants to buy US dollars and sell Hong Kong dollars for carry trade activities, driving the Hong Kong dollar to gradually weaken, and the weak-side CU was triggered again in March. Despite the triggering of the weak-side CU, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. The Aggregate Balance has been maintained at around HK$76 billion since August (Chart 4.2), and after the weak-side CU was triggered in March, it declined slightly to HK$70.9 billion (as of 19 March). The HKD funds that have flowed out since April 2018 account for only a small portion of the approximately HK$1 trillion that has flowed in since 2008. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Fund flow indicators The nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar broadly followed the movements of the US dollar and continued to rise during the review period (Chart 4.3). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was very small and thus had limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index, the trend of the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index broadly followed the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates The latest balance of payments statistics show that portfolio investment continued to record outflows in the third quarter of 2018. Amid weak market sentiment and increased volatility in the equity markets, outflows of equity portfolio investment by local residents accelerated, more than offsetting the portfolio investment inflows of non-local residents in the third quarter (Table 4.A). In contrast, debt securities investment by both local and non-local residents recorded inflows in the third quarter. Looking ahead, in the face of uncertainties such as ongoing US-China trade tensions, Brexit negotiations, and the pace of US monetary policy normalisation becoming more difficult to predict, fund flow volatility may intensify. In addition, the significant negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar may stimulate carry trade activities, leading to fund outflow. Under the LERS, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may weaken and may trigger the weak-side CU again. Both fund outflow and the possible triggering of the weak-side CU are normal operations under the LERS. Despite the ongoing US interest rate normalisation process and the triggering of the weak-side CU multiple times between April and August, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2018. The HKD Monetary Base contracted slightly by 0.7% in the second half, standing at HK$1,632.9 billion at the end of 2018 (Chart 4.4). The contraction in the Monetary Base was mainly due to the triggering of the weak-side CU in August 2018, which caused the Aggregate Balance to decrease from HK$109.5 billion at the end of June 2018 to HK$76.4 billion at the end of 2018, while the Certificates of Indebtedness, government-issued notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes rose slightly. The HKD Monetary Base remained broadly stable in the first two months of 2019, with the Aggregate Balance showing no significant change since August. Subsequently, due to the triggering of the weak-side CU in March, the Aggregate Balance declined slightly to about HK$70.9 billion (as of 19 March). Chart 4.4 Components of the Monetary Base As for the broader Hong Kong dollar money supply indicators, money supply growth generally slowed in the second half, partly reflecting increased uncertainties in the macroeconomic and financial conditions. Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (HKD M3) grew by 3.6% in the first half but only edged up 0.1% in the second half (Chart 4.5). As the main component of HKD M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits changed little compared with the end of June (Chart 4.6). Among Hong Kong dollar deposits, demand deposits and savings deposits declined, partly due to reduced investment-related transactions in the second half; on the other hand, time deposits continued to record strong growth as deposit interest rates were raised. Analysis of the corresponding assets shows that HKD M3 growth slowed due to changes in banks' capital and reserves (recorded under "net other items"). Chart 4.5 HKD M3 and changes in its corresponding assets Foreign currency deposits grew at a faster pace in the second half. US dollar deposits grew strongly by 8.8% in the second half, becoming the main driver of foreign currency deposits growth as banks attracted more deposits after raising the preferential deposit interest rates on the US dollar (Chart 4.6). Other foreign currency deposits edged up 1.4% in the second half, with renminbi deposits continuing to record growth. Overall, total deposits of AIs grew moderately by 3.3% in the second half, slightly faster than the 1.6% increase in the first half. Chart 4.6 Deposit growth Despite the still-large HKD Monetary Base and deposit size, HKD interbank interest rates began to face some upward pressure in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting US interest rate hikes. Seasonal liquidity demand occasionally pushed up short-term interbank rates, causing the latter to be more volatile than long-term interbank rates (Chart 4.7). The 3-month and 12-month HIBORs averaged 2.32% and 2.74% respectively in December, about 30 basis points higher than the June averages. Entering 2019, HKD interbank interest rates generally declined as seasonal demand receded. The 3-month and 12-month HIBORs fell to averages of 1.65% and 2.39% respectively in February. Chart 4.7 HKD and USD interbank interest rates The Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted downward in the second half of 2018, broadly following the movements of the US dollar yield curve. Relative to the end of June 2018, the 3-year and 10-year Hong Kong government bond yields fell by 45 and 37 basis points respectively to 1.56% and 1.83% at the end of February 2019 (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8 Government bond yields, composite interest rate and average lending rate of new mortgages During the review period, the composite interest rate, which measures the average HKD funding cost of retail banks, rose slightly. Reflecting changes in interbank and deposit funding costs, the composite interest rate rose from 0.62% at the end of June to 0.89% at the end of December 2018, before easing to 0.83% at the end of January 2019 (Chart 4.8). Given the rising cost of funding, retail banks raised their Best Lending Rates by 12.5 to 25.0 basis points following the upward adjustment of the target range for the US federal funds rate in September. After the target range for the US federal funds rate was raised again in December, retail banks did not make further adjustments to the Best Lending Rates. On the other hand, the average lending rate of new mortgages rose in line with the Best Lending Rates, standing at about 2.45% at the end of January 2019. Looking ahead, the USD counterparts interest rate trajectory, fund flows, and local financial markets activities (such as new share subscription activities) will continue to be the main drivers of HKD interest rates. Given that the HKD Monetary Base remains large and the banking system holds a substantial amount of Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, as banks can use Exchange Fund Bills and Notes as collateral to borrow HKD funds through the Discount Window, the pace of increase in HKD interest rates should be relatively moderate. Against the backdrop of intensifying US-China trade tensions, the CNH and onshore renminbi exchange rates have depreciated against the US dollar since the beginning of 2018 (Chart 4.9). However, amid the optimism brought about by the resumption of high-level US-China trade talks, the CNH and onshore renminbi exchange rates stabilised in November. Meanwhile, the spread between the onshore renminbi and the CNH was not significant during the review period. Chart 4.9 Onshore and CNH exchange rates At present, the ongoing US-China trade tensions have not yet had a significant impact on the Funding positions in the offshore interbank market. As liquidity conditions remained broadly stable, the overnight CNH HIBOR was below 4% for most of the review period, rising only occasionally due to seasonal factors (Chart 4.10). The 3-month CNH interbank rate hovered around 4% between September and December 2018, before falling to 3.02% at the end of February 2019, which may reflect the recent monetary easing measures introduced by the PBoC. Nevertheless, it remains to be seen how the progress of the US-China trade talks will affect the liquidity of the CNH interbank market in 2019. Chart 4.10 Overnight and 3-month CNH HIBOR fixings Hong Kong's CNH liquidity pool expanded steadily in the second half of 2018. The balance of RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit grew slightly faster than the 2.6% increase in the first half, rising by 3.7% in the second half to RMB657.7 billion at the end of 2018 (Chart 4.11 and Table 4.B). This was mainly driven by RMB customer deposits, which grew by 4.5% in the first half and recorded 5.2% growth in the second half. Among these, corporate customer deposits grew faster than personal customer deposits. However, the balance of certificates of deposit fell further by 14.1% in the second half, mainly due to reduced issuance of certificates of deposit and a relatively larger amount of certificates of deposit maturing in October.

Benefiting mainly from an increase in net interest income, the profitability of retail banks continued to improve in the second half of 2018 compared with the same period in 2017. Their capital and liquidity positions also remained robust. Reflecting the upward pressure on HKD interbank interest rates and retail deposit rates arising from the normalization of US interest rates, the overall HKD funding cost of retail banks rose notably, but remained at a relatively low level. Amid an uncertain external environment, bank credit contracted moderately in the second half of 2018. Nevertheless, credit growth has shown signs of stabilization since November, and asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will face multiple headwinds due to the persistent uncertainty surrounding China-US trade relations, the global economic slowdown, the uncertain pace of the US monetary policy tightening cycle, and geopolitical risks. Given the continuing rise in corporate leverage, banks should remain vigilant about the impact on their credit risk relating to corporate loans should the external environment deteriorate further.  Retail banks' overall pre-tax operating profit grew by 14.3% compared with the same period in 2017, while the return on assets also rose from 1.14% to 1.23% (Chart 5.1). This strong performance was mainly driven by a substantial increase in net interest income, which was sufficient to offset the increases in loan impairment provisions and operating expenses. For 2018 as a whole, retail banks' overall pre-tax operating profit grew by 19.4%, while the return on assets rose from 1.16% in 2017 to 1.27%. Chart 5.1 Retail banks' profitability. Retail banks' net interest margin widened further in the fourth quarter to 1.67%, compared with 1.5% in the same period a year earlier (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Retail banks' net interest margin. Broadly reflecting further US interest rate hikes and the decline in interbank HKD liquidity following the triggering of the weak-side CU in August 2018, Hong Kong banks' interbank funding costs continued to face upward pressure in the second half of 2018. Specifically, the 3-month HIBOR rose by 23 basis points in the second half of 2018 (Chart 5.3). As banks generally raised time deposit rates to secure long-term stable funding, HKD retail deposit rates also rose during the review period. In addition, following the US interest rate hike decision at the end of September, banks raised their Best Lending Rates and correspondingly increased their savings deposits rates. Given the rise in both wholesale and retail funding costs, the composite interest rate (a measure of the average cost of HKD funds of retail banks) rose from 0.62% in June 2018 to 0.89% in December, but remained at a relatively low level by historical standards. Chart 5.3 Interest rates. (a) Period-end figures. (b) Period average figures of newly approved loans.  At a broader level, the overall HKD and USD funding costs of Hong Kong's licensed banks continued to show an upward trend. In the second half of 2018, banks' average overall HKD and USD funding costs rose by 36 basis points, compared with a rise of 40 basis points in the first half (the red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 HKD and USD funding costs and maturities of licensed banks. The cumulative increase in HIBORs outpaced the rise in Hong Kong banks' overall funding costs, which may have a positive impact on retail banks' HIBOR-based mortgage loans, a type of loan that the industry has also actively promoted in the past few years. However, the improvement in the net interest margin may become more limited in the future, as most HIBOR-based mortgage loans have already reached the capped rate benchmarked against the Best Lending Rates. As the timing of future increases in the Best Lending Rates remains unclear, amid the normalization of US interest rates, the continuing upward trend in banks' funding costs may weigh on the overall net interest margin. Looking ahead, increased uncertainty in the external environment may cloud banks' earnings outlook. In particular, against the backdrop of slowing global economic growth, the persistent uncertainty surrounding China-US trade relations may dampen business confidence and reduce demand for bank credit. Should this lead to a significant decline in loans and a deterioration in asset quality, it may weigh on banks' profitability.  The capital base of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong, well above international minimum standards. At the end of 2018, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions rose further to 20.3% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 17.9%, of which 16.0% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital. Chart 5.5 Capital base of locally incorporated authorized institutions. 1. Consolidated position. 2. From 1 January 2013, locally incorporated authorized institutions were required to comply with the revised capital framework under Basel III. Therefore, capital ratios from March 2013 onwards are not directly comparable with the figures up to December 2012. In addition to the risk-based capital adequacy ratio, Basel III also introduced a non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement to limit excessive leverage in the banking system. The minimum leverage ratio requirement took effect in Hong Kong in 2018, and the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a robust level of 8.0% at the end of December 2018, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions.  Measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions rose from 156.6% in the second quarter of 2018 to 167.6% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the 90% statutory minimum requirement applicable in 2018. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions also rose from 51.3% in the second quarter to 54.3% in the fourth quarter, also well above the 25% statutory minimum requirement. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio. 1. Consolidated position. 2. Quarterly average figures. The Net Stable Funding Ratio, one of the liquidity standards under Basel III, indicates that the funding position of authorized institutions was stable. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 135.6% in the fourth quarter of 2018 (Chart 5.8), well above the 100% statutory minimum requirement. The average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.3%, also exceeding the 50% statutory minimum requirement applicable in 2018. The ample liquidity and sound funding position of authorized institutions indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is able to withstand various liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio.  Customer deposits remained the primary source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting the banking system's stable funding structure. At the end of 2018, the proportion of customer deposits to the total liabilities of all authorized institutions rose slightly from 54.5% six months earlier to 55.7% (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all authorized institutions. 1. Due to rounding, figures may not add up to the total. 2. Figures refer to the percentage of total liabilities (including capital and reserves). 3. Debt securities include negotiable certificates of deposit and all other negotiable debt instruments. As total loans and advances declined during the second half of 2018 while total deposits increased over the same period, the loan-to-deposit ratio in all currencies of all authorized institutions fell from 75.7% at the end of June 2018 to 72.6% at the end of the year (Chart 5.10). Similarly, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions fell from 65.2% to 58.3% over the same period. In contrast, as the growth in HKD deposits was much lower than that of HKD loans, the HKD loan-to-deposit ratio rose slightly from 85.4% at the end of June 2018 to 86.9% at the end of the year. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratios of all authorized institutions.  The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks declined slightly in the second half of 2018. We estimate that, under an assumed shock of an across-the-board 200-basis-point rise in interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of the interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks would be equivalent to 2.44% of their total capital base at the end of 2018 (Chart 5.11). Nevertheless, given that the pace of further US interest rate hikes is unclear, banks should closely monitor their interest rate risk management.
