Interest rate shock refers to the impact of a standardized 200-basis-point parallel interest rate shock on institutions' interest rate risk exposure. 2. The impact of the interest rate shock refers to the impact on the economic value of the banking book and trading book, expressed as a percentage of the banks' total capital base.  Against the backdrop of persistent uncertainty over the China-US trade conflict, tightening global financial liquidity, and slowing global economic growth, credit growth slowed markedly in the second half of 2018. However, credit growth has shown signs of stabilization since November 2018. On a half-yearly basis, total loans and advances of all authorized institutions fell by 0.9% in the second half of 2018, after rising by 5.3% in the first half (Chart 5.12). This decline was attributable to the slowdown in the growth of domestic loans (including loans and trade finance used within Hong Kong) and the decline in loans for use outside Hong Kong. The growth of domestic loans slowed to 0.1% in the second half, while loans for use outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.0% over the same period, compared with growth of 5.3% and 5.2% respectively in the first six months. For 2018 as a whole, the growth rate of total loans slowed markedly from 16.1% in 2017 to 4.4%. Chart 5.12 Loan growth.  Looking ahead, credit demand may remain weak in the near term. The HKMA's Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook in December 2018 showed that, among all the authorized institutions surveyed, 82% expected loan demand to remain unchanged over the next three months, while the proportion of authorized institutions expecting a decline in demand rose to 18% (Table 5.A). Although total loans declined slightly in the second half of 2018, the asset quality of banks' loan portfolios remained sound. The gross CLR and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans of all authorized institutions edged down to 0.55% and 0.36% respectively at the end of December 2018, compared with 0.61% and 0.40% respectively at the end of June 2018. For retail banks, the gross CLR declined slightly to 0.50%, while the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans rose slightly to 0.32% (Chart 5.13). Both ratios were at low levels by historical standards. Chart 5.13 Asset quality of retail banks. 1. Classified loans refer to loans classified as "substandard", "doubtful" or "loss". 2. Figures before December 2015 reflect the position of the Hong Kong offices and overseas branches of retail banks. From December 2015, the coverage of the figures was expanded to include the major overseas subsidiaries of retail banks.  On a half-yearly basis, the growth of personal loans slowed from 5.3% in the first half of 2018 to 3.9% in the second half. This was mainly due to the slowdown in the growth of private loans (including credit card advances and other loans for private purposes), which offset the rapid growth of residential mortgage loans (Table 5.B). As Hong Kong's nominal GDP grew at a slower pace than personal loans, the household debt-to-GDP ratio rose slightly from 71.2% in the second quarter of 2018 to 71.9% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.14).

The coronavirus pandemic that erupted since early 2020 has simultaneously dealt blows to both demand and supply, posing challenges to the global economy that differ from those of previous crises. Although major central banks and some governments have rolled out stimulus measures since early March to arrest the economic shocks brought about by the pandemic, financial markets remained volatile and global financing conditions also tightened. Despite the uncertainties in the external and local environments, Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and orderly. Against the backdrop of a stronger Hong Kong dollar exchange rate, a stable Aggregate Balance, and moderate growth in total deposits, no significant outflow of funds from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system was observed during the review period. After a moderate rebound in the first half of 2019, the growth in total loans slowed in the second half. The residential property market has generally softened since mid-2019, though its trend has been somewhat volatile. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face a number of downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, future China-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social incidents. Given the persistent rise in corporate leverage levels and personal debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should these risk factors intensify. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, global economic growth has shown initial signs of stabilisation, benefiting from major central banks stepping up their policy-easing efforts, the easing of China-US trade tensions, and the diminished risk of a "no-deal Brexit" in the UK. However, since late January, the increasing number of global coronavirus infection cases has raised market concerns and triggered sharp volatility in global financial markets. To address the evolving risks of the pandemic, several major central banks substantially cut interest rates and enhanced liquidity tools, while some governments also introduced targeted measures to support the real economy. Nevertheless, amid rising credit spreads and plunging stock markets, global financing conditions tightened. Looking ahead, the downside risks to the global economic outlook have increased. The coronavirus pandemic will hit global economic activity, and the extent of the economic impact will depend on the severity and persistence of the pandemic. In the medium term, relations between the US and its major trading partners may once again become tense, while post-Brexit trade negotiations between the UK and the EU may prove difficult. Weak global demand continued to weigh on economic growth in East Asia1. Exports from the East Asian region to major destinations such as the US, European economies, and Mainland China remained weak in the second half of 2019. Some major telecommunications equipment exporters in the region recently reported growth in their earnings, but whether the technology product cycle will rebound broadly remains to be seen. Financial markets reacted positively to the China-US Phase One trade agreement announced in December 2019, and the trade truce reduced uncertainties in global trade to some extent. Even so, the East Asian region will continue to face adverse factors such as weak firms’ earnings and high private sector leverage ratios. Meanwhile, the outbreak of the coronavirus has raised concerns that the region's economy may come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. Travel bans imposed by several economies in the region may hit Asia's tourism industry, especially those more reliant on tourism service exports. As the region's supply chains are closely linked with those of Mainland China, the manufacturing sector may also be affected by the outbreak. As for Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 due to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the China-US Phase One trade agreement helped to temporarily reduce the external uncertainties facing the Mainland economy, downward pressures remained in the face of the coronavirus outbreak, the ongoing economic rebalancing, and the global economic slowdown. The Central Economic Work Conference held in December 2019 set economic stabilisation as a priority for 2020, while also emphasising the control of financial risks. The latest consensus forecasts indicate that the Mainland's economic growth will slow to 5.2% in 2020. During the review period, the Mainland authorities continued to announce targeted monetary and fiscal policies to support the private sector, especially small private enterprises. Despite the relevant measures, some media reports and market analysts pointed out that private industrial enterprises may have faced a decline in shareholders' equity in recent years, which was seen as a sign of "the retreat of the private sector." Box 2 studies the driving factors behind equity changes at Mainland industrial enterprises using 2018 listed corporates data, and finds that private enterprises or small enterprises are not intrinsically more susceptible to downsizing or "retreat." While the study finds that negative earnings are the largest driving factor, other factors, especially structural factors, are also worth noting (see Box 2 for details). Local economic activity contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. Real GDP declined continuously over the past three quarters, indicating that the local economy has entered recession. Weighed down by this, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the whole of 2019, worse than the 2.9% growth in 2018 and the first annual contraction since 2009. The slowdown in local demand, especially the contraction in private consumption, was the main factor dragging down GDP in the second half of 2019. Local social incidents severely affected consumption activity, resulting in a weak economic outlook, which in turn dampened consumer and business sentiment. With the renewed escalation of China-US trade frictions, the slowdown in global economic growth, and the severe downturn in inbound tourism, Hong Kong's external trade performance continued to be sluggish. Given that the economy is facing significant headwinds, the government rolled out several rounds of economic stimulus measures between August and December 2019. To give banks greater room to step up support for the local economy and to help mitigate the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on 14 October a reduction in banks' countercyclical capital buffer ratio from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby releasing an additional HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion in lending capacity for enterprises, especially small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). The economic performance in 2020 is expected to face very significant challenges, and the pandemic has also recently introduced notable downside risks. As sectors such as retail, accommodation services, food services, tourism, and transport have yet to recover from the damage caused by the social incidents, the pandemic will deal a double blow to these sectors. However, a series of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget can provide assistance to households and enterprises (especially SMEs), including a one-off cash payout to adult permanent residents and concessionary low-interest loans with a 100% government guarantee for enterprises under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme."2 On 16 March 2020, the HKMA further reduced banks' countercyclical capital buffer ratio from 2.0% to 1.0%, which will give banks greater room to step up support for the local economy, especially sectors and individuals that are under greater short-term pressure due to the impact of the pandemic. Analysed by GDP components, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak due to fragile consumer and business sentiment. Although government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to be relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. On the external front, the China-US Phase One trade agreement is expected to have a slightly positive impact on the local economy in the short term.3 However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong's external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may cause disruptions to supply chains in the region and slow cross-border economic activity (such as tourism), thereby limiting Hong Kong's export performance. The government forecasts that real GDP growth in 2020 will range between -1.5% and 0.5%, while the average growth forecast of international institutions and private sector analysts is -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is affected by numerous uncertainties and risks such as the slowdown in global economic growth, China-US trade relations, Mainland China's economic performance, and local social incidents. The labour market faced greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020, with total employment declining, the unemployment rate rising, and the real wage index also falling year-on-year. Specifically, the unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.7% in February 2020, partly reflecting the impact of the social incidents and the pandemic outbreak on the retail, accommodation, and food service sectors. Looking ahead, given the weak economic outlook and the coronavirus outbreak, the unemployment rate will climb further. Box 3 will explore the recent developments and short-term outlook of the labour market in greater detail. Local inflationary pressures continued to build up to the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to the impact of rising fresh pork prices; subsequently, economic activity weakened and inflation momentum gradually slowed. Due to weak economic conditions, the consolidation of private residential rentals, and moderate import inflation, inflation is expected to ease in the short term. Market consensus forecasts indicate that headline inflation in 2020 will range between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the government forecasts underlying inflation at 2.5%. Supported by increased equity-related demand for the Hong Kong dollar (including IPOs), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually strengthened since mid-October 2019. Entering December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened further, partly due to buoyant IPO activity and partly due to the tightening of liquidity towards year-end prompting the unwinding of Hong Kong dollar short positions. After the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased somewhat, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened slightly towards the end of February. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly during the review period, and the CUs were not triggered. The Aggregate Balance remained stable at around HK$54 billion. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, short-term HKD interbank interest rates have been volatile, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand as well as increased capital market activity such as IPOs. Box 4 studies how market attention to future IPO activity affects the 3-month HIBORs. Meanwhile, the composite interest rate gradually rose from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020, reflecting banks' continued increases in preferential deposit rates to attract deposit funds. As some banks raised the rate caps set with reference to the Best Lending Rates, the average lending rate for new mortgages rose to around 2.6% in October, but as the Best Lending Rates in the market were lowered from November onwards, the average lending rate for new mortgages fell slightly to around 2.5% by January 2020. Against the backdrop of a stronger Hong Kong dollar exchange rate, a stable Aggregate Balance, and moderate growth in total deposits, no significant outflow of funds from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system was observed during the review period. However, we need to monitor the impact should the coronavirus pandemic deteriorate further amid the uncertain external environment. With ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system, the HKMA has the ability, resources, and determination to cope with capital outflows and to maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. During the review period, on market expectations of a China-US trade agreement, both the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates strengthened, but faced weakening pressure since late January 2020 due to the coronavirus outbreak. In the latter part of 2019, the CNH generally traded at a premium to the onshore renminbi, and the discount briefly widened at the end of January 2020, but the spread remained moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong's CNH liquidity pool rebounded slightly after edging down in the previous review period. As at the end of January 2020, RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit balances increased to RMB637.4 billion. Other renminbi business in Hong Kong also grew, with local renminbi bank loans and RMB trade settlements recording strong growth. The average daily turnover of the RMB RTGS system for the whole of 2019 remained at a high level of RMB1,133.9 billion. Despite the uncertainties in the external environment, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the continued opening up of the Mainland's capital account, increased allocation of renminbi assets by international investors, and the deepening of regional economic and financial cooperation under the "Belt and Road" and "Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area" initiatives.

Towards the end of 2019, global economic activity showed signs of stabilisation, raising market hopes for a global economic recovery. However, since late January 2020, the continuous rise in coronavirus infection cases globally has dashed hopes of a recovery, deepening investors' concerns about a global economic recession and triggering a sell-off in global financial markets. To address the economic shock, major central banks and some governments have rolled out stimulus measures since early March. In view of the spread of the epidemic, downside risks to the outlook for global economic growth have increased. In East Asia, weak global demand since the second half of 2019 has cast a shadow over the outlook of economies in the region. The coronavirus outbreak is expected to weigh on economic growth in the region in the near term, with the tourism industry being particularly hard hit. On the other hand, the East Asian region also continues to face the challenges of weak corporate profitability and high private-sector leverage ratios. As for Mainland China, economic growth in the second half of 2019 continued to slow amid weak domestic demand and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US helps temporarily reduce external uncertainties, downward pressures persist in the face of the coronavirus outbreak, ongoing economic rebalancing, and the impact of the global economic slowdown, while the monetary and fiscal policy responses adopted by the authorities will provide some cushion. Amid persistent trade tensions and policy uncertainty, manufacturing and investment remained sluggish, and global economic growth was still weak in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, economic growth showed preliminary signs of stabilisation at the start of the last quarter (Chart 2.1), partly benefiting from the earlier policy easing by the Fed and the ECB, as well as the easing of global trade tensions following the signing of the "Phase One" trade agreement between China and the US. Chart 2.1 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index. However, since late January, the continuous increase in coronavirus infection cases globally, and the subsequent shock to the economy, have raised market concerns, resulting in a sell-off wave in global financial markets (Chart 2.2). Given that Mainland China is a major global export destination and holds an important position in the global supply chain, when the epidemic disrupts production activities on the Mainland and drags down its economic growth, it will cause significant spillover effects that may spread across the globe (Chart 2.3). Since late February, the surge of coronavirus infection cases in regions outside Mainland China may exacerbate the disruptions to the supply chain and pose risks of directly dragging down local economic activity. 5 Chart 2.2 MSCI All Country World Index and the Bloomberg Barclays Global Corporate Bond Index Option-Adjusted Spread. Chart 2.3 Exports of goods and services to Mainland China by selected major advanced economies in 2018 (as a percentage of their GDP). To address the potentially severe economic shock that the epidemic may cause, some central banks (including the Fed, the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England) have cut interest rates since early March, while some governments have also introduced targeted measures to support households and businesses. However, financial markets still face enormous sell-off pressure, leading to a significant tightening of global financing conditions, which may in turn exacerbate the downward pressures on the global economy (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Bloomberg Advanced Economies Financial Conditions Index. Apart from developments in the epidemic, other downside risks and uncertainties also loom over the global economic outlook. In particular, on the trade tensions front, although policy risks have declined following the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US, subsequent negotiations may be fraught with difficulties as many thorny structural issues remain to be resolved. In Europe, trade negotiations between the EU and the UK are not expected to go smoothly, thereby prolonging the uncertainties following Brexit. In addition, oil prices have plunged sharply since March, which will put pressure on major oil-exporting emerging market economies. In East Asia, real economic activity remained sluggish in the second half of 2019 due to weak global demand. Exports from the East Asian region to various major destinations such as the United States, European economies and Mainland China remained weak in the second half of 2019 (Chart 2.5). Although there are preliminary signs that the downturn cycle of technology products in the region is bottoming out and rebounding, including reports by large electronics companies in the region of improved profitability at the end of 2019, 6 whether there is a substantive rebound in technology product exports in the region remains to be seen. Chart 2.5 East Asia: Merchandise exports to major destinations. Sustained weak economic growth and trade uncertainties have also weighed on investor sentiment, with gross fixed capital investment in most East Asian economies declining in 2019 (Chart 2.6), which may affect the region's potential economic growth in the long run. To support economic growth in an environment of moderate inflation, after cutting interest rates in the first half of 2019, the central banks of Indonesia, the Philippines and South Korea lowered their policy rate again in the second half of the year, while the Bank of Thailand also lowered its policy rate for the first time since 2015. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Gross fixed capital formation. The coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that economies in the region may come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. As many economies in the region have imposed entry and exit restrictions on Mainland China, the tourism industry has borne the brunt, with economies that are more reliant on Mainland Chinese tourists and tourism service exports being more heavily affected by this epidemic (Chart 2.7). A persistent and intensifying epidemic would also affect supply chains in the region that are closely linked to Mainland China. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Tourism exports and Chinese tourists. In the near term, this epidemic will continue to affect economic activity and investor sentiment. Drawing on the experience of the 2003 SARS outbreak, these effects may be transient, but the actual situation will depend on the severity and spread of the epidemic, as well as the effectiveness of government actions to contain the outbreak. Meanwhile, East Asian economies also face multiple headwinds. First, although the market expects corporate profitability to deteriorate in the near term (Chart 2.8), accommodative global monetary conditions have encouraged yield-seeking activities, thereby pushing up asset prices without fundamental support. As a result, equity markets in the region are more susceptible to shifts in investor sentiment. Chart 2.8 Expected earnings of constituent stocks in benchmark equity indices. Second, weak corporate profitability and economic growth may make it more difficult for private institutions in the region to repay their debts. Although declining local interest rates can provide breathing room for indebted companies and households, they may also plant the seeds for further debt accumulation. Moreover, as described in Box 1, when more index-tracking funds flow into the region's financial markets, the risk of debt overhang for private institutions may also be exacerbated, although this impact may be limited to companies with sound financial fundamentals and their long-term borrowings. Third, in terms of external factors, in the face of an increasingly hardline US trade policy on protective barriers, the risks faced by East Asian economies may also increase. Despite the recent progress on the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US, trade tensions between the two countries persist as fundamental trade issues between them remain. As the net trade surplus of many economies in the region with the United States continues to increase (Chart 2.9), it can be seen that multinational companies, in order to avoid tariffs, may continue to seek more supply channels outside the China-centred supply chain. As of November 2019, the cumulative net trade of nine emerging Asian economies (excluding China) with the United States had increased to about US$167 billion in US dollar terms. If the net trade with the United States continues to expand, the relevant Asian economies may become the next targets of trade conflicts; for example, the US government imposed tariffs of up to 456% on steel imports from Vietnam in July 2019. 7 In view of this, despite the trade truce between China and the US, the trade outlook for the region remains highly uncertain. Chart 2.9 Net trade of goods with the United States. Over the past decade, the intensified integration of international financial markets has led to a significant increase in global cross-border portfolio investment flows. A recent study shows that up to 70% of these cross-border investment flows are driven by index-driven funds. 8 Index-driven funds include not only funds that closely track investment indices (commonly referred to as passive funds), but also funds that are actively managed with reference to investment indices. 9 By introducing overseas investors that the relevant economies would otherwise be unable to attract or reach, these funds help promote the development of financial markets in emerging market economies. Thus, such funds enable emerging market economies to diversify their investor base, which helps the long-term growth and stability of the markets. However, is there really such a thing as a free lunch? In the case of passive bond funds, there are market concerns that investment by such funds may weaken the fiscal discipline of the corporate bond issuers they invest in, thereby leading to high leverage levels among the relevant companies. 10 In addition, some hold the view that the growth of index-driven funds in recent years has intensified the volatility of global portfolio investment flows, making emerging market economies—which are already highly sensitive to global factors and affected by other common factors—even more vulnerable. 11 This Box assesses the impact of index-driven investment on financial stability with regard to these two propositions. Passive bond funds allocate their investment funds to the relevant bonds according to the weight of the constituent bonds within the benchmark index. Therefore, compared with actively managed bond funds, the mechanical investment decisions adopted by passive bond funds may leave the issuers of index-constituent bonds lacking the incentive to act in the interest of the fund's investors. 13 Worse still, from a financial stability perspective, such behaviour may encourage excessive borrowing, posing significant risks to credit and debt repayment abilities in the corporate sector of emerging market economies, whose leverage ratios have risen sharply since the global financial crisis (Chart B1.1). Chart B1.1 Corporate leverage in emerging market economies. Using the weight of emerging market economy companies within a mainstream index that tracks emerging market economy corporate bonds as a proxy for the extent to which their bonds are invested in by passive bond funds, 14 we find that an increase in such investment will push up the long-term (rather than short-term) leverage ratio of the corporate issuers of the relevant bonds. The solid blue bars in Chart B1.2 represent the estimated impact. In addition to promoting the development of the corporate bond market in emerging market economies, the broadening of the long-term bond investor base brought about by passive bond funds is also conducive to the development of companies in emerging market economies. We also find that the above effect only has a significant impact on emerging market economy companies with sounder fundamentals (in particular, stronger debt repayment abilities and lower leverage ratios) (the solid green bars in Chart B1.2). Facing higher financial distress costs, highly leveraged companies or those with weaker debt repayment abilities do not appear to fall further into a debt trap as a result of investment by passive bond funds. In summary, the above study shows that the growth of passive bond fund investment may not necessarily significantly increase the risks to debt repayment abilities in the corporate sector of emerging market economies.

Owing to weaker private consumption, reduced investment spending, and lacklustre export performance, the Hong Kong economy contracted in the second half of 2019 and entered its first recession since 2009. Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face considerable challenges, and the coronavirus outbreak has recently posed significant downside risks. The economic outlook is being affected by numerous uncertainties and risks, including slowing global economic growth, China-US trade relations, the economic performance of Mainland China, and the development of local social incidents. Given the various headwinds facing the economy, the unemployment rate is likely to climb further in 2020. Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease somewhat, though the outlook faces potential risks on both the upside and downside. The Hong Kong economy contracted markedly in the second half of 2019. On a year-on-year basis, real GDP contracted by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters respectively (Table 3.A). Dragged down by the economic contraction in the second half, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the year as a whole, worse than the 2.9% growth in 2018, and marking the first annual contraction since the global financial crisis of 2009. Chart 3.1 Real GDP Growth Rate and Contributions of Major Expenditure Components On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activity slowed markedly in the second half (Chart 3.1). Specifically, real GDP fell by 0.4%, 3.0%, and 0.3% in the second, third, and fourth quarters respectively, indicating that the economy had entered a recession. On the domestic front, private consumption was the main factor dragging down GDP in the third quarter. Local social incidents seriously affected consumption activity, thereby weakening the economic outlook and undermining consumer confidence, so private consumption contracted markedly from the third quarter. 33 Owing to increased economic uncertainties and worsening business sentiment, total investment spending remained weak and dragged down GDP in the fourth quarter. 34 On the external front, as China-US trade tensions intensified, global economic growth weakened, and visitor arrivals plummeted, Hong Kong's external trade performance remained sluggish (Chart 3.2). 35 Under the impact of the sharp contraction in exports of services, net exports dragged down GDP in the third quarter, but supported GDP growth in the fourth quarter, partly reflecting an improvement in the merchandise trade balance. Chart 3.2 Real Imports and Exports Given the significant headwinds facing the economy, the Government introduced multiple rounds of measures between August and December 2019 to ease the financial burden on citizens, safeguard employment, and support enterprises, in particular small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and severely hit sectors such as retail, food services, transport, and tourism. 36 To provide banks with greater room to step up their support for the local economy and help smooth the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on 14 October a reduction of the banks' countercyclical capital buffer ratio from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional lending capacity of HKD 200 billion to 300 billion to enterprises, including SMEs. Economic performance in Hong Kong in 2020 is expected to face considerable challenges, and the outbreak has recently posed significant downside risks. As some sectors have yet to recover from the damage caused by the social incidents, the outbreak will deal a double blow to these sectors. Nevertheless, a series of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget can provide assistance to households and enterprises (in particular SMEs), including the distribution of a one-off cash payout to adult permanent residents and the provision of special concessionary low-interest loans with 100% government guarantee to enterprises under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. 37 On 16 March 2020, the HKMA further reduced the banks' countercyclical capital buffer ratio from 2.0% to 1.0%, which will provide banks with greater room to step up their support for the local economy, particularly for sectors and individuals under greater pressure in the short term due to the impact of the outbreak. Analysing by GDP components, given fragile consumption and business sentiment, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak. While government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to be relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. On the external front, the first-phase China-US trade agreement is expected to have a slight positive impact on the local economy in the short term. 38 However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong's external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may cause disruptions and breakdowns in the regional supply chain and a slowdown in cross-border economic activities (such as tourism), thereby constraining Hong Kong's export performance. The Government forecasts real GDP growth in 2020 to range between -1.5% and 0.5%, while the average growth forecast by international institutions and private-sector analysts is -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is affected by the numerous uncertainties and risks described in the preceding chapters. The labour market faced greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.3% in December 2019, and climbed further to 3.7% in February 2020 (Chart 3.3). Among these, the unemployment rate in the retail, accommodation, and food services sectors rose to a near-decade high of 6.1%, partly reflecting the heavy blow caused by the social incidents. 39 As economic momentum weakened, total employment fell by 0.5% year-on-year in the second half of 2019 and continued to decline to 3,768,800 in February 2020. Of these, the decline in employment mainly came from the trade, wholesale, retail, accommodation, food services, and construction sectors. Real wages also fell by 0.3% year-on-year in the third quarter. Looking ahead, in view of the weak economic outlook described above, the labour market will continue to face more challenges, and the unemployment rate is very likely to climb further. Box 3 will explore in greater detail the recent developments and short-term outlook of the labour market. Chart 3.3 Labour Market Conditions Local inflationary pressures continued to build up until the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to the impact of rising fresh pork prices; subsequently, as economic activity weakened, inflation momentum gradually slowed. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying composite consumer price index grew by 3.3% in the third quarter, while the increase slowed slightly to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. The annualised three-month underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also softened from a high of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The slowing of inflation momentum was due to reduced price pressures on various consumer price index components. In terms of tradable goods, rising fresh pork prices kept underlying food inflation notable, though price pressures on consumer goods such as clothing and footwear and on durable goods remained mild. In terms of services, as the growth in newly signed residential rentals earlier slowed, the growth of the rental component of the consumer price index also showed a downward trend (Chart 3.5). Labour cost pressures rose slightly, but remained at a mild level in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4 Different Indicators Reflecting Consumer Price Inflation Chart 3.5 Rental Component of the Composite Consumer Price Index and Market Rentals Chart 3.6 Unit Labour Cost Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease somewhat in the short term. On the domestic front, weak economic conditions and a widening negative output gap will continue to constitute downward pressures on local inflation. As residential rentals continue to slow, the housing rental component of inflation should ease further. On the external front, imported inflation is expected to remain mild due to weak global economic growth and soft energy prices. Market consensus forecasts point to a headline inflation rate ranging between 0.6% and 3.7% in 2020, while the Government forecasts an underlying inflation of 2.5% and a headline inflation of 1.7%. This inflation outlook is affected by risk factors on both the upside and downside. On the one hand, given that the estimated negative output gap has widened since the third quarter of 2019, if the economy deteriorates more severely than expected (for example, due to a prolonged coronavirus outbreak), inflation may be further suppressed. On the other hand, if the disruption to fresh pork supply becomes more severe, it will bring upward pressure on inflation. Despite the marked slowdown in the Hong Kong economy, the unemployment rate remained at a low level of 2.8-2.9% in the first nine months of 2019. It was only as the social incidents persisted that the unemployment rate climbed more noticeably to 3.3% at the end of 2019. Affected by the coronavirus outbreak, the labour market will face greater headwinds in 2020. Against this backdrop, this box analyses the recent developments and short-term outlook of the labour market, including exploring why the overall labour market was broadly resilient (with the unemployment rate barely changing) in the first three quarters of 2019, and what implications this has for future developments. This article also examines some of the risk factors that could lead to a sharp rise in the unemployment rate. It is worth noting that, partly because adjusting labour demand entails costs, the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator. In fact, the unemployment rate tends to lag the year-on-year growth of real GDP by about two to three quarters (Chart B3.1). This lagging nature can explain why, when real economic activity deteriorated sharply in the third quarter, the unemployment rate remained low at around 2.9%. Chart B3.1 Real GDP Growth Rate and Unemployment Rate In terms of labour demand, although the China-US trade tensions and local social incidents dealt heavy blows to employment in the trade sector and in the retail- and tourism-related sectors respectively, some major sectors were still able to support the overall labour market. Specifically, employment in the financial, business, public administration, social, and personal services sectors continued to grow in 2019, partly offsetting the decline in employment in the trade and retail sectors (Chart B3.2). Despite the economy entering a recession, Hong Kong's financial system remained sound, and financial activities in areas such as fintech development and new share offerings were also very active. These factors may all help support the job market in the financial and business services sectors. In addition, the public administration, social, and personal services sectors, including education, healthcare, and social work activities, appear to be less sensitive to the economic cycle. An analysis of correlation coefficients shows that, although employment in many sectors is highly correlated with real GDP, employment in the public administration, social, and personal services sectors reacts more neutrally to the economic cycle. In other words, even as the economy slows, employment in these sectors may not be greatly affected by cyclical factors. Chart B3.2 Changes in Employment by Sector in 2019 In terms of labour supply, the labour force participation rate 40 fell from 61.2% in 2018 to 60.5% in 2019, providing a buffer against the rise in the unemployment rate. Chart B3.3 shows the various supply and demand factors affecting changes in the unemployment rate (blue line). As shown in the chart, the labour force participation rate (green bars) exerted downward pressures on the unemployment rate in 2019. 41 On the other hand, the increase in employment in the first half of 2019 (purple bars) also helped restrain the unemployment rate. However, as the economy contracted markedly in the second half, the reduction in employment exerted upward pressure on the unemployment rate. Taken together, although employment declined during the economic recession, the lower labour force participation rate helped ease the pressure of a rising unemployment rate in the second half of 2019. Chart B3.3 Factors Leading to Changes in the Unemployment Rate Some changes in the structure of the labour market are also worth noting. In particular, the increased proportion of voluntary part-time employees may help companies retain staff. In fact, the proportions of self-employed persons and underemployed persons in total employment have in recent years declined to 6% and 1% respectively, while the number of voluntary part-time employees has continued to rise, becoming the second-largest group in total employment (about 7% in 2017). 42 Therefore, companies may be able to retain or hire more staff by adjusting the working hours of part-time employees. Our calculations show that the average weekly working hours have decreased, falling from a recent high of 48 hours in 2010 to about 44 hours at present, partly reflecting that there are now more part-time workers among the employed population.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened from October onwards, with the upward momentum strengthening further in December, keeping the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate at the strong side of the CUs range in recent months. The strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar came partly from equity-related demand, and partly from the unwinding of Hong Kong dollar short positions prompted by tightening liquidity towards year-end. Overall, Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets continued to function smoothly and in an orderly manner. Although the coronavirus outbreak may affect market sentiment and lead to intensified fund flow volatility amid an uncertain external environment, Hong Kong possesses substantial foreign reserves and a robust banking system, and is therefore able to withstand the pressure of fund outflow without affecting the city's financial stability. Supported by increased equity-related Hong Kong dollar demand (including IPOs), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually strengthened from mid-October (Chart 4.1). Entering December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar strengthened further, with the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate staying at the strong side of the CUs range from mid-December through February. The strengthening of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate was partly attributable to buoyant IPO activity, and partly to the unwinding of Hong Kong dollar short positions prompted by tightening liquidity towards year-end. After the Lunar New Year holidays, liquidity conditions eased somewhat, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened slightly, closing at 7.7956 on 28 February. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly during the review period. As neither the strong-side nor weak-side CUs were triggered during the review period, the Aggregate Balance remained unchanged at around HK$54 billion (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes The Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index largely tracked the movement of the US dollar and edged up slightly during the review period (Chart 4.3). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and thus had limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index, the movement of the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index largely followed that of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates In measuring Hong Kong's fund flows, it is necessary to distinguish between two distinct but interrelated concepts of fund flows: (1) HKD fund flows; and (2) cross-border fund flows. HKD fund flows focus on the currency dimension of fund flows and help assess monetary stability, particularly under the LERS. On the other hand, cross-border fund flows focus on the movement of funds across geographical locations through the Hong Kong banking system, which helps assess the stability of Hong Kong's overall financial system. The two concepts of fund flows require different monitoring indicators. In monitoring HKD fund flows, attention should be paid to the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate and the Aggregate Balance. If the public or investors convert their Hong Kong dollar assets into foreign currency assets on a large scale, demand for the Hong Kong dollar would naturally decline, leading to a weakening of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate. Under the LERS, if the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakens to the weak-side CU exchange rate of HK$7.85 per US dollar, the HKMA stands ready to buy Hong Kong dollars in response to banks' requests, and the Aggregate Balance would decrease accordingly. Since April 2019, the Aggregate Balance has remained largely unchanged, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has been at the strong side of the CUs range in recent months, so no significant fund outflow from the Hong Kong dollar was observed during the review period. In monitoring cross-border fund flows, Hong Kong's total bank deposits serve as a useful indicator. When there is substantial fund outflow from Hong Kong's banking system, bank deposits would inevitably decrease. During the review period, total deposits grew at a moderate pace, indicating that there was no significant cross-border fund outflow. Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets continued to function smoothly and in an orderly manner, indicating that the impact of the coronavirus outbreak on the city's monetary environment remained limited. Nonetheless, we need to closely monitor the risks brought about by the coronavirus outbreak. Hong Kong possesses substantial foreign reserves and a robust banking system, and the HKMA has the ability, resources and determination to cope with fund outflow and maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. Despite the uncertain external environment and the local economic slowdown, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained relatively accommodative during the review period. The HKD Monetary Base remained substantial, rising 4.0% since end-June to HK$1,689.4 billion at end-January 2020 (Chart 4.4). As the CUs were not triggered during this period, the Aggregate Balance remained largely unchanged at around HK$54 billion. Other components of the Monetary Base, including outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, Certificates of Indebtedness, and government-issued notes and coins in circulation, rose steadily. Chart 4.4 Components of the Monetary Base During the review period, the broad HKD money supply indicators remained largely stable. Broad HKD money supply (HKD M3) grew 3.5% in the first half of 2019, and thereafter edged up 0.2% during the seven-month period since end-June 2019. Analysis of the corresponding assets shows that the growth of HKD M3 since end-June mainly reflected an increase in banks' net foreign currency assets, as well as a rise in the Monetary Base (via the increase in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued notes and coins in circulation) (Chart 4.5). During the seven-month period since end-June, Hong Kong dollar deposits (the major component of HKD M3) remained largely unchanged (Chart 4.6). Among Hong Kong dollar deposits, time deposits continued to grow moderately, partly reflecting the rise in Hong Kong dollar deposit interest rates. Chart 4.5 Changes in HKD M3 and corresponding assets During the seven-month period since end-June 2019, foreign currency deposits grew moderately by 2.3% (Chart 4.6), driven mainly by US dollar deposits, which increased 3.5% during this period. Other foreign currency deposits fell 1.0% over the same period, among which renminbi deposits recorded a slight decline in Hong Kong dollar terms. Overall, total deposits with AIs grew steadily by 1.2% since end-June. Supported by the increase in total deposits, Hong Kong's total broad money supply also rose at a relatively stable pace, with total money supply M2 and M3 increasing 1.6% and 1.5% respectively since end-June (Chart 4.7). As monthly monetary statistics may fluctuate due to various short-term factors (such as seasonal and IPO-related fund demand, as well as business and investment-related activities), the statistics should be interpreted with caution. Chart 4.6 Deposits with AIs by currency Chart 4.7 Total broad money supply (M2) Although the monetary environment remained relatively accommodative, short-term HKD interbank interest rates fluctuated, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand as well as increased capital markets activity since the fourth quarter of 2019, particularly the increasingly active IPO activity in the Hong Kong stock market, with the overnight HIBOR fluctuating considerably in late October and mid-November (Chart 4.8). 44 During the review period, other short-term HIBORs generally rose. Subscriptions to large IPO listings exert significant pressure on the overnight interest rate, and Box 4 shows through empirical analysis that market attention to future IPO activity also affects the 3-month HIBOR. This situation would arise if market participants anticipate the future subscription deadlines of large new listings and prepare medium-term funds in advance for early deployment. Chart 4.8 HKD and USD interbank interest rates As for the HKD yield curve, it moved downward following the USD yield curve. Compared with end-June 2019, the yield of 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds fell 60 basis points to 1.04% on 28 February 2020 (Chart 4.9). Meanwhile, the yield of 3-year Hong Kong Government Bonds fell 50 basis points to 1.00% over the same period. Chart 4.9 Government bond yields, composite interest rate and average lending rate for new mortgages As for the retail level, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of HKD funds for retail banks, gradually rose from 0.94% at end-July 2019 to 1.01% at end-January 2020. This rise mainly reflected banks' continued upward adjustment of preferential deposit rates to attract deposit funds, thereby raising the Hong Kong dollar weighted deposit rate. At end-October 2019, following the downward adjustment of the target range of the US federal funds rate, a number of retail banks lowered their Best Lending Rates by 12.5 basis points. As a result, the Best Lending Rates of retail banks currently stand in the range of 5.00% to 5.50%. On the mortgage front, for HIBOR-based mortgages, major banks raised the interest rate cap determined by the Best Lending Rates, so the average lending rate for new mortgages in October rose to around 2.63%. 45 The Best Lending Rates in the market have been lowered since November, and the average lending rate for mortgages accordingly declined slightly to 2.53% in January 2020. In view of the evolving risks that the coronavirus outbreak poses to US economic activity, and to support the US Federal Reserve in achieving its policy objectives, the Federal Reserve lowered the target range of the federal funds rate by a total of 150 basis points to 0-0.25% on 3 March (US time) and 15 March (US time). Although the HIBORs follow the movements of USD counterparts in the long run, short-term HIBORs may be affected by local factors that could influence Hong Kong dollar demand, such as the city's IPO activity. As the Aggregate Balance of the banking system has decreased since April 2018, the sensitivity of HIBORs to changes in the supply of and demand for HKD funds may have increased. However, this does not mean that the current Aggregate Balance level of HK$54 billion is insufficient to meet interbank payment settlement needs. In fact, Hong Kong's interbank market has been functioning in an orderly manner. Should there be a short-term liquidity squeeze, banks can make use of the liquidity facilities provided by the HKMA. In view of the possible escalation of the China-US trade conflict, both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates weakened significantly in late August and September 2019, with the CNH against the US dollar falling to a ten-year low of 7.19 on 2 September (Chart 4.10). Entering October, market expectations of a resumption of China-US trade negotiations reversed the renminbi's depreciation trend, and both the CNH and onshore renminbi strengthened in the fourth quarter, briefly breaking through the 6.9 level in mid-January 2020 following the signing of the China-US phase-one trade deal. However, since end-January, due to the coronavirus outbreak, both the CNH and onshore renminbi have again faced weakening pressure. The CNH was mostly at a discount to the onshore renminbi from May to August, and largely at a premium in the latter part of 2019, with the discount widening briefly at end-January 2020, but the spread between the two remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates Despite the fluctuations in the renminbi exchange rate, the liquidity conditions in the CNH interbank market remained largely stable. During the review period, the 3-month CNH HIBOR continued to hover between 3-4% (Chart 4.11). The overnight CNH HIBOR experienced brief fluctuations in late August and late November due to the MSCI A-share adjustments, and around the Lunar New Year holidays at end-January 2020.

Amid increasing uncertainties in the global and local economic environment, the profitability of retail banks in Hong Kong recorded a slight decline in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, the capital and liquidity positions of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong and sound by international standards. Asset quality remained healthy by historical standards. Although the growth in total loans slowed in the second half of last year, it still outpaced deposit growth of the corresponding period during the review period. Correspondingly, both the average loan-to-deposit ratio in all currencies and the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio of all AIs increased. However, given that the aggregate balance of the banking system remained stable and deposits remained largely steady, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face a number of downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the future course of US-China trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social incidents. In view of the continued rise in corporate leverage and personal debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should these risk factors intensify.  In the second half of 2019, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell slightly by 1.5% compared with the same period in 2018. Correspondingly, the return on assets edged down to 1.13% in the second half of 2019, lower than the 1.23% recorded in the same period of 2018 (Chart 5.1). Although the net interest margin of retail banks narrowed slightly from 1.67% in the second half of 2018 to 1.63% in the same period of 2019 (Chart 5.2), the net interest income of retail banks continued to record moderate growth during the review period. However, both the loan impairment provisions and operating expenses of retail banks increased, resulting in a slight decline in profitability. Chart 5.1 Retail bank profitability Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks.  Although the US Fed Funds target rate was cut three times by 25 basis points each in the second half of 2019, no significant downward pressures have yet emerged in the HKD wholesale funding market. On the contrary, affected by a number of local factors (including seasonal funding demand, increased liquidity demand due to large IPOs, and tighter liquidity conditions in the interbank market), short-tenor HKD interbank interest rates have been on an upward trend since the fourth quarter of 2019. At the same time, during the review period, longer-tenor HKD interbank interest rates remained largely stable, with the three-month HIBORs standing at 2.43% at the end of 2019, close to the level six months earlier (the blue line in Chart 5.3). At the retail level, since the interest rate on HKD savings deposits remained close to zero, retail banks had limited room to follow the US in cutting rates after the US lowered its policy rate. On the other hand, as HKD liquidity in the banking system tightened during the review period, banks continued to compete for long-term stable deposit funds. Reflecting the increase in the weighted cost of Hong Kong dollar deposits, the composite interest rate (an indicator measuring the average HKD funds cost of retail banks) gradually rose from 0.95% six months earlier to 1.09% at the end of 2019, though it remained at a relatively low level by historical standards (the green line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates.  From a more comprehensive perspective, given that the decline in the USD funding cost of Hong Kong licensed banks offset the slight increase in their HKD funding cost, the average overall HKD and USD funding cost of Hong Kong licensed banks edged down by 14 basis points in the second half of 2019 (Chart 5.4). During the review period, banks' net interest income benefited from the slight decline in their overall funding cost and the relatively high level of HKD interbank interest rates, providing support to the profitability of the banking sector over the same period. Since June 2019, all licensed banks required to comply with the new local framework for interest rate risk in the banking book will submit returns under the new framework, while exempted licensed banks will continue to submit returns under the existing interest rate risk framework. The overall funding cost and tenor are calculated as a weighted average of the relevant figures of these two categories of licensed banks. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards cannot be directly compared with figures for previous months.  Looking ahead, a number of downside risk factors in the external and local environment will continue to cast a shadow over banks' profit outlook. Relevant factors include uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the future direction of US-China trade relations, and the intensification of geopolitical tensions. An intensification of these risk factors could dampen the already weak global economic growth momentum and reduce demand for bank credit. Given the widespread adoption of accommodative monetary policies by major central banks, the low interest rate environment globally may persist, which could put pressure on banks' future net interest margins. At the local level, local social incidents since mid-2019 have continued to weigh on business investment and market confidence. Against a backdrop of an already weak economic environment, if the situation persists or even intensifies further in the future, the outlook for credit demand and banks' asset quality could deteriorate.  In terms of overall market developments, following the granting of eight virtual banking licences by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the Hong Kong banking sector has begun to launch virtual banking services. As these new market participants may increase their market share by launching more convenient products and more attractive deposit rates to attract new customers, this could put upward pressures on the cost of funding of existing banks. Although the short-term impact may remain moderate as the business scale of virtual banks is currently still limited, their long-term impact may depend on whether existing banks will accelerate the adoption of financial technology to maintain competitiveness. The results of Box 5 show that the extent of Hong Kong banks' adoption of financial technology is statistically correlated with improvements in their cost efficiency and profitability levels.  The capital position of the Hong Kong banking sector remained sound and well above the minimum international standards. As at the end of 2019, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions rose further to 20.7% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 18.5%, of which 16.5% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. Chart 5.5 Capital position of locally incorporated authorized institutions.  In addition to the risk-based capital adequacy ratio, there is also the non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement under Basel III, which is used to limit excessive leverage in the banking system. The leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a sound level of 8.2% at the end of 2019, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions.  Measured by the "Liquidity Coverage Ratio" requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions rose from 152.8% in the second quarter of 2019 to 159.9% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum of 100%. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions also rose moderately from 54.6% in the second quarter of 2019 to around 56.3% in the fourth quarter of 2019, also well above the statutory minimum of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio.  The Net Stable Funding Ratio, as one of the liquidity standards under Basel III, indicates the stable funding position of AIs. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 131.7% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.5%, also exceeding the statutory minimum of 75% applicable in 2019. The ample liquidity and sound funding position of AIs indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is able to withstand a variety of liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio.  Customer deposits remained the main source of funding for AIs, reflecting the maintenance of a stable funding structure in the banking system. At the end of 2019, the proportion of customer deposits in the total liabilities of all AIs remained largely unchanged, edging down from 56.4% six months earlier to 56.3% (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all AIs.  The average Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio of all AIs rose from 89.3% at the end of June 2019 to 90.3% at the end of 2019 (Chart 5.10), as the level of HKD loan and advances remained largely stable while deposits fell slightly during the review period. At the same time, as foreign currency loans grew faster than deposits, the average foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio also rose from 58.9% to 60.4% over the same period. Overall, the average loan-to-deposit ratio of all AIs in all currencies rose from 74.5% at the end of June 2019 to 75.4% at the end of the same year. Given that the aggregate balance of the banking system has remained stable since April 2019 and deposits have remained largely steady, there were no clear signs of significant fund outflows from the HKD or the Hong Kong banking system during the review period. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all AIs.  The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at a relatively low level in the fourth quarter of 2019. We estimate that, under a shock of a 200-basis-point increase in HKD and USD interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of the interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks would be equivalent to 1.56% of their total capital base at the end of 2019 (Chart 5.11).
