Against the backdrop of US-China trade tensions, the global economic slowdown, and ongoing local social incidents, bank credit growth slowed in the second half of 2019 after a moderate rebound in the first half. On a half-yearly basis, loan growth (measured by the change in the total loans and advances of all AIs) grew moderately by 4.2% in the first half of 2019, and subsequently slowed to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 5.12). The slowdown in loan growth was due to a slowing trend in the growth of both domestic loans (including loans for use in Hong Kong and trade financing) and loans for use outside Hong Kong during this review period. Domestic loans and loans for use outside Hong Kong grew by 2.5% and 2.2% respectively in the second half of 2019, lower than the growth of 4.5% and 3.5% in the first half. Nevertheless, total loan growth for the whole of 2019 still rose moderately to 6.7%, higher than the 4.4% for the whole of 2018.

The rollout of COVID-19 vaccines brought hopes of reopening economies, boosting the global growth outlook. Coupled with sustained fiscal and monetary policy-easing, financial markets repeatedly hit new highs. However, the global outlook remained clouded by uncertainties, and the pace of recovery across economies was expected to be uneven. In the medium term, the disconnect between financial markets and the real economy, high indebtedness, and the lasting economic scars inflicted by the pandemic will be the challenges facing policymakers going forward. The HKD foreign exchange and money markets continued to function smoothly and in an orderly manner. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side of the CUs, driven mainly by equity-related demand. During the review period, total deposits increased, with no signs of large-scale fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Partly reflecting the weak economic activity and lower credit demand caused by the recurring pandemic, total lending by the banking sector declined slightly in the second half of the year, yet still recorded a mild increase for 2020 as a whole. Meanwhile, the residential property market was broadly stable. Looking ahead, uncertainties surrounding the pace of economic recovery and persistent geopolitical risks will continue to pose challenges to Hong Kong's banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic weakens the repayment ability of corporates and households, the banking sector should continue to closely monitor the impact of relevant downside risks factors on asset quality. Global economic growth rebounded in the third quarter of 2020 as economies reopened, but a resurgence in COVID-19 infections from the fourth quarter onwards slowed global growth again. Nevertheless, with the breakthrough in vaccine development at the end of 2020, markets expected the pandemic to eventually end, favouring a return to normalcy and accelerated growth for the global economy. Coupled with sustained fiscal and monetary policy-easing, global financial markets rose to new highs in early 2021, even as signs of a disconnect with the real economy began to emerge. Against this backdrop, uncertainties will continue to cloud the global economic outlook. Whether vaccines can be widely distributed remains to be seen. At the same time, supply bottlenecks and the earlier aggressive easing policies could lead to higher-than-expected inflation, in turn prompting central banks to reduce monetary easing earlier and ending market expectations of a "lower-for-longer" monetary policy. In the long run, policymakers will need to assess the costs and benefits of extending relief measures and address the many economic legacies triggered by the pandemic, including high global indebtedness and lasting economic scars. In East Asia, GDP growth in the second half of 2020 improved, supported by a rebound in export demand. With increased risk appetite, portfolio investment inflows into the region rebounded, and search-for-yield activities re-emerged. Despite these positive developments, East Asia still had to contend with persistent uncertainties brought by the pandemic. First, in the global competition for vaccine procurement, the region's less developed economies may lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity, hindering the recovery of their tourism and services industries. Second, the supply, coverage, or efficacy of vaccines may prove variable, and coupled with weaker fiscal positions of regional governments, this could dampen market sentiment and trigger a reversal of fund flows. As for Mainland China, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumption activities gradually returned to normal. For 2020 as a whole, the Mainland economy grew by 2.3%, making it the only major economy to record positive growth. Looking ahead, the economic outlook still largely hinges on the development of the pandemic and changes in China-US tensions. The latest consensus forecasts show that the Mainland economy will grow by 8.4% in 2021. The renminbi recorded several months of depreciation at the start of 2020, and subsequently strengthened for the rest of the year as economic recovery accelerated, the US dollar weakened, and the Mainland bond market recorded strong fund inflows. Detailed studies show that during the COVID-19 outbreak, fundamental factors rather than market sentiment played a more important role in driving fluctuations in the renminbi exchange rate (see Box 1 for details). Hong Kong's economy improved in the second half of 2020, but real GDP remained well below its pre-pandemic level. With a slight increase in local demand and a further expansion of exports of goods, seasonally adjusted real GDP began to rebound in the third quarter, ending five consecutive quarters of contraction. The year-on-year contraction in real GDP also narrowed markedly, from 9% in the first half of 2020 to about 3% in the second half. However, for 2020 as a whole, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record, and the first-ever back-to-back annual decline in history following the 1.2% contraction in 2019. The latest sectoral GDP data show that the contraction in consumption- and tourism-related industries was worse than the overall economy amid the pandemic. To respond to the persistent pandemic, the Government launched two further rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-epidemic Fund in the second half of 2020 to help industries and members of the public affected by the pandemic and enhance Hong Kong's capacity to combat the epidemic. In the recent 2021/22 Budget, the Government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures to boost the economy, including the issuance of a one-off HKD5,000 electronic consumption voucher and the provision of a 100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme for the unemployed. In March 2021, the HKMA, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, announced an extension of the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to October of the same year, and announced an extension of the repayment period for trade finance loans under the scheme. These extension measures are expected to help ease the cash-flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers. COVID-19 vaccines are expected to enable economic activity to return to normal, and the local economy is projected to resume positive growth in 2021 (for the year as a whole), but the strength and pace of the economic recovery will be affected by numerous uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the progress and efficacy of the vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination takes time, the local economy will still face significant challenges in early 2021. On external factors, the Mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong's exports of goods and services, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programmes. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of between 3.5–5.5% in 2021, while the average growth forecast of international institutions and private-sector analysts is 4.4%. Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The unemployment rate climbed further, reaching a 17-year high of 7.2% in February 2021, while the underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, a post-SARS high. To respond to the continuously deteriorating labour market conditions, the Government launched the Employment Support Scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing employers with time-limited (June to November 2020) wage subsidies to help them retain employees. After the Employment Support Scheme ended, the Government introduced other targeted measures (such as one-off subsidies) under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to further support industries hard hit by the pandemic. In the near term, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure due to weak economic conditions. Box 2 explores the potential impact of the rise and fall of inbound tourism on the local labour market. Local inflationary pressures continued to ease over the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. Underlying consumer price inflation fell markedly on a year-on-year basis to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020 respectively, and further declined to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 respectively. The three-month-on-three-month annualised underlying inflation, which reflects inflation momentum, fluctuated slightly in recent months but also stayed at a relatively low level. As global and local economic conditions remained challenging, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong may remain mild in the near term, particularly as local inflation will continue to be restrained by the earlier slowdown in the growth of newly signed residential rentals. Market consensus forecasts point to headline inflation at a mild level of 1.4% in 2021, while the Government forecasts underlying inflation and headline inflation of 1.0% and 1.6% respectively for 2021. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side of the CUs, driven mainly by equity-related fund demand, including from buoyant IPO fundraising activities and southbound fund inflows via the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. Fundraising activities remained active in the first two months of 2021, keeping the Hong Kong dollar on the strong side. During the review period, the strong-side CUs were triggered 47 times in September and October 2020, with HKD263.3 billion flowing into the Hong Kong dollar. The strong-side CUs were triggered a total of 85 times in 2020, with cumulative inflows of HKD383.5 billion. Overall, Hong Kong dollar transactions continued to be smooth and orderly. From a geographical perspective, total deposits increased during the review period, indicating no signs of large-scale fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Although uncertainties related to the development of the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and persistent China-US tensions may intensify fund flow volatility, Hong Kong has ample foreign reserves and a sound banking system, and is therefore capable of withstanding fund flow volatility. As the triggering of the strong-side CUs increased the Aggregate Balance, HKD interbank interest rates generally remained at extremely low levels. The composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of HKD funds for retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at end-June 2020 to 0.23% at end-February 2021, and as funding cost declined, the average lending rate for new mortgages also fell from 2.02% in June to 1.56% in January. On the other hand, the Best Lending Rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. As the onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rate strengthened, the offshore renminbi (CNH) appreciated against the US dollar from late May 2020. During most of the review period, the CNH exchange rate carried a premium over the CNY exchange rate, with the average premium in the fourth quarter at about 100 pips, still moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to expand in the second half of 2020, and as at end-January 2021, RMB customer deposits and outstanding certificates of deposit rose to RMB826.3 billion. As for other renminbi business, RMB bank lending in Hong Kong decreased, while RMB trade settlements grew, and the average daily turnover of the RMB RTGS system remained at a high level of RMB1,191.5 billion for 2020 as a whole. Hong Kong possesses an efficient financial infrastructure, providing investors with numerous cross-border fund-flow channels connecting with the Mainland. With the continued opening of the Mainland's capital account, growing demand from international investors for renminbi assets, and the deepening of regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit. Supported by the rise in global equity markets and active purchases of Hong Kong stocks by Mainland investors via the Stock Connect (Southbound Trading), Hong Kong's stock market rebounded after a sharp correction early in the review period. Global equity markets rose for reasons including the unprecedented monetary easing measures adopted by major economies; market optimism over positive progress in vaccine development, which was seen as potentially helping to accelerate the recovery of economic activity; and a reduction in global geopolitical uncertainties. Against this backdrop, the Hang Seng Index recovered lost ground after its sharp fall in 2020, rising by 15.1% during the review period, and briefly broke through the 31,000-point mark in mid-February 2021, hitting a 32-month high. Supported by stable issuance, the HKD and CNH debt market continued to expand in the second half of 2020. Following substantial net fund outflows in the first half of 2020, market confidence recovered rapidly as governments around the world rolled out unprecedented economic stimulus measures, and bond fund inflows into the local market rebounded. Although bond yields recovered moderately over the same period, global bond yields, including those in Hong Kong, still hovered near historic lows.

With breakthroughs in vaccine development, markets expected that the COVID-19 pandemic would eventually come to an end and that the global economy could accelerate its growth thereafter. Coupled with expectations of a "lower-for-longer" global monetary policy, investors were not deterred by the resurgence of the pandemic at the end of 2020, and financial markets rose to new highs in early 2021. However, the strong expectations of financial markets became disconnected from the still-challenging macroeconomic environment. Should the strength of the economic recovery fall short of expectations, or should policy support be withdrawn earlier than anticipated (for example, due to inflation exceeding expectations), asset prices could become volatile. Looking ahead, policymakers will have to grapple with the difficult question of when to withdraw policy support, as well as tackle the many problems left behind by the pandemic, including elevated debt levels and long-lasting economic scarring. Persistent uncertainties surrounding the pandemic continue to cast a shadow over the economic recovery in East Asia, and the more slowly developing emerging market economies in the region may face greater challenges in vaccine procurement and distribution. If the progress of vaccination programmes is impeded, it could reverse the current optimistic sentiment and destabilise capital inflows and financial markets. As for Mainland China, with consumption activities gradually returning to normal, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020. Looking ahead, the growth outlook remains fraught with uncertainty and will depend to a large extent on developments in the pandemic and changes in US-China tensions. Therefore, the government announced that it would continue to maintain a supportive policy stance and emphasised the importance of controlling systemic risks. Benefiting from the purchasing power unleashed by the reopening of the economy, most major economies recorded better-than-expected real GDP growth in the third quarter of 2020. However, since the fourth quarter, COVID-19 infection numbers have climbed again, prompting governments to reinstate lockdowns and social distancing measures, and global growth momentum has weakened once more. At the end of 2020, more transmissible virus variants emerged and subsequently spread around the world, making the situation even more severe. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development and the approval of multiple vaccines for use at the end of 2020, markets expected that the pandemic would eventually come to an end and that the global economy would return to normal and accelerate its growth. Another driving force supporting the global economic recovery came from continued policy stimulus measures, including the commitment by major central banks to a "lower-for-longer" monetary policy amid weak inflation, as well as the sustained fiscal easing of major advanced economies, particularly the fiscal stimulus packages passed by the US Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. Accordingly, in January 2021 the International Monetary Fund revised its 2021 global GDP growth forecast upward to 5.5%, 0.3 percentage point higher than the forecast made in October 2020 (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 Real GDP growth forecasts made by the International Monetary Fund in January 2021 and October 2020. Against this backdrop, market optimism strengthened, and the share prices of cyclical industries that typically benefit from economic recovery rose, driving global share prices and valuations to new highs in early 2021 (Chart 2.2). Chart 2.2 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratios of major stock indices. However, while financial markets performed strongly, the macroeconomic situation remained full of challenges, and the disconnect between the two could lead to volatility in asset markets in the face of multiple risks. First, the prospect of the pandemic being brought under control depends on whether vaccines can be widely distributed, which remains to be seen. As of mid-March 2021, the overall global vaccination rate remained low (Chart 2.3). Although global mechanisms (such as COVAX) promote a more equitable distribution of vaccines, given the limited vaccine supply, the problem of a low vaccination rate in lower-income emerging market economies is expected to be more severe. If the pandemic is not brought under control as hoped, various places may need to extend social distancing measures and other restrictions, thereby undermining the prospects for global recovery. Chart 2.3 Proportion of the population that has received at least one dose of vaccine in selected economies (as of 15 March 2021). Second, the rebound in financial markets is built on continued monetary and fiscal policy support, especially the "lower-for-longer" monetary policy. However, there is a risk that support measures may be withdrawn faster than expected. For example, under the combined effects of supply bottlenecks, strong money and liquidity growth, and aggressive fiscal easing, inflation expectations in the US and Europe have already risen (Chart 2.4). If future inflation proves stronger than expected, central banks may need to scale back their policy-easing, and inflation data exceeding expectations could also lead to greater volatility in financial markets. Chart 2.4 5-year/5-year inflation swap rates in the US and the Euro area. Third, significant uncertainty surrounds future US-China relations. The wave of US-China "decoupling," particularly in the financial and technological spheres, has intensified since the outbreak of the pandemic. Given the increasingly hawkish attitude of both the Democratic and Republican parties in the US toward Mainland China, this trend may not necessarily be reversed under the Biden administration. Should US-China tensions unexpectedly escalate, this could trigger financial market turmoil in the future. Looking ahead, policymakers will need to grapple with the difficult question of whether and when to withdraw pandemic support measures. While withdrawing such measures prematurely could jeopardise the economic recovery and create a "cliff effect," these measures are costly in the long run, including imposing a fiscal burden and delaying the necessary reallocation of resources after the pandemic—for example, allowing "zombie companies" whose business models are no longer viable to survive on continued government support. In addition, policymakers must also address the many problems left behind by the pandemic. First, due to declining corporate revenues and surging government spending, global debt levels rose sharply in 2020 (Chart 2.5). Although, given that global interest rate levels are currently extremely low, the problems arising from the surge in debt may not be imminent, the continued accumulation of debt in the public and private sectors could raise concerns in the markets over fiscal sustainability and financial stability. Chart 2.5 Global debt as a proportion of GDP. Another lingering problem concerns the potential long-term economic losses or lasting scarring caused by the pandemic. For example, elevated uncertainty could cause businesses to reduce investment, while workers plagued by long-term unemployment may permanently exit the labour market, resulting in a substantial waste of human resources. As for East Asia, real GDP growth stabilised in the second half of 2020 after a sharp decline in the second quarter (Chart 2.6). The momentum of the economic recovery came mainly from a rebound in exports, with export demand for electronics and technology equipment being the strongest. At the same time, the hardest-hit service industries (such as tourism and consumer services that require face-to-face contact with customers) remained in difficulty. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Real GDP growth in 2020. Although uncertainties still exist in the economic recovery, portfolio investment funds have flowed back in. Since the second half of last year, improved market sentiment and higher yields relative to advanced economies' bonds have attracted greater bond fund inflows into the region (Chart 2.7). As signs of economic recovery emerged and vaccine production plans were rolled out, equity funds also flowed into East Asia at a faster pace in the final quarter of 2020. Regional currencies also appreciated accordingly on the back of portfolio fund inflows, causing the Bloomberg JPMorgan Asia Dollar Index to rebound by about 10% from its low in March of last year. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Portfolio investment fund flows. East Asia continues to face persistent uncertainties surrounding the pandemic. First, although the rollout of vaccines has brought hope to the hard-hit service industries and economies in the region, competition around the world for early batches of vaccines has pushed up procurement costs, and vaccine distribution also poses challenges to the region's logistics and public health capabilities. As a result, the region's slower-developing economies may achieve herd immunity later than advanced economies, and uneven vaccination across economies may prolong border closures and delay the recovery of tourism-related industries. Second, since investor optimism is largely driven by the vaccine rollout, if the progress or effectiveness of vaccination falls far short of expectations, the current capital inflows and the rebound in financial asset prices may come to an end. A sudden drop in capital inflows could trigger another wave of market turmoil. With COVID-19 successfully brought under control and consumption gradually picking up, the Mainland economy recovered rapidly in the second half of 2020. Meanwhile, benefiting from strong demand for pandemic-related products (such as medical supplies and high-tech products), exports also maintained growth (Chart 2.8). Over the course of 2020, despite the unprecedented shock the economy suffered under the COVID-19 pandemic, Mainland China's GDP still recorded growth of 2.3%. Chart 2.8 Mainland China: Contribution of each demand component to GDP growth. Looking ahead, the latest consensus forecasts indicate that the Mainland economy will grow strongly by 8.4% in 2021, with private consumption expected to be the main driver of economic growth. However, whether the economy can sustain its recovery will, to a certain extent, still depend on developments in the pandemic. Although industrial production activities on the Mainland have already normalised, the service industries remain partly disrupted as the pandemic resurfaced in several northern provinces. On the external front, although exports resumed growth in the second half of 2020, global demand remains uncertain due to a new wave of the pandemic breaking out in most developed economies. In addition, US-China tensions may not necessarily ease in the short term, but the earlier-signed Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership and the concluded China-EU Comprehensive Agreement on Investment help further integrate China with other economies and could partly offset the adverse impact of US-China decoupling on the economic recovery. Considering that the economic outlook remains full of uncertainty, the government announced at the Central Economic Work Conference in December 2020 that the existing policy stance would not change significantly in 2021 in order to support economic growth, while also emphasising the importance of controlling systemic risks, such as maintaining the stability of macro leverage and the debt sustainability of local governments. In addition, the latest Government Work Report set the 2021 growth target at above 6%. In the long run, the "14th Five-Year Plan" designates technological self-reliance and self-strengthening and dual circulation as priority development directions, with the aim of raising per capita GDP to the level of moderately developed economies by 2035. The impact of the COVID-19 outbreak on the repayment ability of bond-issuing enterprises appears to have been limited, and the overall default rate in the Mainland bond market remained at a relatively low level in the second half of 2020. However, due to a sharp rise in defaults on state-owned enterprise bonds, the total amount of defaulted bonds in 2020 increased (Chart 2.9). Although the rise in state-owned enterprise defaults mainly reflected the Central Government's determination to break the "rigid redemption" of state-owned enterprises in order to promote more reasonable market risk pricing, the constrained fiscal space of some local governments may also have been a factor, particularly the local governments of less developed regions. Chart 2.9 Mainland China: Scale and proportion of onshore bond defaults. In the second half of 2020, the cost of funding for corporate issuers increased, particularly for some higher-risk issuers. Although the continued economic recovery and the gradual normalisation of interest rate levels contributed to some extent to the higher cost of funding for lower-rated issuers, several corporate default events occurred in the final quarter of 2020, causing credit spreads to widen significantly as a result (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 Mainland China: 5-year corporate bond yields. As for the housing market, Mainland housing prices continued to rise in the second half of 2020, especially in first-tier cities. By contrast, housing prices in lower-tier cities rose at a much slower pace (Chart 2.11). As for the housing oversupply problem that had plagued third-tier cities in previous years, it was largely brought under control in 2020, partly because third-tier cities recorded strong sales amid buoyant market sentiment. As of the end of 2020, the inventory-to-sales ratio of third-tier cities remained at around 13 months, far below the peak of 31 months in early 2015.

Although real GDP remained well below its pre-pandemic level, the Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 as local demand recovered and exports of goods expanded further. With expectations that COVID-19 vaccinations would help economic activity return to normal, the local economy—following the most severe contraction on record in 2020—is expected to return to growth in 2021. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of the vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination takes time, the local economy will still face considerable challenges in early 2021. Consequently, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure in the near term, while local inflationary pressures should stay mild. The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 (Table 3.A), but economic activity remained well below its pre-pandemic level. The year-on-year decline in real GDP narrowed to 3.6% in the third quarter and further to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. Nevertheless, for 2020 as a whole, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record, and marked the first time in history that a contraction occurred in two consecutive years, following a 1.2% contraction in 2019. The latest GDP figures by industry also showed that economic activity in the vast majority of industries recorded year-on-year declines in recent quarters, with consumption- and tourism-related industries contracting more sharply than the overall economy. On a quarter-on-quarter comparison, real GDP began to recover from the third quarter of 2020, ending five consecutive quarters of decline (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). Local private consumption returned to positive growth in the third and fourth quarters; however, amid the local third and fourth waves of the pandemic, the authorities reimposed social distancing measures, and consumer confidence remained weak. As business sentiment temporarily improved, overall investment spending also grew in the second half. Partly benefiting from stronger export performance (particularly exports to Mainland China), Hong Kong's merchandise trade expanded further (Chart 3.2). As global tourism remained at a standstill, trade in services stayed weak. Overall, net imports (the trade deficit) dragged down GDP in the second half, partly reflecting the slower recovery of exports of goods compared with imports. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contributions of major expenditure components. Chart 3.2 Real imports and exports. To address the ongoing pandemic, the Government launched two further rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-epidemic Fund totalling HKD 30.4 billion between September and December 2020, to help industries and citizens affected by the pandemic and to enhance Hong Kong's anti-epidemic capacity. The Government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures to boost the economy in the recent 2021/22 Budget, including launching a one-off HKD 5,000 electronic Consumption Voucher Scheme and providing 100% guaranteed personal concessionary loans for the unemployed. Together with the "Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism" for small and medium-sized enterprises, the HKMA announced in March 2021 that the "Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme" would be extended again to October of the same year, and announced an extension of the repayment period for trade finance loans under the scheme. These extension measures are expected to help ease the cash-flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers. With COVID-19 vaccines expected to help economic activity return to normal, the Hong Kong economy is projected to resume positive growth in 2021 (for the year as a whole), but the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of the vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination takes time, the local economy will still face considerable challenges in early 2021. On external factors, the Mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong's exports of goods and services, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programmes, thereby affecting Hong Kong's merchandise trade and inbound tourism. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of between 3.5% and 5.5% for 2021 as a whole, while the average growth forecast of international institutions and private-sector analysts is 4.4%. Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate climbed further to 7.2% in February 2021, a 17-year high (Chart 3.3). The underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, a post-SARS high. Total employment stabilised after falling to a low level (Chart 3.3), while Government figures showed that the number of job vacancies continued to decline. The nominal average wage index of employed persons, which reflects labour earnings, slowed to 2.0% year-on-year in the third quarter of 2020, the lowest in nearly 11 years. To address the continuously deteriorating labour market conditions, the Government launched the "Employment Support Scheme" under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing employers with time-limited wage subsidies (June to November 2020) to help them retain their employees. After the "Employment Support Scheme" ended, the Government introduced other targeted measures (such as one-off subsidies) under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to further support industries hit hard by the pandemic. In the near term, given the weak economic conditions, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure. The underlying consumer price inflation rate declined markedly on a year-on-year basis to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020 respectively, and fell further to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 respectively (Chart 3.4). The three-month-on-three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, although fluctuating slightly in recent months, also remained at a low level. Specifically, price pressures on basic food items eased somewhat, and the cost of dining out decreased noticeably, reflecting that more restaurants offered takeaway discounts while dine-in services were restricted. As global and local economic conditions remain challenging, Hong Kong's inflationary pressures should stay mild in the near term. In particular, affected by the slower growth of newly signed residential rentals earlier, local inflation will continue to be restrained. Market consensus forecasts put headline inflation for 2021 at a moderate level of 1.4%, while the Government forecasts underlying inflation of 1% and headline inflation of 1.6% for 2021. As the COVID-19 pandemic raged, inbound tourism quickly fell into a slump, and there are market concerns that this crisis could have scarring effects on the future recovery of the labour market. To this end, this box empirically analyses the impact of the boom in inbound tourism on Hong Kong's labour market, thereby exploring the potential impact of the current tourism slump. Since 2000, inbound tourism has experienced significant ups and downs (Chart B2.1). Specifically, visitor arrivals declined during the 2003 SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) outbreak. Following the launch of the "Individual Visit Scheme" in July of that same year, visitor numbers began to surge. Under the initial Individual Visit Scheme, Mainland residents could apply on an individual basis for one or two trips to Hong Kong per year, each stay not exceeding seven days. The Individual Visit Scheme was expanded from April 2009 onwards, allowing eligible residents holding Shenzhen household registration to apply for multiple-entry "Individual Visit" visas (the "multi-entry permit") within a year. Since then, the number of Mainland tourists has increased substantially. Driven by new cross-boundary infrastructure connecting with Mainland China, visitor arrivals reached a record high at the end of 2018 and early 2019. Subsequent local social incidents halved the number of visitors in the second half of 2019, and amid the COVID-19 pandemic, inbound tourism has been at a standstill since late January 2020. Chart B2.1 Visitor arrivals and related policies. We take the tourism boom brought about by the Individual Visit Scheme as an example to examine the impact of inbound tourism on local employment and earnings. We consider the Individual Visit Scheme launched in 2003 to be analogous to a random economic shock, as it was nearly exogenous in timing and its introduction could not have been anticipated by Hong Kong citizens. Our main analytical data come from population data in the Hong Kong Population Census or By-census. Specifically, we use 5% samples from the 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011 and 2016 Population Censuses or By-censuses. In addition, we define tourism-related industries as the food and beverage, retail, hotel and transportation industries. First, we adopt the "difference-in-differences" method as an analytical framework, comparing the differences in employment outcomes before and after the implementation of the Individual Visit Scheme between younger workers (aged 20-40) in the "treatment group" and older workers (aged 41-65) in the "comparison group". We classify the younger group into the "treatment group" because they are still in the early stages of their careers and can more flexibly make major changes to their employment choices in response to the exogenous growth of inbound tourism. As the impact of the tourism boom brought about by the Individual Visit Scheme on the labour market may change over time, we also adopt the "event study" method to identify time-varying effects. Our empirical findings show that, compared with the older group, younger workers (especially women and those with only secondary education) were more likely to enter tourism-related industries after the implementation of the Individual Visit Scheme. Among these, the impact of the Individual Visit Scheme on the probability of young women engaging in tourism-related industries was particularly significant and persistent, remaining at close to 5 percentage points from 2006 onwards (in terms of the average difference in the probability of entry compared with the older group) (Chart B2.2). We also use a similar method to compare the earnings of those engaged in tourism-related industries (treatment group) with those in non-tourism-related industries (comparison group). The estimation results show that, after the implementation of the Individual Visit Scheme, the earnings growth of workers in tourism-related industries was higher than that of employees in non-tourism-related industries. In addition, compared with similar employees in other industries, female workers and lower-educated workers in tourism-related industries experienced higher and rising earnings gains (3-20 percentage points) (Chart B2.3). Chart B2.2 Impact of the Individual Visit Scheme on female employment. Chart B2.3 Impact of the Individual Visit Scheme on the earnings of women and lower-educated workers. The above results are broadly consistent with international experience, revealing that tourism is an important source of employment, especially for young people, women and lower-educated workers. As far as Hong Kong is concerned, our findings are also consistent with previous analyses, namely that the strong growth of inbound tourism increased market demand for lower-skilled workers and improved the resilience of the lower-skilled segment of the labour market. As inbound tourism falls from boom to bust, these worker groups may be more affected and warrant close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate continued to stay close to the strong-side CUs level, and the strong-side CUs were triggered multiple times between September and October 2020. Strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including from buoyant IPO fundraising activities, as well as southbound inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. As the Aggregate Balance increased to over HK$450 billion, HIBORs declined across the board. Despite uncertainties related to the development of the COVID-19 pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and continued tensions in China-US relations, which may intensify fund flow volatility, Hong Kong has ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system, and is capable of withstanding the pressure from fund flow volatility. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate stayed close to the strong-side CUs level, mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including from buoyant IPO fundraising activities, as well as southbound inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Chart 4.1). Although part of the funds raised from IPOs were remitted out, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate traded within a narrow range of 7.7505 to 7.7544 in November and December, owing to improved market sentiment in the local stock market and market expectations of rising funding demand towards year-end. As fundraising activities remained active in the first two months of 2021 (Chart 4.2), the Hong Kong dollar traded at 7.7568 against the US dollar on 26 February 2021. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. During the review period, the strong-side CUs were triggered multiple times, leading to an increase in the Aggregate Balance, reflecting substantial inflows into the Hong Kong dollar. Between September and October 2020, the strong-side CUs were triggered 47 times. Under the design of the LERS, the HKMA sold a total of HK$263.3 billion, increasing the Aggregate Balance from HK$193.1 billion at the end of August to HK$457.5 billion at the end of February (Chart 4.3). The strong-side CUs were triggered a total of 85 times throughout 2020, with cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. From a cross-border perspective, total deposits increased, indicating no signs of substantial capital outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments figures showed that non-residents' direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, without showing any abnormal fund flows. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate. Chart 4.2 Equity funds raised on HKEX. Chart 4.3 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index generally declined in line with the softening of the US dollar against major currencies (Chart 4.4). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and had limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index, the movement of the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index broadly followed that of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.4 Nominal and real effective exchange rates. Looking ahead, uncertainties related to the development of the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and continued tensions in China-US relations may intensify fund flow volatility. As an international financial centre, various fundraising activities (such as IPO fundraising) take place in Hong Kong, resulting in substantial inflows into and outflows from Hong Kong. On the one hand, related fundraising activities can attract international investors to transfer funds to Hong Kong. On the other hand, funds raised by listed corporates may subsequently be transferred out of Hong Kong for business needs. Hong Kong has ample foreign reserves and a sound banking system, and is capable of withstanding fund flow volatility without affecting financial stability. Amid continued inflows into the Hong Kong dollar, the local monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2020 and in recent months. Over the eight months since the end of June 2020, the HKD Monetary Base increased by 20.8% (Chart 4.5). By component, the increase in the Monetary Base during this period reflected the increase in the Aggregate Balance resulting from the multiple triggering of the strong-side CUs. On the other hand, other components, including the Certificates of Indebtedness, government-issued notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base. During the review period, large-scale IPO fundraising activities boosted Hong Kong dollar deposits arising from IPO subscription loans, so Hong Kong dollar broad money (Hong Kong dollar M3) and its Hong Kong dollar deposits component rose significantly during July to October 2020 and January 2021 (Chart 4.6). As IPO fundraising activities concluded and customers repaid IPO subscription loans, Hong Kong dollar deposits and broad money returned to normal levels at the end of 2020. Entering January 2021, Hong Kong dollar M3 increased significantly again, mainly driven by the large-scale IPO fundraising activities at the end of January. Overall, over the seven months since the end of June, Hong Kong dollar M3 grew by 21.7%, and excluding the impact of the IPO fundraising activities at the end of January, Hong Kong dollar M3 grew moderately by 9.1%. On the asset counterpart side, excluding IPO subscription loans, the growth of Hong Kong dollar M3 was mainly due to the increase in the Monetary Base driven by the triggering of the strong-side CUs (Chart 4.7). As the main component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits rose by 22.9% over the same period, and excluding the impact of the IPO fundraising activities at the end of January, Hong Kong dollar deposits grew moderately by 9.1%. Although Hong Kong dollar time deposits recorded a decline due to low deposit interest rates, this was fully offset by the rapid growth of demand and savings deposits partly driven by investment demand. Chart 4.6 AIs' deposits by currency. Chart 4.7 Hong Kong dollar M3 and changes in asset counterparts. Overall foreign currency deposits grew steadily by 3.6% over the seven months since the end of June. US dollar deposits edged down by 0.3%, partly reflecting the weakness of the US dollar, while other foreign currency deposits grew strongly by 15.5% over the same period, mainly reflecting an increase in renminbi deposits. Overall, due to short-term fluctuations in Hong Kong dollar deposits caused by IPO fundraising activities, AIs' total deposits rose sharply by 13.2% during the review period (Chart 4.6). Excluding the IPO fundraising activities at the end of January, total deposits grew moderately by 6.4%. It should be noted that, as monthly monetary statistics may be subject to fluctuations arising from various short-term factors (such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demand, as well as business- and investment-related activities), the statistics should be interpreted with care. As the Aggregate Balance increased, HIBORs generally remained at extremely low levels during the review period (Chart 4.8). Although there were large-scale IPO fundraising activities in the second half of 2020, HIBORs did not experience significant fluctuations, owing to the ample liquidity in the banking system. Overall, the local interbank market continued to function normally. Chart 4.8 HKD and USD interbank interest rates. The Hong Kong dollar yield curve broadly followed the movement of the US dollar yield curve and steepened during the review period, with short-term bond yields declining while long-term bond yields rose (Chart 4.9). Compared with the end of June, the yield of the 3-year Hong Kong Government Bond edged down by 4 basis points to 0.23% at the end of February, while the yield of the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond rose by 67 basis points to 1.30% over the same period. Chart 4.9 Government Bond yields, composite interest rate, and average lending rate of new mortgages. At the retail level, HKD interest rates mainly declined in line with HKD interbank interest rates. The composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of HKD funds of retail banks, further declined from 0.71% at the end of June to 0.23% at the end of February 2021 (Chart 4.9). As funding cost decreased, the average lending rate of new mortgages also fell from 2.02% in June 2020 to 1.56% in January 2021, broadly following the movement of the 1-month HIBOR. On the other hand, the Best Lending Rates of retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Under the LERS, HKD interest rates are influenced by their USD counterparts. Given the prolonged low levels of US interest rates, HKD interest rates should continue to stay low, with occasional fluctuations arising from capital markets activities and seasonal liquidity demand. Facing an extremely uncertain macro-financial environment, the ample liquidity in the banking system should provide a sufficient buffer to maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. The CNH and onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rates against the US dollar strengthened since the end of May (Chart 4.10), broadly reflecting the better economic outlook of Mainland China relative to the rest of the world, as well as the weakness of the US dollar. FTSE Russell's announcement at the end of September to include Mainland government bonds in the World Government Bond Index further supported the strengthening of the renminbi through investment demand. During most of the review period, the CNH exchange rate traded at a premium relative to the CNY exchange rate, with an average premium of about 100 pips in the fourth quarter, which remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates. During the review period, liquidity conditions in the CNH interbank market remained stable. Although the overnight CNH HIBOR experienced brief fluctuations due to occasional northbound remittance demand and seasonal liquidity demand towards year-end, it remained below 4% most of the time (Chart 4.11). The 3-month CNH HIBOR followed onshore renminbi interest rates and declined in late December, then rose again in late January, partly due to tighter onshore liquidity and seasonal factors. Chart 4.11 Overnight and 3-month CNH HIBOR fixings. In the second half of 2020, Hong Kong's CNH liquidity pool continued its growth trend. Since the fourth quarter, the growth of renminbi deposits accelerated, partly reflecting the appreciation of the renminbi and the relatively higher interest rates of the renminbi compared with other currencies. Compared with the end of June 2020, RMB customer deposits and outstanding certificates of deposit grew at an accelerated pace, reaching RMB826.3 billion at the end of January 2021, up 21.9% (Chart 4.12 and Table 4.A). Among these, RMB customer deposits grew by 24.7%, mainly driven by the strong growth of corporate customers' deposits. On the other hand, certificates of deposit outstanding decreased by 25.0% over the same period. Chart 4.12 Renminbi deposits and certificates of deposit in Hong Kong. As for other renminbi business, over the seven months since the end of June 2020, outstanding renminbi loans declined by 2.4% to RMB159.2 billion. On the other hand, RMB trade settlements in Hong Kong continued to grow strongly. Within the relevant transactions, remittances from Hong Kong to the Mainland grew at a higher rate than remittances from the Mainland to Hong Kong (Chart 4.13). Throughout 2020, the average daily turnover of the RMB RTGS system reached RMB1,191.5 billion, compared with RMB1,133.9 billion in 2019.

Amid the persistent economic recession caused by the recurring COVID-19 pandemic and the impact of the prolonged low-interest-rate environment, the retail banks in Hong Kong saw a further decline in profits in the second half of 2020, with a slight deterioration in asset quality. Nevertheless, the Hong Kong banking sector remained resilient on the back of its still-strong capital and liquidity positions. During the review period, in order to continue supporting the overall economy through difficult times, the HKMA decided to extend a number of relief measures. Looking ahead, although the rollout of vaccines may raise hopes that the global pandemic can be brought under control and economic activities can resume, the pace of economic recovery remains uncertain. The above uncertainties and ongoing geopolitical tensions would be unfavourable to business activities and would continue to pose challenges to the Hong Kong banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic would weaken the repayment ability of corporates and households, the banking sector should continue to closely monitor the impact of the relevant downside risks on its asset quality. In the second half of 2020, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 38.5% compared with the same period in 2019. Correspondingly, the return on assets fell to 0.62% in the second half of 2020, compared with 1.13% in the same period of 2019 (Chart 5.1). The net interest margin of retail banks narrowed from 1.63% in the second half of 2019 to 1.01% in the same period of 2020 (Chart 5.2), reducing net interest income and outweighing the slight increase in non-interest income, thereby leading to a decline in profits. For the full year of 2020, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 29.4%, and the return on assets declined from 1.19% in 2019 to 0.77%. Chart 5.1 Retail bank profits. Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks. Largely owing to substantial fund inflows driven by equity markets activity, Hong Kong dollar liquidity became more ample. HIBORs softened further in the fourth quarter of 2020. Among them, the three-month HIBOR fell by 43 basis points in the second half of the year to 0.35% at the end of 2020 (the blue line in Chart 5.3). The composite interest rate (an indicator measuring the average HKD funds cost of retail banks) followed a broadly similar trend, falling markedly from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.28% at the end of 2020 (the green line in Chart 5.3). The decline in the composite interest rate mainly reflected the drop in interbank funding costs and the lowering of time deposit rates by some major retail banks. Chart 5.3 Interest rates. From a broader perspective, the average overall HKD and USD funding costs of Hong Kong's licensed banks fell moderately by 53 basis points in the second half of 2020 (the red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 HKD and USD funding costs and maturities of licensed banks. Looking ahead, as the global low-interest-rate environment is likely to persist and continue to be unfavourable to banks' net interest margin performance, the profit outlook of the banking sector will remain challenging. In addition, although breakthroughs in vaccine development have strengthened market optimism about the global economic outlook, considerable uncertainties surrounding the distribution and efficacy of vaccines mean that the trend of economic recovery remains highly uncertain. The above risk factors will continue to affect the loan quality and profitability of the banking sector in the near term. The capital adequacy of the Hong Kong banking sector remained sound and well above the minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions stood at 20.7% at the end of December 2020, higher than the international minimum requirement of 8% (Chart 5.5). During the period, the Tier 1 capital ratio was 18.7%, of which 16.7% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. In addition, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a sound level of 8.2% at the end of December 2020, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.5 Capital adequacy of locally incorporated authorized institutions. Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions. Measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions was 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. During the same period, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions was 57.9%, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio. The most recent ratio figures under the Net Stable Funding Ratio requirement also indicated that the funding position of authorized institutions was stable. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions and the average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions stood at high levels of 138.6% and 139.5% respectively in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.8), well above their statutory minimum requirements of 100% and 75% respectively. The ample liquidity and sound funding position of authorized institutions indicated that the Hong Kong banking sector was able to withstand liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio. Customer deposits remained the primary source of funding of authorized institutions, reflecting the stable funding structure maintained by the banking system. At the end of 2020, customer deposits accounted for 56.1% of the total liabilities of all authorized institutions, broadly similar to the level six months earlier (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all authorized institutions. As total deposits of all authorized institutions increased in the second half of 2020 while total lending declined during the same period, the average all-currency loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions fell from 76.0% at the end of June 2020 to 72.3% at the end of 2020 (Chart 5.10). The increase in total deposits largely reflected growth in both Hong Kong dollar deposits and foreign currency deposits. Correspondingly, as at the end of 2020, the average Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio and foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell to 83.5% and 61.0% respectively, compared with 86.4% and 65.5% respectively six months earlier. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions. The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at a relatively low level in the fourth quarter of 2020. Assuming a shock of a 200-basis-point increase in HKD and USD interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of the interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks was estimated to be equivalent to 1.41% of their total capital base at the end of December 2020 (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11 Impact of HKD and USD counterparts interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks. Against the backdrop of a persistent economic recession caused by the recurring pandemic and the tightening of social distancing measures, total loans and advances registered a moderate decline in the second half of 2020. However, for the full year of 2020, the total credit of the banking sector still recorded positive growth, though the pace of growth slowed markedly from 6.7% in 2019 to 1.2%. On a half-yearly basis, total loans and advances of all authorized institutions, after growing by 3.0% in the first half of 2020, declined by 1.8% in the second half (Chart 5.12). The decline in total lending was due to decreases in both domestic loans (including loans used within Hong Kong and trade finance) and loans used outside Hong Kong. Among them, total domestic loans edged down by 0.9% in the second half, while total loans used outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.9%, compared with growth of 2.6% and 4.2% respectively in the preceding six months. Chart 5.12 Loan growth. By currency, Hong Kong dollar loans, after declining by 2.0% in the first half, remained broadly at a level similar to that at the end of June by the end of 2020. Foreign currency loans, after growing significantly by 10.6% in the first half of 2020, declined by 4.5% in the second half, partly reflecting a decrease in USD loan demand as global liquidity conditions improved. The banking sector was slightly more optimistic about the near-term outlook for credit demand than six months earlier. The HKMA's Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook in December 2020 showed that the proportion of surveyed authorized institutions expecting loan demand to increase in the next three months rose to 37%, while the proportion expecting loan demand to decline during the same period fell to 13% (Table 5.A). As the pandemic adversely affected the repayment ability of households and companies, the loan quality of banks deteriorated slightly, but remained sound by historical and international standards. In addition, the pace of deterioration in loan quality slowed in the second half of 2020. The gross CLR of all authorized institutions rose moderately from 0.79% six months earlier to 0.9% at the end of 2020, while the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans of all authorized institutions rose from 0.49% at the end of June 2020 to 0.57% at the end of 2020. For retail banks, the gross CLR and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans rose to 0.82% and 0.48% respectively (Chart 5.13).

Entering 2022, the global economy performed weakly, but inflationary pressures continued to intensify across regions, especially in the US. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties, including the risk of a large-scale outbreak of the pandemic, and if US inflation proves more persistent and broad-based than expected, monetary policy tightening may be stronger than anticipated. If the US Federal Reserve tightens monetary policy substantially and leads to a tightening of global financing conditions, it would place pressure on the recovery of the more vulnerable emerging market economies. Recently, the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine may have significant impacts on the global economy through trade and financial channels, and further complicate the outlook for global monetary policy. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened, but trading remained smooth and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, and there were no significant signs of funds flowing out of the Hong Kong banking system. For 2021 as a whole, the growth of total bank loans accelerated somewhat. On the other hand, the residential property market has softened since mid-2021. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may pose a threat to the sustained economic recovery, and coupled with the potentially faster-than-expected pace of US monetary policy normalisation, these risk factors will pose challenges to banks' credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. The global economy began to slow in late 2021, with the weakness continuing into 2022, owing to the spread of the highly contagious Omicron variant which led to increased restrictions on the movement of people globally, coupled with persistent supply bottlenecks that put production under pressure. At the same time, amid supply-demand imbalances and labour shortages, global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and have spread to a broad range of goods and services in the major advanced economies (especially the US). Recently, with the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine, the surge in commodity prices could further exacerbate the threat of global inflation, while heightened financial market volatility may cause global financing conditions to tighten in an undesirable manner, further complicating the outlook for global monetary policy. Looking ahead, there are significant uncertainties surrounding the global economic outlook. In the short term, if there is a large-scale outbreak of the pandemic, the reimposition of lockdown measures and renewed worsening of supply bottlenecks cannot be ruled out. In the US, with the growing risk that inflation will prove more persistent and broad-based than expected, the Federal Reserve's stance has turned hawkish, accelerating the timetable for tapering asset purchases and raising interest rates, and beginning to discuss shrinking its balance sheet. If the Federal Reserve needs to tighten monetary policy substantially, global financing conditions may also tighten, leading to a deterioration in borrowers' debt repayment abilities, while disorderly capital outflows would place pressure on the recovery of the relatively vulnerable emerging market economies. Recently, the Russia-Ukraine military conflict may expose global commodity prices to the risk of sustained increases, aggravate shortages in the supply of industrial goods, and increase financial market volatility. Heightened market volatility may also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risk. Box 1 discusses whether swing pricing (a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds to manage their liquidity) can reduce the liquidity risk of these funds during periods of market stress, and discusses the potential limitations of this tool. In emerging Asia, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, though the recovery momentum in some Southeast Asian economies slowed temporarily as strict anti-pandemic measures were reimposed in the third quarter, while the technology-exporting economies in the region (South Korea and Singapore) continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products. Although the market generally expects a broad-based recovery in emerging Asia in 2022, the region's short-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds. First, new variants of the virus remain a concern, especially for economies in the region with lower vaccination rates and tight public health resources. Second, the Federal Reserve's accelerated policy normalisation could trigger capital outflows from the region and aggravate currency depreciation pressures; and for economies in the region that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policy to support economic recovery, the trade-off between curbing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity will become more difficult. Third, the slowdown in major economies, coupled with the possible shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, will place pressure on the outlook for trade growth. Fourth, the rise in the prices of various commodities triggered by the Russia-Ukraine conflict will feed through to inflation in the region while simultaneously eroding consumption. Due to the rapid global spread of virus variants (Delta and Omicron), coupled with persistent production bottlenecks, the global economy slowed markedly in late 2021, and growth drivers remained weak heading into 2022. Global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and have spread to a broad range of goods and services in major advanced economies (particularly the United States). Rising inflation concerns prompted the Federal Reserve to shift its monetary policy stance to a more hawkish one, heightening the risk that a premature tightening of global financing conditions could pressure currently elevated asset valuation, and posing challenges for emerging market economies whose recoveries generally continue to lag. More recently, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine has pushed up energy prices and other commodity prices, triggered global financial market volatility, and exacerbated some of the aforementioned risks. In emerging Asia, despite the spread of the Delta variant within the region, the economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, with the region's major technology-product exporting economies continuing to outperform other economies. Although the Omicron variant is not expected to severely impede the region's economic recovery at present, any uncertainty associated with new virus variants will continue to cast a shadow over the region's economic outlook. In addition, the normalisation of Federal Reserve policy could trigger adjustments in the region's asset prices, and slowing growth in major economies could also weigh on growth in the region's exports of goods. The conflict between Russia and Ukraine, on the one hand, has led to rising commodity prices and increased inflation risk, and on the other hand, will weaken consumption and increase global economic uncertainty, which will make decisions on monetary policy normalisation by the region's central banks more complex. Mainland China's economic growth slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a new wave of COVID-19 outbreaks, power supply restrictions, and tightening measures in the housing market. Looking ahead, the Mainland economy may continue to face downward pressures arising from a cooling housing market and Omicron variant outbreaks. In view of this, the government has set stabilising growth as its top priority for this year, and macroeconomic policy will provide greater support. The global economic recovery slowed markedly in the final quarter of 2021, as the highly transmissible Omicron variant overlapped with the spread of the Delta variant, triggering a new wave of infections and leading to tighter restrictions on the movement of people around the world. In addition, supply chain problems (such as shipping bottlenecks and shortages of key production raw materials such as semiconductors) continued to weigh on production. Entering 2022, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in January projected that global GDP growth would slow from 5.9% in 2021 to 4.4% in 2022, reflecting the persistent drag from the pandemic and supply constraints, reduced policy support in the United States and other major advanced economies, as well as slowing growth drivers in Mainland China offsetting the expected growth rebound in the rest of Asia (Chart 2.1). Core inflation (excluding food and energy prices) rose significantly in major advanced economies, especially in the United States, which has adopted larger-scale policy stimulus since the pandemic. Amid supply bottlenecks, released pent-up demand, and labour shortages, inflationary pressures have spread to a broad range of goods and services (Chart 2.2). In addition, the recent military conflict between Russia and Ukraine has pushed up the prices of various commodities, which may intensify already-elevated global inflationary pressures. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties, with downside risks being greater, and will depend on the development of the pandemic and related supply chain disruptions, how the impact of geopolitical tensions on global trade, inflation, and financial market sentiment evolves, as well as major central banks' policy responses to inflation. On the pandemic front, most governments have thus far adopted targeted measures in response to the recent surge in Omicron cases, focusing on restricting high-risk activities, encouraging remote work, and promoting vaccination. Compared with previous lockdown policies, these more relaxed measures should help reduce supply chain disruptions, which have shown initial signs of improvement since late 2021 (Chart 2.3). However, should a large-scale outbreak occur, the reimplementation of lockdown measures cannot be ruled out, which would in turn cause supply bottlenecks to deteriorate again. Chart 2.3 Purchasing Managers' Index – Suppliers' Delivery Times sub-index. If the pandemic remains under control, supply bottlenecks are expected to gradually improve, providing some relief for goods inflation. However, several developments may make the current elevated global inflation more persistent than expected, including the risk that the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine and sanctions imposed on energy imported from Russia push up commodity prices, the lagged reflection of rising production costs in final selling prices, the possibility that the earlier surge in global residential property prices may subsequently drive up rents, the upside risk to wage growth posed by tight labour markets, as well as rising inflation expectations. In particular, given that US inflation recorded its largest increase in decades, the Federal Reserve shifted to a more hawkish policy stance at its December 2021 Federal Open Markets Committee meeting, no longer characterising high inflation as "transitory," and doubling the pace of asset purchase tapering from a monthly reduction of US$15 billion to US$30 billion, with a view to ending the asset purchase programme before March 2022 and beginning to discuss shrinking the balance sheet. In fact, recent market pricing suggests that the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates multiple times during 2022. By comparison, given the Euro area's closer trade and financial links with Russia and Ukraine, the ECB may face more significant policy trade-offs. Against this backdrop, coupled with global debt levels and asset valuation remaining persistently elevated under prolonged policy easing, should inflationary pressures persistently require the Federal Reserve to tighten policy faster than expected, borrowers' debt repayment abilities could face deterioration risks, triggering financial market volatility. Recently, as geopolitical tensions in Eastern Europe intensified, risk aversion in financial markets has risen, and signs of US dollar shortage have emerged, including a widening of cross-currency swap spreads. Under a premature tightening of global financing conditions, emerging market economies with weaker fundamentals and still affected by the pandemic may be vulnerable to renewed growth slowdown, currency depreciation, and capital outflow pressures. Heightened market volatility may also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risk. Feature 1 will discuss whether swing pricing (a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds) can reduce the liquidity risk of these funds during periods of market stress, and will discuss the potential limitations of this tool. In emerging Asia, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, but the spread of the Delta variant weakened growth drivers in the third quarter, especially in some Southeast Asian economies (Chart 2.4). At the same time, as major technology-product exporters in the region, South Korea and Singapore continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products, which further widened the imbalance in the recoveries across the region. In addition, inflationary pressures in several emerging Asian economies remained mild. Chart 2.4 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index. The market generally expects emerging Asian markets to recover broadly in 2022, but the region's near-term economic outlook is facing multiple headwinds: First, although the Omicron variant has spread within the region since late 2021, its economic impact has been milder than that of previous waves of infection; however, some economies in the region where the vaccination rate still lags and public health resources are relatively strained will continue to face the threat of new virus variants emerging. Second, the normalisation of Federal Reserve policy may trigger capital outflows and create currency depreciation pressures for the region's currencies. For economies in the region that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policy to support economic recovery, the trade-off between curbing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity will become more difficult. At the long end of the yield curve, given their high historical correlation (Chart 2.5), the risk of a sudden surge in US long-term yield could also spread to long-term bond yields in emerging Asia, heightening the risk of adjustments in the region's asset markets.
