Third, the region's goods trade outlook faces uncertainties from slowing major economies, as well as the possibility that demand may shift from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, and these factors may weaken the region's export growth. Chart 2.6 United States: Imports from emerging Asia and real GDP. Fourth, although the region's economies have relatively limited trade and financial links with Russia and Ukraine, the rising commodity prices triggered by the conflict will be transmitted to the region's inflation while simultaneously weakening consumption. Coupled with increasing global economic uncertainty, decisions on monetary policy normalisation by the region's central banks will become more complex. For some economies in the region with weaker growth momentum and inflation that is more sensitive to energy prices, their central banks will face particularly difficult trade-offs. The pandemic has also alerted the region's economies to the long-term need to rebuild more sustainable and resilient growth models, in order to prepare for other risks such as climate change. To this end, investors need to place greater emphasis on environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Feature 2 examines whether equity markets returns are affected by changes in climate risk, and how such sensitivity is affected by companies' environmental performance. The COVID-19 pandemic caused an enormous shock to global financial markets in March 2020. During this period of market turbulence, some open-ended funds experienced large outflows (Chart B1.1), placing pressure on their ability to manage their liquidity. Chart B1.1 Outflows from some open-ended funds during the March 2020 episode. In addition to investors' liquidity needs, another reason for the large outflows may also be that investors adopted the "first-mover advantage" to redeem funds early, thereby avoiding bearing the redemption costs that may surge under market stress. To curb outflows caused by the first-mover advantage, some open-ended funds adopt swing pricing — an open-ended fund pricing rule that reduces investors' first-mover advantage. Although many open-ended funds used swing pricing during this episode, there has been no empirical research indicating whether swing pricing can effectively reduce outflows from open-ended funds. Against this backdrop, this feature conducts empirical research to understand whether swing pricing was able to reduce outflows from open-ended funds during the March 2020 episode, thereby reducing their liquidity risk. In addition, this feature will also seek to identify factors that may limit the effectiveness of swing pricing during periods of market stress. Based on these assessments, we will put forward policy recommendations in relation to financial stability. The first-mover advantage refers to investors redeeming ahead of other investors, thereby passing on the redemption costs to them. The first-mover advantage mainly exists in open-ended funds that adopt traditional pricing rules, whereby the subscription and redemption costs of the fund's investors (such as the transaction costs arising from portfolio adjustments) are reflected in the open-ended fund's price after the transaction is conducted. Under this pricing mechanism, investors who redeem shares first do not have to bear such transaction costs. This creates an incentive for them to redeem funds early, especially when large redemption costs are expected. Therefore, during periods of market stress, the first-mover advantage becomes more pronounced due to the expectation that redemption costs will rise. This amplifies the redemption pressures and liquidity risk faced by open-ended funds.

The profitability of retail banks in Hong Kong declined in the second half of 2021. The classified loan ratio edged up slightly in the second half of 2021, but it remained low by both historical and international standards. Underpinned by robust capital and liquidity positions, the Hong Kong banking sector remained resilient. During the review period, in order to further help the economy weather difficult times, the HKMA extended a number of support measures. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant could pose a threat to the economic recovery, and coupled with the risk that the normalization of US monetary policy may proceed faster than expected, both will pose challenges to banks' credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of the relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolio. In the second half of 2021, retail banks' overall pre-tax operating profit fell by 16.1% compared with the same period in 2020. The weak profit performance was mainly due to a decline in net interest and non-interest income and an increase in operating expenses. As a result, the return on assets fell to 0.50% in the second half of 2021, compared with 0.61% in the same period of 2020 (Chart 5.1). For 2021 as a whole, retail banks' overall pre-tax operating profit decreased by 18.6% compared with 2020, while the return on assets declined from 0.77% to 0.59%. Chart 5.1 Retail banks' profitability reflected the continuing impact of the low-interest rate environment, and retail banks' net interest margin also remained at a low level of 0.98% in the second half of 2021 (Chart 5.2). However, given that liquidity in the banking system remained very ample, HIBORs continued to stay at a relatively low level. Specifically, the three-month HIBOR rose slightly by 9 basis points from six months earlier to 0.26% at the end of December 2021 (see the blue line in Chart 5.3). Retail banks' funding cost remained stable during the review period. Among them, the composite interest rate (a measure of retail banks' average cost of HKD funds) rose moderately by 3 basis points from 0.18% six months earlier to 0.21% at the end of 2021 (the green line in Chart 5.3). Although the normalization of US monetary policy may signal an improvement in banks' profitability, the improvement in the short term may be partly offset by two factors. First, although the Fed has indicated that it will raise interest rates multiple times in 2022, past experience shows that movements in local interest rates may lag behind their USD counterparts (especially when interbank liquidity in Hong Kong remains very ample). Therefore, it may take more time for the improvement in banks' net interest margin to materialize. In addition, the surge in Omicron variant cases may also bring uncertainties to the pace of economic recovery, thereby putting pressure on banks' asset quality and profitability. Climate change affects every aspect of life, and everyone has a responsibility to do their part to mitigate its impact. In this regard, the HKMA has devoted significant effort to advancing Hong Kong's climate goals and to enhancing global climate resilience and sustainable development. Following last year's inclusion of our first sustainability report as a chapter in the HKMA Annual Report 2021, this year we are, for the first time, publishing the Sustainability Report 2022 separately. I hope this report will give readers a deeper understanding of the HKMA's work strategies and priorities in strengthening the resilience of Hong Kong's banking system to climate change, building a green finance ecosystem, and how we put into practice our role as a responsible investor and a sustainable organisation. During the year, we made significant progress in advancing sustainability work across the HKMA's major functions. You will learn about our specific measures and work in this report, the highlights of which include the following: The day-to-day operations of banks face climate risk. As a banking regulator, the HKMA has taken concrete measures to strengthen banks' resilience to climate change. In 2022, we formulated a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into the supervisory process, and studied how to harness the power of technology to help banks assess the impact of physical risks. Given that banks are launching more and more green and sustainable products, we also shared with the industry good practices on how to properly manage these products, in order to help banks strengthen their climate risk management capabilities. The HKMA actively participates in various collaborative initiatives on addressing climate risk and promoting the development of sustainable finance. Locally, we are working with other financial regulators through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group) to develop a local green classification framework; the framework will increase the transparency of the financial markets and make green finance policies more consistent. At the international level, we are actively participating in various international organisations to help formulate policies to address climate change and to assess their impact on financial stability. Hong Kong is well positioned to meet Asia's demand for green and sustainable financing. Although 2022 was a rather difficult year for the global bond market, the issuance of green and sustainable debt in Hong Kong continued to record strong growth, rising by 42% to a total issuance of US$80.5 billion, making it the largest centre for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuance in Asia². The relevant issuers included the Shenzhen Municipal People’s Government and the People’s Government of Hainan Province, whose issuances once again demonstrated Hong Kong's unique role in facilitating the flow of green and sustainable funds between the Mainland and the international market. The flourishing development of Hong Kong's green bond market is also partly attributable to the Government Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the HKMA has assisted the Government in issuing green bonds worth nearly US$16 billion, with the proceeds allocated to more than 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, energy efficiency and energy conservation. We also assisted the Government in achieving two "firsts": in May 2022, we assisted the Government in issuing its first batch of government green Retail Bonds totalling HKD20 billion, which was then the largest green retail bond issuance in the world. In addition, we assisted the Government in issuing its first batch of tokenised green bonds in February 2023. These were the world's first tokenised green bonds issued by a government, and this issuance also marked a milestone as it successfully combined our strengths in the bond market, green and sustainable finance, and financial technology. Standards, data and talent are indispensable elements in driving the sound development of the climate finance ecosystem, and their establishment relies on the efforts and cooperation of different sectors. To this end, the HKMA works with other relevant government departments, regulators, academic institutions and the financial industry, mainly through the Steering Group, to develop the aforementioned elements. In addition to the development of the local green classification framework mentioned above, the Steering Group also promotes skills training in the industry and improves Hong Kong's data resources through its Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance. Moreover, the Steering Group has also made good progress in other areas such as the mandatory disclosure of climate-related information and carbon market opportunities. In 2022, the HKMA further strengthened the Exchange Fund's work on responsible investment, in particular setting a target for the Exchange Fund's investment portfolio to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. At the same time, we also enhanced our risk management work to improve the Exchange Fund's climate resilience and risk-adjusted long-term returns. In addition, to fully capture the opportunities that climate change may bring, we are committed to promoting sustainable investment by the Exchange Fund, seeking out investment opportunities that help support climate transition and mitigate climate change, so as to enhance the long-term returns of the portfolio. At the end of 2021, the weighted average carbon intensity of the Exchange Fund's equity portfolio had decreased by 43% compared with the 2017 level. In fact, the Exchange Fund's risk exposure to high-carbon assets has consistently been lower than that of the overall market. Going forward, we will continue to move towards our net-zero emissions goal by continuously strengthening the integration of environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors into the investment management process, actively exercising our rights as an asset owner, continuously working with stakeholders, and focusing on the decarbonisation and transition of the portfolio. At the HKMA, the "Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee", which I chair, is responsible for formulating the HKMA's sustainability strategy. Our strategic direction is based on three pillars: the environment, staff, and social responsibility. In terms of the environment, we are committed to promoting a green working environment and advocating a more environmentally friendly market to the general public; in terms of staff, as a responsible and caring employer, we actively foster a healthy and inclusive working environment; and in terms of social responsibility, we are committed to improving the level of public financial literacy, promoting financial inclusion, and actively giving back to society. Compared with the level when we began tracking our carbon footprint in 2015, our per capita greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption and paper consumption in 2022 all achieved double-digit reductions. More importantly, we have formulated a roadmap to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or before. In the short term, our target is to completely eliminate Scope 1 emissions and, using 2015 as the baseline, to reduce Scope 2 emissions by 63% by 2030 or before. Addressing climate change and promoting sustainable development require the continuous efforts and cooperation of many parties. On this important global issue, we understand that we must practise what we preach and lead by example, and work together with like-minded peers and international organisations. In the next section, we will outline the HKMA's short-term plans and work priorities in addressing climate change under its major functions. Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or before is an arduous task, and we will spare no effort to achieve this goal. We are confident that, through the joint efforts of all our colleagues, the financial industry and the general public, we will be able to successfully address the climate challenges of the future. Eddie Yue, Chief Executive

In 2023, the HKMA will continue to promote the sustainable development of Hong Kong's financial industry and fulfil its responsibilities as a responsible investor and a sustainable organisation. At the same time, through participation in international and regional organisations, the HKMA will also strive to promote the broad development and best practices of green and sustainable finance. As the regulator of the banking sector, we will endeavour to strengthen the climate resilience of the banking sector and further improve our green finance ecosystem to support banks' green transition. Specifically, the HKMA will engage with banks to understand their progress in implementing the supervisory requirements on climate risk management, incorporate climate factors into our supervisory review process, and revise the banking sector's "Green Baseline" common assessment framework. At the same time, the HKMA will support banks' efforts to enhance their climate resilience and risk management capabilities, for example by exploring various measures and technological solutions to help banks identify, measure and monitor their climate risk exposures. The HKMA will also collaborate with banks to launch the next round of climate risk stress-tested exercise as part of the regular supervisor-driven stress-tested exercise for 2023 to 2024. Participating banks will be required to assess their ability to cope with climate risk based on an enhanced stress-tested framework, which covers a range of stress scenarios such as extreme weather and adverse economic conditions. To foster the healthy development of banks in providing green and sustainable investment products, the HKMA will keep abreast of local and international market and regulatory developments, maintain communication with the industry, and provide guidance on the sales process in a timely manner. We will also conduct off-site thematic assessments to gain a comprehensive understanding of the green and sustainable investment products offered by banks. Meanwhile, to strengthen the building of a green finance ecosystem to support the green transition of the financial industry, the HKMA is planning to consult the industry on the structure and core elements of formulating a local green classification framework. In terms of market development, to promote Hong Kong as a green and sustainable finance hub in the region, the HKMA will assist the Government in expanding the issuance scale of green bonds under the Government Green Bond Programme, and broadening the scope of the programme to cover sustainability bonds; at the same time, it will attract more green financing activities to be conducted in Hong Kong through the "Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme". The HKMA will also assist in implementing the government-funded "Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Training Scheme" to expand Hong Kong's talent pool in green finance. In addition, the HKMA will continue to encourage more Mainland local governments, institutions and enterprises to conduct green financing through Hong Kong, and explore the feasibility of combining green finance with technology. On the other hand, we will continue to work with other agencies and departments through the "Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group" on cross-sectoral topics such as skills training and data, green taxonomy, climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities. Through the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks, the HKMA will jointly launch various dedicated programmes with the International Finance Corporation across the Asia region, including conducting green finance research, providing unique market analysis, offering targeted professional training for banks, and providing practical guidance to help banks develop roadmaps to make green finance a core business. Looking ahead, the Alliance will work closely with its founding members, global partners and knowledge partners to launch a membership programme to expand its influence in the Asia region. At the same time, the Alliance will also enhance the professional capabilities of industry practitioners, promote the sharing of green finance knowledge, and lead the launch of project initiatives in new areas. As a responsible investor, the HKMA has set a target for the Exchange Fund's investment portfolio to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or before, as its commitment to participating in global climate action and implementing the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures. Looking ahead, the HKMA will continue to incorporate environmental, social and governance factors into its investment management process, strive towards the goal of net-zero emissions, and fully support global climate action. As a responsible and sustainable organisation, the HKMA cares for its staff as well as the public and the surrounding environment. We have formulated a sustainability roadmap and set climate targets for our own operations as our commitment to participating in global decarbonisation and climate action. The HKMA will continue to prioritise reducing carbon emissions and encourage staff to fully support energy saving and waste reduction. In addition, we will provide further guidance to staff on incorporating sustainability principles into the procurement process. To achieve digital transformation and enhance operational agility, the HKMA will explore ways to modernise its internal systems and applications to further improve work efficiency, while minimising as far as possible the potential risks that may arise during the digital transformation process.

Climate change is a significant risk facing the financial system. The HKMA has been committed to strengthening Hong Kong's financial system to build a greener and more sustainable future, contributing to Hong Kong's climate goals as well as the global sustainable development agenda. Banks encounter the impacts of various sustainability- and climate-related matters in their day-to-day business operations. To continue performing their vital functions in the financial system and to channel more funds towards green and sustainable projects, banks must proactively manage climate risk. As the banking sector regulator, the HKMA places particular emphasis on building banks' capabilities to respond to and manage climate risk, and on accelerating banks' efforts to support the transition to a low-carbon economic model. The HKMA also supports banks in enhancing their capabilities in detecting environmental crimes, and participated in the recently published Hong Kong Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment, which covers areas such as environmental crimes and illegal wildlife smuggling. In 2022, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (Basel Committee)1 published the Principles for the Effective Management and Supervision of Climate-related Financial Risks, and responded to frequently asked questions, clarifying how the existing Basel framework covers the aforementioned risks. In response to these international developments, the HKMA will continue to work towards incorporating climate-related factors into the supervisory framework. Following the issuance of the Supervisory Policy Manual module GS-1 "Climate Risk Management" in 2021, the HKMA has also maintained communication with banks, exchanging views on expectations, progress and challenges regarding the implementation of the relevant supervisory requirements. To further strengthen the supervision of banks' climate risk management, the HKMA has developed a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into the banking supervisory process, which was communicated to the banking sector in June. As part of implementing the two-year plan, the HKMA issued a revised Supervisory Policy Manual module SA-1 "Risk-based Supervisory Approach", and enhanced the CAMEL2 rating system by incorporating climate risk into the risk-based supervisory process. Meanwhile, based on the experience gained from the 2021 pilot exercise, the HKMA refined the climate risk stress test scenarios and assessment framework. The HKMA has also developed a plan to incorporate the next round of climate risk stress-tested exercises into the regular supervisor-driven stress tests, so as to enable a more comprehensive assessment of the banking sector's resilience under extreme climate scenarios. Under this two-year plan, the HKMA is also enhancing its green assessment framework for banks to reflect the latest developments on sustainability-related topics (including climate risk management and transition planning). At the same time, the HKMA is reviewing the supervisory review process used to assess and monitor banks' capital adequacy and to determine their Pillar 2 capital requirements, with the aim of encouraging banks to strengthen their risk management frameworks to address the risks associated with climate change and the transition to carbon neutrality. Given the growing prevalence of banks issuing green and sustainable products, the HKMA conducted a thematic review, primarily examining banks' development and ongoing management of these products. The HKMA identified some good practices during the thematic review, and issued a circular in December to share them with the industry, enabling banks to gradually enhance their climate risk management capabilities. The application of technology can improve data availability and strengthen banks' ability to manage climate risk. The HKMA has begun developing a common platform for banks to assess the impact of physical risks on real estate. In addition, the HKMA, together with other central banks and regulators, completed a project under the Bank for International Settlements Innovation Network, exploring how technological solutions can assist in conducting physical risk assessments. The HKMA also attaches great importance to promoting sustainable and world-leading anti-money laundering work practices; this work employs advanced analytics and regulatory technology, complemented by fully automated regulatory data collection. Over the past 12 months, the HKMA has streamlined the anti-money laundering regulatory data collection process to reduce the manpower burden and paper usage of banks. To enhance transparency across financial markets and to make green finance policies more consistent, the HKMA has collaborated with other financial regulators to establish a local green classification framework. The green classification framework, commonly referred to as a green taxonomy, classifies economic activities as green or sustainable, providing a reference for authorities and market participants to determine whether a particular activity or its related products are genuinely green or sustainable. To this end, the HKMA has kept in contact with the industry and other relevant stakeholders to explore in depth the features and challenges of the framework, and is preparing to make recommendations and conduct a consultation on the structure and core elements of the framework in the first half of 2023. The HKMA is well aware that climate change may pose potential risks to the financial system, and therefore has incorporated a broader range of climate factors and scenarios into its financial risks analysis and research to strengthen its current monitoring work. The HKMA takes climate change into account in its ongoing monitoring of financial stability risks, and incorporates analysis of climate-related risks into its various financial stability reports. Through its active participation in the Scenario Design and Analysis workstream under the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the HKMA has helped to further enrich climate scenarios, enabling central banks and regulators to better understand the macroeconomic and financial impacts of climate change. On the research front, the HKMA carried out several applied research projects in 2022, examining in depth two major topics, namely greenwashing behaviour in corporate green bond markets3, and the role of disclosure in mitigating climate risk exposures4. The findings of the above research help inform the formulation of policies and regulatory measures to address the impact of climate risk on financial stability. Domestically, these studies help strengthen the HKMA's ongoing monitoring and assessment of the impact of climate risk on financial stability. Externally, the HKMA has shared its research findings with a wide range of stakeholders through various channels, including international central bank research conferences and the HKMA's Half-yearly Monetary and Financial Stability Report. The HKMA's Liquidity Facilities Framework is a collateralised standby funding arrangement that provides timely liquidity support to banks in need. The HKMA is studying the incorporation of sustainability considerations when assessing eligible collateral under this framework. The HKMA actively participates in international and regional discussions on addressing climate risk and mainstreaming sustainable finance. Through such participation, the HKMA helps foster international and regional policy dialogue on addressing climate change and its impact on financial stability, and draws lessons from it to help strengthen the climate resilience of Hong Kong's financial system.

To consolidate Hong Kong's position as a green and sustainable finance hub in the region, the HKMA has stepped up its efforts to raise market awareness and participation, provide the necessary infrastructure and enablers, and support international initiatives to align with global standards. The Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group), co-led by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), is responsible for coordinating the financial sector's response to climate and environmental risks, accelerating the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, and supporting the Government's climate strategy. The Steering Group's work is primarily based on its strategic plan, which sets out six key focus areas and five action points to consolidate Hong Kong's financial system and build a greener and more sustainable future (Figure 1). Strengthening climate-related financial risk management to consolidate Hong Kong's position as a global risk management centre; promoting the flow of climate-related information at all levels to facilitate risk management, capital allocation and investor protection; enhancing the relevant skills of industry practitioners and raising public awareness and understanding; encouraging product innovation and research measures to steer funds towards green and sustainable projects; capturing the business opportunities brought by the Mainland and developing Hong Kong into the green finance centre of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (Greater Bay Area); and strengthening regional and international cooperation. Actions taken so far to advance the development of sustainable finance in Hong Kong: The Steering Group has made good progress since its establishment. The Steering Group's current work priorities include skills training and data collection under the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance (see below), the green taxonomy (see "Establishing a green classification framework to facilitate green fund flows" in the chapter "Building a Sustainable Financial System" on page 9), climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, as well as carbon market opportunities. Specifically, the Steering Group announced in March a preliminary feasibility assessment of Hong Kong's carbon market opportunities, and will support the development of Hong Kong into a regional carbon trading centre, including developing a high-quality international voluntary carbon market and capturing the opportunities arising from Greater Bay Area cooperation. In December, the Steering Group announced its collaboration with CDP to enhance Hong Kong's data availability and strengthen sustainability reporting. As part of this collaboration, the two parties developed a climate and environmental risk questionnaire targeting non-listed corporates and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which both facilitates companies in conducting sustainability reporting and assists financial institutions in collecting and analysing company-level data for use in risk assessment and related business decisions. This is an important step for the Steering Group in expanding the coverage of its data work to include small and medium-sized enterprises, an important but previously hard-to-reach segment of the economy. The Steering Group established the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance in July 2021 to coordinate the work of financial regulators, government departments, industry stakeholders and academic institutions in training and policy formulation, and to build up resources and databases. In the first half of 2022, the Centre launched three information repositories themed on data, training information and internship opportunities respectively, to help the financial sector and other sectors access green and sustainable finance-related data and learning resources. The resource repository provides data sources for assessing Hong Kong's physical risks. To help develop industry talent, the Centre assisted the Government in December in launching the "Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme", which provides subsidies for practitioners, students and graduates participating in green and sustainable finance-related training and skills upgrading. Other measures to promote skills training include launching the "Sustainable Finance Internship Initiative" to create more internship opportunities for students, as well as developing a new "Green and Sustainable Finance" module for banking practitioners under the HKMA's "Enhanced Competency Framework". "Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme": The HKMA has also been actively supporting the development of green and sustainable finance in the region. In November 2020, the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA launched the "Alliance for Green Commercial Banks", bringing together financial institutions, banking sector organisations, research institutions and innovative technology providers in the region to jointly develop a collaboration platform for green commercial banking. The Alliance aims to enable commercial banks and other financial institutions to fully realise their potential, develop green finance into a mainstream core business, and promote the participation of the financial system in global climate change-related activities. It operates by providing financial institutions with a one-stop mutual learning platform to access the knowledge, tools and information they need to formulate their own green finance roadmaps and transform into credible green financial institutions; bringing together green finance leaders, connecting green financial institutions across different emerging markets to facilitate communication and explore frontier issues; and advancing the global green finance agenda to unlock unlimited green and climate-related investment opportunities. In June, five of the world's leading financial institutions became founding members of the Alliance, and worked closely with the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA to encourage clients to adopt green strategies, promote best practices for green products and services, and unlock new business opportunities to help achieve the green economic transition. In addition, three global partners and one knowledge partner committed in 2022 to providing climate expertise in areas ranging from innovation and standardisation to academic research. Details of the Alliance and its membership structure are set out on the relevant webpage (English version): Founding members, the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA signing the memorandum of understanding. On another front, since March 2021 the Alliance has held 18 training events and roundtables, attracting more than 6,000 participants from around the world, including the Asia-Pacific region, Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the Americas. In addition, the Alliance, together with the Hong Kong Institute for Monetary and Financial Research (the Research Institute), published in June 2022 its first frontier-issue research report titled "Climate Risk: Definition, Measurement, Current Practices and Regulation". The HKMA has been promoting the issuance of green and sustainable debt and building up the local ecosystem of related professional services. The total amount of green and sustainable debt (including bonds and loans) issued in Hong Kong in 2022 reached US$80.5 billion, an increase of 42%. +42% green and sustainable debt issuance (US$80.5 billion). To demonstrate the Government's determination to tackle climate change, as well as to promote green finance and its commitment to developing Hong Kong into a more sustainable and liveable city, the Government launched the "Government Green Bond Programme" in 2018, with the HKMA assisting in the implementation of the related green bond issuances. To date, the Government has issued close to US$16 billion equivalent of green institutional and retail bonds, with the proceeds allocated to more than 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, energy efficiency and energy conservation. To enhance the transparency and accountability of the Programme, the Government publishes an annual "Green Bond Report" detailing the allocation of proceeds raised from the green bonds and the expected environmental benefits. To enable the public to participate in Hong Kong's sustainable development through investment and share in the results it brings, the first batch of retail green bonds totalling HK$20 billion was issued in May, receiving enthusiastic support from the public and becoming the largest green retail bond issuance in the world at the time. This issuance also broadened the range of green and sustainable finance products in Hong Kong, consolidating Hong Kong's position as a premier green finance hub in the region and internationally. The Government also continued its regular green institutional bond issuance in the 2022-23 financial year, and issued US$5.75 billion equivalent of green bonds in January 2023. This triple-currency issuance covered US dollar, euro and renminbi, with tenors ranging from 2 to 30 years, continuing to provide an important benchmark for potential issuers in Hong Kong and the region. This issuance was well received by the global investment community and successfully attracted new investors who had not previously participated in the Government's past green bond issuances, reflecting investors' confidence in Hong Kong's long-term credit standing and economic fundamentals. In response to investor demand, the Government doubled the issuance size of the renminbi bond to RMB10 billion. The share of international investors and Mainland investors participating in the issuance through the Bond Connect "Southbound" also increased, demonstrating Hong Kong's role as a premier CNH business hub and further consolidating Hong Kong's leading position as an international financial centre. The HKMA also assisted the Government in February 2023 in issuing a tokenised institutional green bond to test the use of distributed ledger technology for bond issuance and settlement. This was the world's first tokenised green bond issued by a government. This primary issuance was settled on a T+1 basis over a private blockchain network, with subsequent processes (including coupon payment, secondary market trading settlement and redemption at maturity) also digitalised. The experience gained from this Government issuance can provide a reference for market participants interested in undertaking similar bond issuances in the future. To provide the industry with credible and convenient market information, the HKMA continued to collaborate with the Climate Bonds Initiative and the International Capital Market Association to publish annual reports on the green debt markets in Hong Kong and the region respectively. The International Capital Market Association's report showed that in 2022 Hong Kong became the largest hub in Asia for arranging the issuance of international green and sustainable bonds, with a total of US$27.8 billion of bonds arranged through Hong Kong, accounting for more than one-third of the regional total. The largest arranging hub for international green and sustainable bonds in Asia, US$27.8 billion. Following its first issuance in 2021, the Shenzhen Municipal People's Government issued another RMB5 billion of offshore local Government Bond in Hong Kong in November 2022, including RMB2.6 billion of green and blue bonds. In the same month, the People's Government of Hainan Province also issued RMB5 billion of offshore bonds in Hong Kong for the first time, including blue and sustainable bonds. The above bond issuance activities once again highlight Hong Kong's unique role in facilitating green and sustainable fund flows between the Mainland and the rest of the world, as well as its long-standing position as a premier fundraising platform in the region. The HKMA continued to promote and implement the "Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme" launched in 2021, and utilised the Scheme to attract more relevant professional service providers (including financial institutions, green consultancy firms and external review institutions) to establish and expand their business in Hong Kong. The Scheme has been well received by the industry. As at the end of 2022, the Scheme had covered the pre-issuance, post-issuance, or both, external review service expenses of more than 180 issuers of green and sustainable debt instruments, helping issuers to ensure and demonstrate strict adherence to market best practices and international standards. From March, the Scheme was enhanced by lowering the minimum loan-size threshold for applying for external review fee subsidies from HKD 200 million to HKD 100 million, helping smaller enterprises obtain green financing. Following the successful completion of a proof-of-concept for tokenised retail green bonds under Project Genesis in 2021, the HKMA collaborated again with the BIS Innovation Hub Hong Kong Centre under Genesis 2.0 to explore the technical feasibility of digitalised carbon forwards (also known as mitigation outcome interests, or MOIs), with a view to enhancing the transparency, objectivity and environmental attributes of the green bond market. The project was completed in October 2022, successfully developing two prototypes that use blockchain and other related technologies to track, deliver and transfer digitalised MOIs.

As one of the world's largest asset owners and managers, the HKMA plays an important role in promoting the development of green and sustainable finance to support the global climate change agenda. The HKMA is also a pioneer in responsible investment, having taken the lead in investing in green and sustainable assets as early as 2015, requiring its external investment managers to adopt the Principles of Responsible Ownership issued by the Securities and Futures Commission, and integrating environmental, social and governance factors into the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The HKMA invests prudently in accordance with the principle of "capital preservation first, long-term value enhancement", believing that attaching importance to environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors can unlock long-term sustainable value for investments and mitigate related risks. In the face of the increasingly severe challenges posed by climate change, the HKMA continues to advance on its responsible investment journey, including setting the target of "Net Zero by 2050" in 2022 and enhancing its risk management strategy, so as to improve the resilience of the asset portfolio and thereby strive for more favourable risk-adjusted long-term returns for the Exchange Fund. The HKMA also actively participates in building a green and sustainable finance ecosystem, partnering with like-minded investors and regulators to jointly promote responsible investment, and collaborating with international organisations to develop ESG investment standards. Transparency of climate-related information plays a pivotal role in managing climate risk. To fulfil its commitment to support the Glasgow Declaration issued by the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) at the 2021 United Nations Climate Change Conference and to green the global financial system, the HKMA makes climate-related disclosures for the Exchange Fund in accordance with the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) under the Financial Stability Board. a. FCLTGlobal — Focusing Capital on the Long Term b. PRI — Principles for Responsible Investment c. NGFS — Network for Greening the Financial System d. TCFD — Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures The Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Financial Secretary, sets the responsible investment framework and guiding principles, which are implemented by the Exchange Fund Investment Office in the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The foremost guiding principle is for the HKMA to give priority to ESG investments whose risk-adjusted long-term returns are comparable to those of other projects, in order to fulfil the investment objectives of the Exchange Fund. Details of the HKMA's responsible investment framework are set out on the HKMA website: The Investment Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, is responsible for overseeing the ESG and climate-related risks involved in Exchange Fund investment projects. The Investment Committee reviews the responsible investment framework and the risk management approach, and monitors the progress of integrating ESG factors into investments and the ESG status of the Exchange Fund through regular meeting reports from the Risk Management and Surveillance Department of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. As shown in Figure 1, the ESG Committee established under the Exchange Fund Investment Office is chaired by the Chief Risk Officer and is responsible for coordinating and overseeing the various ESG initiatives of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. The motions and work progress discussed at each meeting of the ESG Committee are reported to the Chief Executive Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. Governance and oversight structure of responsible investment The dedicated team of the Risk Management and Surveillance Department works closely with the various investment teams of the Exchange Fund Investment Office on integrating ESG factors, and assists the senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office in managing the ESG and climate-related risks and opportunities of various investment projects: Public market investments The Credit, Rules and Surveillance Committee, comprising the senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, monitors the ESG status of the fixed income portfolio through regular reports from the Risk Management and Surveillance Department. In addition, the Risk Management and Surveillance Department also participates from an ESG perspective in the selection, appointment and monitoring process of external investment managers for equity portfolios (see the section "Striving to actively exercise ownership" under "Risk Management" on page 27). Private market investments The Investment Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, considers the ESG-related assessments made by the Risk Management and Surveillance Department and the private market investment teams on each investment proposal. Concrete evidence² continues to demonstrate the significant impact of climate change and related risks. According to the latest report³ of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (the Climate Change Convention), even assuming full implementation of the "Nationally Determined Contributions" targets announced by various regions, it is estimated that global temperatures will still rise by as much as 2.1 to 2.4 degrees Celsius by 2100, making it difficult to achieve the goal of the Paris Agreement to limit the global average temperature rise to below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Should various regions adopt more aggressive policy measures to close the temperature gap, the resulting transition risks⁴, the asset repricing by the market based on anticipated future trends, coupled with inherent physical risks, would all intensify the pressure on asset valuation. In light of updates to the global warming trajectory and model assumptions, the HKMA, drawing on the expertise of external consultants, has further assessed the resilience of the Exchange Fund's "portfolio" under the "rapid transition" scenario (Figure 2), in addition to the scenarios assessed in 2021. The "rapid transition" scenario incorporates higher transition risk factors in the short, medium and long term, assuming that policy changes and technological developments together drive a rapid decline in carbon emissions, while various assets are suddenly divested in order to keep the average temperature rise within 1.5 degrees Celsius before 2100. This scenario broadly corresponds to the disorderly scenario recommended by the NGFS for forward-looking climate impact assessments. The "portfolio" is able to remain robust in the medium to long term, as a larger proportion of its asset allocation is in sovereign bonds, which are less sensitive to transition impacts. Sector distribution is key. Low-carbon electricity and renewable energy assets can benefit from the relevant transition. Transition risks and asset repricing may impact performance (especially equity assets) in the short term. The "portfolio" as a whole will suffer increasingly aggravated impacts from physical risks that gradually emerge over time. Energy and traditional utilities remain the most vulnerable sectors. Climate scenarios, like other model approaches, have their limitations. The analysis is based on the sector distribution of the market benchmark at the strategic asset allocation level, and does not take into account the effect of actively selecting specific securities within a particular sector. More in-depth research reveals that, compared with the market benchmark of the strategic asset allocation, the investment projects within the "portfolio" are generally more resilient to transition shocks or suffer more moderate impacts. This result once again affirms that the HKMA's responsible investment, with its focus on combating climate change, can enhance the resilience of the asset portfolio. The trajectory of climate change remains uncertain, and scenario analysis methods will continue to evolve as data quality improves and policies develop. The HKMA will regularly review the relevant scenarios and refine its assessments, so as to more clearly ascertain the resilience of the Exchange Fund in the face of climate change. As a long-term investor, the HKMA fully understands the risks and opportunities that climate change may bring. The HKMA is committed to further expanding sustainable investment, and seizing opportunities relating to climate transition, mitigating climate risk and enhancing the long-term returns of the asset portfolio. The HKMA sustained its good momentum in 2022, increasing its holdings of green, social and sustainable bonds by a further 50%. On the equity investment front, the HKMA invested in a governance-themed active equity portfolio, and adopted a decarbonisation strategy favouring low-carbon-emission companies for its passive equity portfolio. In addition, the HKMA is exploring, together with the dedicated partners of the Exchange Fund's "Long-Term Growth Portfolio", the establishment of a dedicated private equity portfolio to promote green and sustainable development in the Asian region (Figure 3). Figure 3 Continued implementation of measures to increase ESG investment The HKMA has invested in a pan-African wind farm operator which, in addition to producing clean energy, also places great emphasis on social and natural biodiversity factors. Before the wind farm was established, local villagers used poisoned bait to prevent predators from preying on their livestock, but this inadvertently endangered certain vulture species that are classified as endangered. Livestock is an important asset for the local villagers, and to help them protect their livestock, the operator built livestock shelters within the wind farm to protect the livestock from natural predators. In addition, the operator employed a bird monitoring team to issue warnings when vultures were spotted being attracted by animal carcasses occasionally left behind by predators, so that the wind turbines could be shut down to prevent the vultures from being struck by the blades. Reducing livestock predation brings about a win-win situation: on the one hand it safeguards the livelihood of the villagers, and on the other hand it reduces the number of vultures killed by being struck by wind turbines, thereby protecting endangered species. Good ESG practices can bring more business opportunities to enterprises and open up sources of revenue, as illustrated by the supply chain-related operations described below. The investee company is an integrated logistics and warehousing operator in Mainland China, specialising in cold chain logistics services for pharmaceuticals, chemical products and high-end consumer goods. The company faces ever-rising ESG operating standards, primarily from multinational corporate customers requiring their service providers to meet ambitious decarbonisation targets consistent with the Paris Agreement. In response to such demands, the company engaged external consultants to help formulate a "Three-Year ESG Plan" to reduce carbon emission intensity by 50% by or before 2030. This comprehensive decarbonisation plan delivered significant results in 2021 alone. The above ESG measures earned the company a "Low-Carbon Green Management Case" award from the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing. These achievements and accolades enabled the company to gain considerable business opportunities from multinational consumer and chemical products corporate customers who place particular importance on ESG practices. The growth of ESG investment is closely linked to the development of the green and sustainable finance ecosystem. The HKMA actively collaborates with like-minded investors and partners to promote responsible investment and enhance industry skills. In 2022, the HKMA successfully held its 4th annual ESG Workshop, exchanging good ESG practices with the 9 participating private market institutions (including dedicated partners, limited partners and enterprises), and promoting sustainable investment opportunities in the Asia-Pacific region and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. On the public market front, the HKMA urged its trading partners (mainly investment banks) to expand their ESG manpower and research capabilities, particularly in Hong Kong. Mr Li Tat-chi, Chief Executive Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, delivered the opening remarks at the HKMA's 2022 ESG Workshop. At the international level, the HKMA actively participates in the work of developing industry ESG investment standards and practices: As one of the first central banks to become a signatory to the Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI), the HKMA participated in the collaborative signatory initiative coordinated by the PRI to develop a standardised responsible investment due diligence questionnaire⁵,⁶ for private equity and venture capital investments, to help private market investors conduct ESG assessments of dedicated partners and investment proposals. The HKMA participated in several working groups to support the research work of FCLTGlobal; this research aims to explore key market practices for long-term portfolios and the decarbonisation of private assets, as well as the application of such practices to long-term investors. As a member of the NGFS and a supporter of the TCFD, the HKMA contributed to the NGFS's "Guide on Climate-related Disclosure for Central Banks" to demonstrate its determination to adopt good ESG practices. The HKMA also led a working group under the NGFS's "Net Zero for Central Banks" workstream, participating in the development of a sustainable and responsible investment approach for the central banking community. The HKMA continues to participate in various industry forums and seminars to share insights on responsible investment and climate change strategies. Ms Lau Wai-kuen (centre), Chief Risk Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, spoke at a sharing session on ESG investment opportunities. Building internal capacity is crucial to continuing to advance the ESG journey. In addition to encouraging staff to enrol in sustainability-related courses and obtain relevant qualifications, the HKMA has also gained relevant knowledge and practical experience through the process in 2021 in which external consultants provided advice on key industry practices for the climate transition of the asset portfolio. On the other hand, the HKMA also uses ESG data compiled by reputable external information providers to supplement its ongoing analysis of the asset portfolio, so as to help strengthen the ESG resilience of the Exchange Fund.

The HKMA is committed to reducing the carbon footprint of its own organisation, with the aim of achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier, and contributing to Hong Kong's overall climate targets. On the one hand, the HKMA strives to promote environmental sustainability, while on the other hand it fulfils its commitments to caring for the physical and mental well-being of its staff, encouraging financial inclusion, and discharging its social responsibilities. The HKMA is dedicated to conducting its daily operations in a responsible and sustainable manner. To this end, the HKMA puts the concept of sustainable development into practice under the three pillars of environment, staff and social responsibility (Chart 1). The Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee is responsible for leading the HKMA in formulating and implementing its sustainability strategy. The Committee is chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, with members including the three Deputy Chief Executives, as well as representatives from the Risk Management and Surveillance Department and the Corporate Development and Operations Department; and it submits regular reports to the Governance Sub-Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee. Under the leadership of the Committee, a number of different teams and working groups are responsible for planning and implementing measures in their respective areas. In 2022, the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee approved the climate targets for the organisation's operations and reviewed the transition roadmap for achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. During the year, the Committee continued to review the progress of the HKMA's green initiatives, including recommendations for strengthening the HKMA's sustainable procurement policies, procedures and methodologies. Sustainability Governance Structure: The HKMA's Corporate Sustainability Journey. In recognition of the HKMA's dedication to caring for the environment, its staff and society as a whole, the Hong Kong Council of Social Service awarded the HKMA the "15 Years Plus Caring Organisation" logo for the 16th consecutive year. The HKMA pays close attention to the carbon footprint of its own organisation and has established internal "Green Office Guidelines" to control the environmental impact of its operational procedures. The HKMA has incorporated environmental considerations into the interior design, operation and maintenance of its offices. In 2022, BEAM Plus awarded the HKMA Gold certification for certain renovated office areas. This was the second green building certification obtained following the Gold certification awarded by LEED in 2021. Awarded BEAM Plus Interior Version 1.0 Gold. The HKMA has implemented a number of energy-saving measures. Total energy consumption in 2022 was 4,996.4 MWh (2.8 MWh per person), a decrease of 24.4% compared with 2015 (Chart 1). Total Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions in 2022 were 2,996.4 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO2e) (1.7 tCO2e per person), a reduction of 38.2% compared with 2015 (Chart 2). Chart 1. Chart 2. Greenhouse gas emission intensity (Scope 1 and 2). The HKMA encourages paperless internal operations. In addition, the HKMA has implemented a print management system whereby staff must log in at the printer to confirm each print request, which helps to reduce unnecessary printouts and toner usage. Where printing is genuinely necessary, double-sided printing and black-and-white printing are also encouraged. The HKMA is also preparing to implement an internal electronic records management system. Total paper consumption in 2022 was 20.5 tonnes (0.0114 tonnes per person), a reduction of 65.3% compared with 2015 (Chart A). Chart A: Paper intensity. The HKMA's waste management efforts continue to adhere to the "4R" principle. In addition to conventional waste, the HKMA also reduces electronic waste by adopting technological solutions such as server virtualisation and private cloud infrastructure. In 2022, the HKMA engaged an external company for the first time to conduct a waste audit to analyse the composition of the waste generated in its offices. The audit found that food waste accounted for a large portion of the total waste, and the HKMA therefore launched a food waste recycling programme (see "Enhancing Waste Management" on page 41). Total non-hazardous waste generated in 2022 (including general refuse and recyclables) was 242.0 tonnes (0.135 tonnes per person), a reduction of 4.8% compared with 2015 (Chart 3). The fluctuating trend was mainly due to the work-from-home arrangements implemented during the peak of the COVID-19 pandemic and the resumption of office operations after the fifth wave. Chart 3. Non-hazardous waste intensity. The HKMA places top priority on waste reduction at source and is committed to reducing, reusing and recycling. In 2022, the HKMA engaged a company for the first time to conduct a waste audit in order to gain a clearer understanding of the composition of the waste generated in its daily operations (plastic, paper, metal, glass, wood, electronics, etc.) and to provide waste reduction recommendations. Based on the results of this audit, the HKMA launched a food waste recycling programme in November, placing food waste collection bins in all pantries. The food waste collected each day is transported to an organic resources recovery centre in Hong Kong, where it is converted into renewable energy to generate electricity. The residue produced during the conversion process can also be turned into compost for use in landscaping and agricultural staple food production. In addition, recycling bins are placed at various locations in the offices for convenient use. The HKMA shares recycling tips with staff and pays greater attention to further improving the sorting of recyclables at source, as well as points to note when handling recyclables such as cardboard boxes, food containers and beverage bottles. In addition, we continue to hold events to raise staff's environmental awareness, explain waste management policies, and encourage staff to make good use of the recycling facilities in the offices. Food waste collected each day is transported to the organic resources recovery centre. Recycling plastic items. The HKMA has two data centres (one operational and one backup). As these two account for a major portion of the organisation's overall energy consumption, the HKMA has adopted green designs and a number of energy-saving measures, including rack-based air-conditioning systems, LED lighting, and 24-hour monitoring of power efficiency. Following the completion of a consultancy study on the green performance of the aforementioned data centres in 2022, the HKMA is preparing to implement recommendations for enhancing overall energy efficiency. It has also begun preparations for obtaining green data centre certification. The HKMA understands the importance of building a culture of sustainability, and therefore regularly launches various programmes and activities to educate and encourage staff to develop habits conducive to sustainability and to adopt green and digital ways of working. The HKMA shares green living tips with staff, as well as annual office-wide energy and paper consumption statistics, to remind them to help address environmental issues at the individual level; it also encourages staff to make suggestions on sustainability matters. Led by senior managers of the Administration Division, a focus group brings together staff from different departments to pool ideas and propose concepts and concrete measures for promoting a green working environment. Members of the focus group also serve as ambassadors when new green measures are rolled out. The HKMA encourages the wider community to adopt more environmentally friendly practices, and has introduced a number of measures to improve the operational efficiency of the HKMA, the financial industry and the economy as a whole, so as to minimise resource consumption. The HKMA's "Submission Through Electronic Transmission" system (STET) is a one-stop platform that allows banks to submit documents to the HKMA electronically, covering various types of periodic returns required to be submitted weekly, monthly, quarterly or annually. Another system, "e-Delivery", is a secure electronic communication channel that allows the HKMA to issue information such as circulars and guidelines to banks. Both systems help save a substantial amount of paper each year. In handling bank complaints and enforcement work, the HKMA has adopted measures to support paperless submission of documents, and bank customers can lodge complaints through electronic channels and by completing online forms. The HKMA is also developing a new generation management information system to facilitate complaint handling and the transition from paper records to digital records. To reduce paper use, the Central Moneymarkets Unit (CMU) has adopted digital signatures in its daily communications with its members, including issuing circulars, account opening and termination letters, and replying to audit confirmations. Looking ahead, the CMU will continue to explore more green measures, including adopting automated electronic processes for internal and external communications. The HKMA encourages the public to make greater use of electronic payment methods instead of cash and physical cheques by promoting the use of the Faster Payment System ("FPS", one of the faster payment systems) and stored value facilities. More information on the FPS and stored value facilities can be found in the chapter "Hong Kong as an International Financial Centre" in the HKMA Annual Report 2022. Distributing electronic lai see is simple and convenient, and can reduce the use of physical lai see packets and banknotes, thereby helping to promote sustainability in Hong Kong. To this end, the HKMA continued to actively promote through various social media and traditional platforms, encouraging the public to distribute electronic lai see via the FPS or other e-wallet services through online or mobile banking services during the Lunar New Year. Major banks and e-wallet operators also organised various activities to attract users to use electronic lai see, such as providing user interfaces full of festive atmosphere, enhancing functions to make use more convenient, and launching lucky draws or cash rebates. The HKMA promoting electronic lai see on social media platforms. For members of the public who choose to distribute physical lai see during the Lunar New Year, the HKMA continued to encourage them to use "good-as-new notes", that is, banknotes that are used but still fresh, for packing lai see. Good-as-new notes can reduce the need to print new banknotes, thereby reducing the impact on the environment. Feedback from the note-issuing banks shows that the public has increasingly accepted good-as-new notes in recent years. The Coin Collection Programme reflects the HKMA's efforts in promoting the recycling of coins. The coins collected through the programme are returned to the market to meet public demand, improving the efficiency of coin circulation and reducing the need for minting. The programme operates two Coin Carts, which to date have served more than 1 million people and collected over 800 million coins with a total face value of approximately HKD 1.3 billion. In 2022, about 78% of users chose to use part or all of their coin value to top up their stored value facility accounts. The HKMA has maintained cooperation with the Hong Kong Council of Social Service, deploying Coin Carts to collect coins on the flag days of non-governmental organisations, in an effort to support social services. Coin-counting machines on the Coin Cart. The Coin Collection Programme was launched in 2014 and was the world's first systematic coin collection programme to adopt the mobile vehicle concept. Over the years, it has received numerous local and international awards, with its innovative and environmentally friendly coin-handling methods being widely recognised. The programme operates two Coin Carts, each equipped with two high-speed coin-counting machines, to collect coins exchanged by the public. Members of the public may choose to exchange their coins for banknotes, to top up their stored value facility accounts (such as Octopus cards or e-wallets), or to donate to the Community Chest as charitable donations. In addition to collecting coins, the Coin Carts are also occasionally assigned for use in various educational activities (such as student visits).

The Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency conducted an independent verification of the climate targets ("Climate Targets") of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority ("HKMA"). The Climate Targets were established with reference to the requirements of the SBTi Corporate Manual ("SBTi Corporate Manual"). The purpose of this verification exercise was to verify whether the Climate Targets were established with reference to the SBTi Corporate Manual. This verification exercise was carried out in accordance with the International Standard on Assurance Engagements 3000 (Revised) "Assurance Engagements Other Than Audits or Reviews of Historical Financial Information" issued by the International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board. The verification procedures were specifically designed to form an opinion and conclusion so as to obtain a reasonable level of assurance. The verification process was determined in accordance with the requirements of the SBTi Corporate Manual. The HKMA is responsible for the collection and presentation of the data. Our verification work is entirely independent and impartial. Based on the results of this verification, the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency provides reasonable assurance and concludes: • The Climate Targets were established with reference to the SBTi Corporate Manual. Shum Siu-yan, Audit Manager, Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency, March 2023.  Verification Statement. The Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency conducted an independent verification of the 2022 environmental data ("2022 Data") of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority ("HKMA"). The 2022 Data includes the total energy consumption in 2022, the Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas emission intensity, the paper consumption intensity, and the intensity and recycling rate of non-hazardous waste generated, as well as the changes in this data compared with the 2015 levels. The HKMA's greenhouse gas emission data was compiled in accordance with the Greenhouse Gas Protocol ("GHG Protocol") jointly issued by the World Resources Institute ("WRI") and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development ("WBCSD"). The scope of the verification covers the relevant data for the period from 1 January 2022 to 31 December 2022, as well as the relevant data used for annual performance comparison for the period from 1 January 2015 to 31 December 2015. The scope of the verification covers a total of 6 office and warehouse assets, with 4 offices located at 1) Two International Finance Centre Office, 2) Hopewell Centre, 3) One Pacific Place, and 4) Kowloon Commerce Centre, and 2 warehouses located at 5) Lok Sing Industrial Centre and 6) Sunley Centre, situated in Kwai Chung and Tsuen Wan respectively. The purpose of the verification was to provide reasonable assurance on the accuracy and reliability of the 2022 Data and to confirm the adequacy of the HKMA's data collection mechanism. Within the scope of the verification, the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency reviewed representative data and supporting evidence selected from the 6 assets. This verification exercise was carried out in accordance with the International Standard on Assurance Engagements 3000 (Revised) "Assurance Engagements Other Than Audits or Reviews of Historical Financial Information" issued by the International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board. The verification procedures were specifically designed to form an opinion and conclusion so as to obtain a reasonable level of assurance. The verification process was determined in accordance with the requirements of the GHG Protocol. The verification process tested the completeness and accuracy of the data by tracing the selected sample data back to its source, and also reviewed the basic procedures for data collection, aggregation, estimation, calculation, and internal checking, and carried out reliability testing. The verification process also included verifying the internal data collection and management mechanisms, conducting interviews with the representatives responsible for preparing the 2022 Data, and selecting representative data and information for examination. The relevant raw data and supporting evidence were also reviewed in detail during the verification process. The HKMA is responsible for the collection and presentation of the data. Our verification work is entirely independent and impartial. The verification team of the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency was not involved in the preparation process of the 2022 Data. Based on the results of this verification, the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency provides reasonable assurance on the 2022 Data and concludes: • The 2022 Data is substantially accurate and reliable; • The HKMA's overall data collection mechanism is adequate. Shum Siu-yan, Audit Manager, Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency, March 2023.

Scaling up and accelerating climate action has become the most pressing issue of our time. We are already almost halfway through the critical decade for the climate crisis. We need to cut global carbon emissions by more than 40% during this decade in order to have any hope of keeping global warming within 1.5 degrees Celsius. Yet greenhouse gas emissions keep hitting new highs. The latest climate science indicates that the window to limit the global temperature rise to within 1.5 degrees Celsius will soon close. Everyone can already clearly feel the impact of the 1.1 degree Celsius temperature increase—record-breaking heatwaves and droughts, severe flooding, storms and other extreme weather events are occurring more frequently across the globe, and each one is more severe than the last. Hong Kong is no exception. Last September, after being battered by a violent super typhoon, we were immediately hit by a once-in-a-century rainstorm. Despite having good infrastructure and being able to respond swiftly to disasters, the impact was still extremely serious—widespread flooding, disrupted traffic, and damage to roads in many places. All of this serves as a clear reminder that decisive and proactive climate action is truly a matter of the utmost urgency. Asia faces particularly significant challenges on the path to a low-carbon transition, especially in balancing economic development with sustainability. We need credible transition strategies that appropriately balance climate action with economic growth and social inclusion. This is by no means an easy task. Owing to the region's rapid economic development, coupled with fast population growth, its carbon emissions account for more than half of the global total. At the same time, the Asia Pacific region is highly densely populated and, given its geographical location, is also vulnerable to rising sea levels and extreme weather. As the economies within the region are at different stages of development, the low-carbon transition, while creating new opportunities for some economies, poses an enormous challenge for others in raising the funding needed for the transition. The market estimates that the Asia Pacific region will require more than US$3 trillion in low-carbon transition investment each year over the next 30 years. As an international financial centres, Hong Kong has both the capacity and the responsibility to harness the power of finance to support the low-carbon transition across Asia. As the regulator of the banking sector, a market facilitator and a responsible investor, the HKMA has consistently devoted significant effort to the sustainable development agenda. Readers will learn from the various chapters of this report about the specific measures and work the HKMA introduced over the past year. In addition, to strengthen the HKMA's internal governance structure and to more effectively coordinate sustainable development work across different functional areas, we established the Green and Sustainable Steering Committee last year. For detailed information on this steering committee, please refer to the newly added "Governance for Sustainability" chapter. Hong Kong's banks play an important role in supporting Asia's transition to net-zero emissions. In addition to fulfilling our traditional functions as a banking sector regulator—ensuring in our day-to-day supervisory work that banks properly manage climate risk—we also play a facilitator role, supporting the banking sector in providing financing for the low-carbon transition. One example is the development of a green classification framework to help banks and other financial institutions identify environmentally sustainable activities, thereby aligning their business decisions with global climate goals. We launched a prototype of the green classification framework for consultation in May, and are now refining the framework based on the feedback received during the consultation period. In addition, as there is growing demand across all sectors for higher-quality and globally more comparable sustainability disclosure information, the HKMA is working with other regulators to develop a clear roadmap for Hong Kong to adopt the disclosure standards launched by the International Sustainability Standards Board in June—a comprehensive global common baseline for sustainability reporting. The HKMA's role as a facilitator is not limited to developing frameworks and rules; we are also committed to addressing the pain points faced by the industry. At present, many banks are constrained by data limitations, making it difficult to conduct physical risk assessments. In view of this, the HKMA will shortly launch a cloud-based physical risk assessment platform, whereby banks need only enter a property address to assess the impact of physical hazards on residential and commercial buildings in Hong Kong under different climate scenarios, thereby helping banks manage the related climate risk. As a major international financial centres in Asia and a sustainable finance hub, Hong Kong has always served as a bridge, channelling international investment into sustainable development projects in Asia and supporting the region's low-carbon transition. In recent years, the total volume of international green and sustainable bonds arranged for issuance in Hong Kong has accounted for more than one-third of the Asian market, clearly leading other regions. It is particularly worth mentioning that in 2023, the Shenzhen Municipal Government and the Hainan Provincial Government issued green and sustainable bonds in Hong Kong for the third and second consecutive years respectively, once again affirming Hong Kong's important role as a green gateway connecting the Mainland with the rest of the world.
